Usage notes for RAG vector indexing  
-  The hierarchical numbering makes it easy to locate related topics by prefix match (e.g., all “2.6.*” entries concern kinematic couplings).

-  The header block provides metadata (product, version, copyright, publisher) for context and provenance.

The table is a two‐part, hierarchical contents‐listing for the SOFiMSHC Geometric Modelling manual. It catalogues all record types (input keywords) available in sections 4 and 5, pairing each code with a short description and its page reference.

1. Overall Structure  
   • Two main blocks, each headed by a bold title and starting page:  
     – “Definition of geometric elements” (section 4, page 4-1)  
     – “Definition of structural elements” (section 5, page 5-1)  
   • Within each block, entries are numbered sequentially (4.1…4.14; 5.1…5.14).  
   • Nested subsections use an extra decimal level (e.g. 5.6.1–5.6.5; 5.10.1–5.10.4).

2. Columns and Fields  
   • First column: section/subsection number.  
   • Second column: record name (keyword) plus a brief title.  
   • Third column: starting page in the manual (format “4-1”, “5-21”, etc.).  
   • Dotted leaders visually guide the eye from the record title to its page number.

3. Section 4 – Geometric Elements  
   • 4.1 Input records (generic header) – p 4-1  
   • 4.2 GAX – Geometric curve or axis – p 4-2  
   • 4.3 GAXA – Axis plan view – p 4-4  
   • 4.4 GAXH – Axis heights – p 4-7  
   • 4.5 GAXB – Straights and circular arcs in 3D – p 4-8  
   • 4.6 GAXC – 3D curve point data – p 4-10  
   • 4.7 GAXN – Knot value of a NURBS-curve – p 4-12  
   • 4.8 GAXP – Axis placements – p 4-13  
   • 4.9 GAXS – Secondary axis – p 4-16  
   • 4.10 GAXV – Variables along axis – p 4-17  
   • 4.11 GAR – Geometric surface – p 4-19  
   • 4.12 GARA – Plane, rotational and sweep surfaces – p 4-20  
   • 4.13 GARC – Coons surface – p 4-22  
   • 4.14 GARS – Area by points – p 4-23  

   This section defines pure‐geometry primitives—axes, curves, surfaces and point‐based areas—each with a distinct “GAX…” or “GAR…” keyword.

4. Section 5 – Structural Elements  
   • 5.1 Input Records – p 5-1  
   • 5.2 SPT – Structural point – p 5-3  
   • 5.3 SPTP – Structural point properties – p 5-6  
   • 5.4 SPTS – Spring element at point – p 5-8  
   • 5.5 SPTH – Halfspace pile at point – p 5-11  
   • 5.6 SLN – Structural line – p 5-12  
       – 5.6.1 Local coordinate system – p 5-13  
       – 5.6.2 Support and coupling conditions – p 5-14  
       – 5.6.3 Element generation – p 5-14  
       – 5.6.4 Hinge conditions – p 5-15  
       – 5.6.5 Intersection properties – p 5-15  
   • 5.7 SLNB – Straights and circular arcs – p 5-17  
   • 5.8 SLNP – 3D curve point data – p 5-18  
   • 5.9 SLNN – Knot value of a NURBS-curve – p 5-19  
   • 5.10 SLNS – Supports and kinematic couplings on a SLN – p 5-20  
       – 5.10.1 Supports and coupling conditions – p 5-21  
       – 5.10.2 Elastic beddings and spring elements – p 5-21  
       – 5.10.3 Orientation of the elements – p 5-22  
       – 5.10.4 Interface-elements – p 5-23  
   • 5.11 SLSC – Explicit sections on structural line – p 5-24  
   • 5.12 SAR – Structural area – p 5-25  
   • 5.13 SARB – Structural area boundaries and constraints – p 5-30  
   • 5.14 SARR – Rotational and sweep surfaces – p 5-32  

   Section 5 extends the geometric primitives into load-bearing and connectivity definitions: points (SPT…), lines (SLN…), coupling (SLNS…), and 2D areas (SAR…), complete with subrecords for local axes, supports, springs, hinges, and boundary conditions.

5. Key Observations for RAG Vector Store  
   • Each record name (e.g. “GAXP”) serves as a unique identifier/key.  
   • Descriptions are standardized short phrases ideal for metadata.  
   • Page numbers anchor the record to its detailed documentation.  
   • hierarchical numbering allows grouping and faceted retrieval (e.g. all “5.6.x” subsections).  

This detailed breakdown captures the table’s taxonomy—geometric vs. structural records, their subcategories and page references—providing clear, metadata‐rich entries for indexing in a RAG vector store.

 SOFiMSHC is a tool for creating and processing geometric models and finite element struc- tures. SOFiMSHC can be used as stand-alone program within Teddy and is integrated as geometry processing module in the SOFiSTiK programs SOFiPLUS, Extensions for Revit and Rhinoceros Interface.
 Basis and starting point of SOFiMSHC is an abstract structural model similar to a CAD model which includes all relevant geometric and structural information necessary for describing a calculation model. After this model is read from database or entered by the user via CADINP, SOFiMSHC analyzes and processes it and creates as result a finite element mesh consisting of beam, area and/or volume elements. In addition to classical building structures, SOFiMSHC also provides a rich set of input facilities for the definition of alignment axes and bridge systems.
 SOFiMSHC basically differentiates between geometric entities carrying geometry related data and structural elements containing all further information needed for definining a calculation model. As for the geometric entities following types are supported:
 • straight lines
 circles and circular arcs in space
 alignment axes for road design defined separately in plan view and elevation
 • polygonal lines
 cubically interpolating splines
 • Hermite interpolation with defined tangents
 • arbitrary NURBS curves (Non Uniform Rational B-Splines)
 • flat surfaces
 surfaces of revolution
 •
 sweep surfaces
 bicubically interpolating surfaces
 arbitrary NURBS surfaces
 The basic geometric elements are usually defined independently from the overall structural model and should be used in as comprehensive units as possible. A bridge with multiple spans, for example, can be defined with one single axis along its whole length. The individual spans and all additional superstructures, however, are modeled with structural elements which inherit their geometry from the underlying axis definition. Once the geometry is changed the structural system will be automatically readjusted.
 The static system itself with all mutual topological relationships comprises the following set of basic structural elements:
 Structural Points are defined at a specific position in space and may have Column Heads, Punching periphery and haunches assigned as structural properties.

Once the geometry is changed the structural system will be automatically readjusted.. The static system itself with all mutual topological relationships comprises the following set of basic structural elements:. Structural Points are defined at a specific position in space and may have Column Heads, Punching periphery and haunches assigned as structural properties..
 Structural Lines connect two structural points and may have a geometric curve as- signed. Structural data includes supports and section definitions, for example.
 Structural Regions are defined by a closed set of inner and outer boundary curves and may also have a geometric surface description assigned. Structural properties contain thickness, element formulation etc.
 Structural Volumes are defined by a set of enclosing structural regions and can be meshed either unstructured with tetrahedral elements or structured by extrusion or rotation with hexahedral elements.
 A number of possibilities are provided within the SOFiSTiK program environment, to access and define the input of SOFiMSHC:
 • Definition using CADINP-ASCII-Files (Teddy + SOFiMSHC)
 Input of structural systems using SOFiPLUS (AutoCAD)
 • Transfer of models from Autodesk Revit Structural (SOFiSTiK Extensions for Revit)
 • Modeling in McNeel Rhinoceros (SOFiSTiK Rhinoceros Interface)
 • Interface to the CDBASE for third party developers and for the import of building infor- mation models (e.g. IFC).
 SOFiMSHC is both used as stand-alone batch program and as backend module in the above mentioned CAD-programs. It contains interfaces to mesh-generators from the University of Munich (DOMESH) and the University of Linz (NETGEN) and to mesh-partitioning software (METIS).

 Basically, the numbers of structural elements should not be selected with a unreasonably high value. The program needs to allocate unnecessary amounts of memory, which might increase the overall running time of the program.
 Attention should be paid to the fact that only numbers below 1 Mio can be entered and ac- cessed within CADINP. This means that even though element numbers above 1 Mio can be created in SOFiMSHC, these elements cannot be accessed from CADINP in order to set ad- ditional properties or apply loads etc. Thus, the group divisor setting the base number of the elements created within a group should be set to a reasonably small value.

The image is a black-and-white line drawing titled “Figure 2.1: Coordinate system.” At its center is the origin, from which three straight lines emerge in different directions to represent the global X-, Y-, and Z-axes of a right-handed Cartesian system. All lines are rendered with uniform stroke width and terminate in simple triangular arrowheads indicating positive directions.

1. Z-axis  
   • Depicted as a vertical line descending straight down from the origin.  
   • The arrowhead at its lower end points straight downward.  
   • Immediately adjacent to the arrowhead is the letter “Z,” aligned horizontally so it reads naturally when viewed upright.

2. Y-axis  
   • Drawn as a slanted line extending upward and to the right at roughly a 45-degree inclination from the origin.  
   • Its arrowhead points toward the upper right of the page.  
   • The letter “Y” is positioned just beyond the arrowhead, centered and legible without rotation.

3. X-axis  
   • Shown as a slanted line extending roughly horizontally to the right but slightly downward—its angle falls between the horizontal and the negative vertical.  
   • The arrowhead points toward the lower right quadrant.  
   • The label “X” appears just past the arrowhead, with no tilt, so that the character is upright.

In the lower right quadrant of the drawing is a small inset illustrating a rotation angle, phi (φ). This miniature sketch includes a short straight line (representing an axis direction) with a small arrowhead at its right end, and a curved arrow swooping around that line in a counter-clockwise sense. The curved arrow terminates near the same axis line, and the Greek letter “Phi” (φ) is placed adjacent to it, marking the rotation in the mathematically positive sense.

Visually, the three principal axes form the standard right-hand rule configuration: if one places the right hand so that the X-axis points toward the fingers and the Y-axis toward the thumb, the Z-axis aligns with the palm’s downward direction (matching the global gravity direction in SOFiMSHC). The slanted projection of the X- and Y-axes onto the plane of the paper yields an apparent two-dimensional handedness that would be judged as right- or left-handed depending on the chosen vertical orientation, but in this figure the convention clearly follows the counter-clockwise ordering “X → Y → Z.”

The overall style is schematic and minimalist, suitable for inclusion in technical documentation describing how global and local coordinate systems are defined in structural-analysis software. All text labels use a sans-serif font, and the arrowheads are isosceles triangles consistent across all axes. The figure conveys both the spatial arrangement of the axes and the sign convention for rotations (phi) in a concise graphic.

Global as well as local coordinate systems are described in SOFiMSHC as cartesian right- handed system X-Y-Z. Rotations are applied in a mathematical positive sense. Within record SYST a global gravity direction can be specified at parameter GDIR. This global gravity or ’downward’ direction affects the default orientation of loads, supports and other geometric at- tributes of structural items within the model if not specified differently at the respective location.
 If the observer is looking from the birds eye view he will believe to see a right or left handed 2D coordinate system depending on the orientation of the vertical axis . We use the designation of the ”first” and the ”second” horizontal axis in the counter clock wise orientation.
 Each geometric or structural object in SOFiMSHC possesses a local orientation or a local coordinate system, which affects the direction of loads, cross-sections or support conditions:
 • Points, for example, have a local coordinate system which defines primarily the local di- rection of supports and kinematic couplings. If no coordinate system is given explicitly the local z-direction defaults to the globally defined gravity direction or, if the point lies within a region or on a structural line, to the local coordinate system defined there.
 • For structural lines, up to three different local coordinate systems can be identified. A first coordinate system is related to the underlying geometric curve and is primarily used to de- fine the orientation of circular arcs or alignment axes. On the structural line, an independant coordinate system can be defined which sets the orientation of cross-sections and beam elements. A third coordinate system may be specified in order to set the local direction of supports, springs or kinematic couplings connected to a line. If one of the three mentioned directions is not explicitly set by the user, it defaults to the previously defined system. If no coordinate system is defined at all, the global gravity direction is used. The local coordinate system of a structural line is normally specified by the user by setting the direction of the local z-axis. As the local x-axis always points into the direction of the curve tangent, the local y-axis is defined automatically.

If no coordinate system is defined at all, the global gravity direction is used. The local coordinate system of a structural line is normally specified by the user by setting the direction of the local z-axis. As the local x-axis always points into the direction of the curve tangent, the local y-axis is defined automatically..
 • Geometric surfaces and structural regions have a local coordinate system assigned which normally varies within the surface for curved shapes. The z-axis of the coordinate system always remains perpendicular on the surface. The coordinate system of a structural region defines, for example, the clock-order of outer boundary edges and the local orientation of the quadrilateral finite elements created on the surface.
 • For volumes there might be a direction of orthotopic material properties, but there is no local coordinate system. However all surfaces describing the volume will have a unique interior
 and exterior side. Thus a separating surface between two volumes will have a different orientation for the two cases.

Curves in SOFiMSHC are defined as parameter curves in three dimensional space. Parameter curves are basically defined by a local parameter s which runs along the curve from its start to its endpoint. A ’curve function’ c(s) maps this local parameter s to global xyz-coordinates and therefore describes the curve in space when s is changed from smin to smax:
 x(s) S>C(s)=]y(s)} S=[Smin: Smax], Z(s)
 (2.1)
 Apart from its shape other parameters might also be specified along a given curve as a func- tion of s, like for example the orientation, the size or the shape of varying cross-sections. SOFiMSHC also allows to define so-called secondary lines, which are connected to a basis curve and whose distance is defined as a function of s.

The provided illustration (Figure 2.2: Axis) presents two depictions of a single alignment axis—its plan (ground) view and its longitudinal (elevation) profile—over a common horizontal station range from 0 m to approximately 32 m. The image is laid out on a white background, with black framing lines at top and right edges. Along the bottom edge runs the horizontal “station” axis, marked at 0, 15, 20, 25, and 30 m. Below that axis the labels “Y,” “Z,” and “X” appear in light gray, suggesting coordinate directions, though only the X-axis scale is explicitly graduated.

1. Ground-plan view (lower half of the graphic)  
   - Two overlaid curves track the same horizontal alignment:  
     • A dashed black line that begins at x = 0 m as a straight, then gently transitions into a shallow curve.  
     • A solid red line that closely parallels the dashed line but lies marginally above it through the transition and arc.  
   - At the leftmost station (x = 0 m), a red arrow symbol indicates the start-tangent direction on plan. The arrowhead sits at the termination of a short vertical red stroke, implying the initial bearing.  
   - At the right end (around x ≈ 30 m), a matching red arrow and short stroke denote the end-tangent direction. This arrow is tilted upward and rightward, showing how the track bearing has changed after the arc and transition.  
   - The two curves meet approximately at x = 0 m and again converge near x ≈ 30 m, diverging slightly between stations 15 m and 25 m—consistent with a reversal clothoid merging a circular-arc segment (radius −100 m to +50 m).

2. Elevation-view overlay (upper half of the graphic)  
   - A single overlaid red curve traces the profile of the same alignment in the vertical plane. It starts at zero elevation (flat tangent), then arcs upward with a smooth, parabolic curvature (easement) before reaching the final tangent slope indicated by the upper red arrow.  
   - The elevation curve is continuous and free of abrupt kinks, reflecting the use of a 100 m radius parabola to transition between grade tangents.

3. Coordinate and Annotation Details  
   - The horizontal axis is common to both views and labeled with “X” beneath the station graduations; no explicit Y or Z graduations are drawn in plan or elevation, but the gray “Y” and “Z” hint at axis orientations.  
   - Both red arrows employ identical glyph designs—vertical strokes with arrowheads—to represent start and end tangent directions in their respective views.  
   - The dashed black plan curve serves as a reference “before transition” or an alternate alignment, with the solid red showing the final design alignment incorporating clothoid easements.  
   - The figure title “Figure 2.2: Axis” appears in bold beneath the graphic.

Overall, the illustration conveys how SOFiMSHC alignment definitions use a combination of straight segments, circular arcs, and transition curves (clothoids in plan, parabolic easements in elevation) to achieve gradual curvature changes. The ground-plan view highlights a reversing clothoid (start radius RA = –100 m to end radius RE = +50 m), while the elevation profile demonstrates a smooth vertical curve with a 100 m parabolic radius. This dual-view presentation underscores the independent yet complementary nature of horizontal and vertical alignment design.

The image consists of two coordinated charts, labeled “Figure 2.2: Plan view” (top) and “Figure 2.3: Elevation view” (bottom), that together illustrate how SOFiMSHC alignment axes are defined in plan and in elevation for a simple compound curve with transition elements.

1. Figure 2.2 – Plan View  
• Axes and Grid  
  – Horizontal axis is labeled X; vertical axis is labeled Y.  
  – Tick marks at chainage 0, 5 m, 10 m, 15 m, 20 m and 25 m appear along the X-axis.  
• Curves and Symbols  
  – A dashed black line traces the “reference” alignment: it begins as a circular arc segment of constant negative curvature (left-turn), then passes through a reversing clothoid, and finally becomes a circular arc of positive curvature (right-turn).  
  – Overlaid in solid red is the actual computed centreline made up of straight-to-arc and arc-to-straight transitions: the red follows the same geometry but emphasizes the transition region.  
  – The transition (clothoid) is centered roughly between chainages 10 m and 15 m on the X-axis. At its start the radius is RA = –100 m (negative sign denoting curvature direction) and it continuously “eases” into a +50 m radius circular arc.  
  – No grid lines are drawn; only the axes and tick labels define the lateral extent.

2. Figure 2.3 – Elevation View  
• Axes and Grid  
  – Horizontal axis again is chainage X from 0 to 25 m by 5 m increments.  
  – Vertical axis is labeled Z (height).  
• Curves and Symbols  
  – A dashed black line represents the basic parabolic vertical curve of radius 100 m, used to round off the grade.  
  – A solid red line overlays the actual elevation alignment: it starts at a slight uphill grade, transitions smoothly (parabolically) up to a small crest just beyond chainage 20 m, then begins a gentle descent.  
  – At approximately chainage 10 m an upright red arrow marks the midpoint of the vertical transition, indicating the point of maximum grade change or vertical deflection.  
  – Labels along the Z‐axis are sparse but the vertical scale matches the modest elevation change (on the order of decimeters to a few meters).

Overall Description  
• Both sub-figures share the same chainage (“stationing”) along X from 0 to 25 m.  
• The plan view demonstrates how a reversing clothoid provides a smooth change of curvature from –100 m radius to +50 m radius in the horizontal alignment.  
• The elevation view shows an independent vertical alignment defined by a parabolic easement of 100 m radius, yielding a continuous, comfortable grade transition.  
• Color and line style distinguish the theoretical reference (dashed black) from the implemented alignment geometry (solid red), making the roles of straights, arcs and transition curves visually explicit.

As a special type of curve SOFiMSHC allows to define alignment axes as primarily used in road and railway design. These curves typically consist of a sequence of straights and circular arcs with transition elements in between. In order to avoid sudden changes in curvature tran- sition curves (or easement curves) are placed between sections with different radii providing a gradual change of curvature from one section to another. Depending on the characteristics of the curvature gradient different types of transition elements can be identified:
 • Clothoid: Curvature varies linearly with distance s along the track
 1
 s
 s
 The definition of alignment axes in SOFiMSHC is carried out separately in plan view and el- evation. In plan view, sections consisting of straights, circular arcs and transition curves are combined into a sequence defining a two-dimensional curve in x,y-coordinates. The elevation of the curve can be defined independently from the plan view by setting height values and elevation radii. Curvatures in the elevation are applied as parabolas.
 The following two pictures show an alignment axis in ground view and elevation. The axis consists in the ground view of a circular arc segment and a reversing clothoid with a start radius of RA = -100m and an end radius RE = +50m. In the elevation view the curve is rounded off parabolically with a radius of 100m.

For defining freeform curves SOFiMSHC provides an implementaton of NURBS based on the openNURBS library. NURBS (Non-Uniform Rational B-Splines) comprise a special class of curves widely used in computer aided design or computer graphics for modelling curves and surfaces of arbitrary shapes. Mathematically, they consist of piecewise rational polynomials of a given order which are connected together under consideration of certain continuity conditions (e.g. tangentially continuous, curvature continuous). Due to their construction using rational polynomials, NURBS are also capable of representing circles, ellipses or hyperbolas mathe- matically exact. A definition of NURBS-curves basically involves the following set of properties and elements:
 The degree decribes the highest polynomial exponent of the NURBS basis functions. De- gree 1 is called linear, degree 2 quadratic, 3 cubic etc. A cubic degree is generally sufficient, but curves with degrees up to 32 may be defined and used.
 Control points are the basic construction points of a NURBS curve or surface. With ex- ception of the first and the last point they are not necessarily located directly on the curve but will stay close to it. Since NURBS curves are constructed using piecewise polyno- mials, the position of a single control point only changes the shape of its adjacent basis polynoms. This so-called ’local property’ of Nurbs - in contrast to pure polynomial curves - allows to modify a curve locally without affecting the whole shape of the curve. In addi- tion to its xyz-coordinates a control points may also have a weight assigned. By changing the control-point weights to values < > 1.0 the basis functions convert to rational polynoms which offers the possibility to model also circular arcs, hyperbolas or ellipses with NURBS.
 Basically, a single knot-value defines the location on a curve where two Nurbs basis func- tions are connected. For a given NURBS curve with N control points they are usually stored internally as monotone list of size (degree+N-1). The knot-vector may be defined by the user in order to set the local curve parametrisation explicitly. In general cases however there is no need to define the knots by the user as SOFiMSHC creates an appropriate distribution automatically. Knots can also be defined repeatedly at the same location. This knot multiplicity changes the default transition condition at the interface between two basis functions such that also kinks and even jumps could be modeled within one single curve.

SOFiMSHC supports different types of geometric surfaces which can be referenced in order to describe the shape of a structural region which is to be meshed. If no geometry is defined explicitly, SOFiMSHC tries to create the shape of a surface from its boundary description. This works, of course, for all plane surfaces and normally also for curved shapes with a less complex boundary description (e.g. four boundary edges in a rectangular like pattern). For complex shapes however, it is more reasonable to specify the geometric shape of a region explicitly.

The general idea of these type of surfaces is that a surface is defined by moving an arbitrary curve in space. In case of a surface of revolution a curve c(v) is rotated around a straight axis.
 The parametric description of the surface s(u,v) is given by
 s(,) = M() · c()
 (2.6)
 where the matrix M(v) defines rotation around an arbitrary axis in space. The parameter v denotes the rotation angle in radians. A sweep surface is defined by moving a curve c(u) along a traction curve t(v). The general form of a sweep surface s(u,v) is given by
 s(,) = t() + M() · c()
 (2.7)
 The curve c(u) may also be rotated by M(v) within the local coordinate system of the traction curve after moving it along t. In most cases however, c(v) is only translated along t(v) without rotation. The rotation matrix M defaults to the unity-matrix then.

As previously mentioned SOFiMSHC basically distinguishes between geometric entities and structural objects. Geometric elements primarily define the shape and the position of objects in space. Structural objects are referencing the shape of the geometry elements and fur- thermore contain all relevant structural information together with necessary mutual topologi- cal relationships. The structural model within SOFiMSHC corresponds to a classical B-Rep (boundary representation) data model which can be found in a similar form in other common CAD-systems. B-rep models describe objects in space by describing the boundary of the ob- jects. Structural lines, for example, are bounded by their endpoints and structural regions are bounded by a closed sequence of structural edges. Structural regions may also have internal boundaries forming openings inside the region.

The 2D-mesh generation is based on the work by Rank et al. for unstructured mesh generation for pure quadrilateral meshes. [ 1] . The first step is to generate a triangular mesh which is then divided into a quadrilateral mesh. This is the reason why along all edges the number of sections will be even.
 However there are specific macros for supports like columns modifying the basic generated mesh in a post processing step.
 The 3D-mesh generation is either done as a structured mapped mesh generation based on the surfaces generated before, or a unstructured mesh generation for pure Tetrahedron meshes. This is adopted from a mesh generator developed at the University of Linz [ 2] . As the quality of Tetrahedron is significantly less than that of Hexahedron we have to generate a more dense element mesh. Both methods may be mixed within one system. E. Rank [1], Schöberl [2], Farin [3], and Piegl and Tiller [4]

In SOFiMSHC, support conditions can be defined for structural points, structural lines and structural regions. The support conditions can be specified in global directions as well as in directions aligned to the local coordinate system of the respective structural entity.
 Support conditions are defined by a set of literals,
 PX Clamped support of displacements in X-direction
 PY Clamped support of displacements in Y-direction
 PZ Clamped support of displacements in Z-direction
 MX Clamped support of rotations about the X-axis
 MY Clamped support of rotations about the Y-axis
 MZ Clamped support of rotations about the Z-axis
 MB Clamped support of warping
 which can also be combined. As an example, the following CADINP statement
 SPT 1 X 0 0 0 FIX PXPY
 defines a structural point at coordinate (0,0,0) whose displacement in the global XY-plane are suppressed, i.e. only displacements in Z-direction are allowed. By prepending the literal ’L’ (e.g. ’LPXPY’) the support conditions will be aligned according to the local coordinate system of the structural entity, e.g.:
 SPT 1 X 0 0 0 NX 0 1 1 FIX LPZ
 Additionally, the following literals, which combine multiple displacement directions, can also be used for defining supports:
 XP = PY + PZ
 YP = PX + PZ
 ZP = PX + PY
 PP = PX + PY + PZ
 XM = MY + MZ
 YM = MX + MZ
 ZM = MX + MY
 MM = MX + MY + MZ + MB
 F = PP + MM

While support conditions basically suppress certain degrees of freedom, coupling conditions define relationships between degrees of freedom of different nodes. As an example,
 SPT 5 X 0 0 0 FIX PXPY->1
 creates a structural point, whose displacements u and uy are coupled to the displacements of structural point no. 1, called the reference point. In the simplest case, the displacements of the base point will be set equal to the displacements of the reference point. However, also more complex relationships are possible, which are usually motivated by mechanical constraints and which will be described further down.
 Couplings can be either defined as previously shown by adding a reference ’-> no’ to the support literal or by using special input records (e.g. SPTP, SLNS), which provide additional options for defining group membership of the constraint or a particular direction, e.g.:
 SPT 5 X 0 0 0
 SPTP KP REF 1 GRP 4
 Depending on the type of the coupling condition, certain degrees of freedom of the coupled node are defined as a function of degrees of freedom R of the reference or ’master’ node. For standard couplings, the following relationships apply:

A point can be coupled to different reference nodes, for example when the couplings are assigned to different groups or different acting directions, as well as multiple points can be coupled to a single master node. The mutual dependencies will be analyzed and resolved when the equation system is set up in the calculation kernels.

With exeption of a rigid coupling of type ’F’, coupling a node ’A’ to node ’B’ is mechanically not equivalent to a coupling of node ’B’ to ’A’. (See, e.g. equations 2.8, 2.9, 2.10)

The input in SOFiMSHC is generally carried out in CADINP language. More information on this can be found in the general SOFiSTiK manual ’FEA / STRUCTURAL Installation and Basics’.

SOFiSTiK programs offer the possibility to carry out all input and output of data in engineering units. A number of unit sets are provided for this purpose, which are preset according to the design code used in the given project. This default can additionally be changed for each program run separately using the keyword PAGE. More information about unit sets can be found in the general SOFiSTiK manual, section ’Units’.
 The description of the input values in this manual will always contain the unit, in which a given record is expected to be given. It shows also, if the input record follows a predefined unit set.
 Three categories of units are distinguished:
 mm Fixed unit. Input is always required in the specified unit.
 [mm] Explicit unit. Input defaults to the specified unit. Alternatively, an explicit as- signment of a related unit is possible (eg. 2.5[m] ).
 [mm]1011 Implicit unit. Implicit units are categorised semantically and denoted by a cor- responding identity number (shown in green). Valid categories referring to the unit ”length” are, for example, geodetic elevation, section length and thickness. The default unit for each category is defined by the currently active (design code specific) unit set. This input default can be overridden as described above. The specified unit in square brackets corresponds to the default for unit set 5 (Eu- rocodes, NORM UNIT 5).

The table lists a series of “records” used in SOFiSTiK input decks.  Each record name appears in the left-hand column; the right-hand column enumerates its allowed “items” (parameters), grouped by their internal type codes (T-numbers).  In a RAG/vector-store context this description can be used as metadata for retrieval, prompt-construction or schema validation.  

1. Overall Structure  
   • Records are identified by a four-letter keyword (e.g. SYST, GRP, COOR)  
   • Items within each record are specified by a name (TYPE, FIX, XREF, etc.) and may carry an optional “T-code” (T11, T22, T31, etc.) that designates their column position or data type in the FORTRAN-style input line.  
   • Some items are flagged OPT (optional).  Those without OPT are mandatory (unless marked otherwise in the detailed manual).  
   • HEAD, END and PAGE exist but are not detailed here (see “Basics” manual).  

2. Record: SYST  
   Purpose: Defines the overall system or project configuration.  
   Items:  
     ­ TYPE (T11) – system type identifier  
     ­ GDIV (T12) – global division code  
     ­ GDIR (T13) – global directory index  
     ­ FIX (T21) – fixation or constraint flag  
     ­ XREF (T22) – X-axis reference  
     ­ YREF (T23) – Y-axis reference  
     ­ ZREF (T31) – Z-axis reference  
     ­ T32, T33 – additional code slots for future expansion  

3. Record: GRP  
   Purpose: Defines a group of elements or nodes.  
   Items:  
     ­ NO – group number (integer key)  
     ­ REF – reference to existing group or geometry  
     ­ BASE – base coordinate or geometry setup  
     ­ TITL – text title of the group  

4. Record: CTRL  
   Purpose: Sets control parameters for a module or process.  
   Items:  
     ­ OPT – optional switch flag  
     ­ VAL – main control value  
     ­ V2, V3, V4 – supplementary control values  

5. Records: IMPO, EXPO, ECHO  
   Purpose: Input/output control for import/export and echoing.  
   • IMPO  
     ­ OPT – optional activation flag  
     ­ FROM – source filename or database  
     ­ PASS – pass-through control  
   • EXPO  
     ­ OPT – optional activation flag  
     ­ VAL – export format or code  
     ­ TO – target filename or medium  
     ­ PASS – pass-through control  
   • ECHO  
     ­ OPT – optional activation flag  
     ­ VAL – level of echo or verbosity  

6. Record: COOR  
   Purpose: Defines coordinate system parameters.  
   Items:  
     ­ TYPE (T11) – coordinate system type (e.g. Cartesian, cylindrical)  
     ­ ID (T12) – coordinate system identifier  
     ­ IDP (T13) – parent system ID (for nested systems)  
     ­ S (T21) – scale factor or sign convention  
     ­ X (T22), Y (T23), Z – zero-point offsets or axis identifiers  

7. Record: XSUB  
   Purpose: Sub-record for defining cross-section or substructure.  
   Items:  
     ­ TYP – cross-section type code  
     ­ FIXA, FIXL, FIXM – fixation parameters for A, L, M directions  
     ­ CD – code descriptor for the substructure  

Usage Notes for RAG Vector Store Integration  
• Each record definition can be stored as a document embedding, keyed by the record name.  
• The item lists, T-codes and OPT flags form structured metadata that supports schema lookup and auto-completion.  
• HEAD, END and PAGE are global file delimiters; see “Basics” for their field definitions.  
• When retrieving or generating input lines, use the T-codes to place each item into the correct column (e.g. T11→column 11–20, T22→column 21–30).
Records HEAD, END and PAGE are described in the general manual SOFiSTiK: ’Basics’.

Below is a structured, detailed description of the input-table fields TYPE, GDIV and GDIR.  This write-up highlights their purpose, valid values, interactions and defaults, and points to related records (e.g. GRP, COOR) where appropriate.

1. General Structure of the Table  
   • Item: the keyword used in the input file (TYPE, GDIV, GDIR).  
   • Description: a narrative of what the keyword controls.  
   • Unit: the expected data type (LIT = literal text, “–” = no unit or integer).  
   • Default: the value assumed if none is specified.

2. TYPE  (Unit = LIT; Default = “!”)  
   Purpose  
     • Defines the overall system type and dimensionality.  Also used in combination with GDIR to fix the orientation of the global axes.  
     • If you declare TYPE other than REST, any previously defined system is deleted and re-initialized.  TYPE REST preserves the existing system definition (modifications are possible; however many results will be cleared unless overridden by CTRL REST).  
   Valid Literals  
     • 3D    → Full spatial (three-dimensional) structural analysis  
     • 2D    → Plane frame or panel analysis (bending + axial)  
     • 2DSS  → Plane stress (membrane) formulation  
     • 2DSN  → Plane strain formulation  
     • 2DAX  → Axisymmetric system (rotational symmetry about X; only POSX/NEGX allowed in GDIR)  
     • 2DSL  → Plane girder or plate bending (out-of-plane bending, shear)  
     • 2DPS  → Prestressed plate system  
     • SECT  → Sectional system for FE-based cross-section analysis (three variants exist, see “Remarks” below)  
     • REST  → Keep current TYPE, do not delete system info  
     • INIT  → Delete system and all results, but keep basic SYSTEM information in memory  
   Remarks  
     • The legacy SPAC codes (e.g. SPAC, FRAM, AXIA etc.) remain valid but have been superseded by the TYPE+GDIR approach.  
     • Choosing a planar TYPE automatically suppresses half of the global unknowns (in-plane or out-of-plane, depending on 2D subtype).  
     • Beam elements with principal axes not aligned to the global axes require a full 3D (TYPE = 3D) definition.  

3. GDIV  (Unit = – ; Default = 0)  
   Purpose  
     • Sets the group divisor, i.e. the divisor used to split element numbers into group identifiers and local element indices.  
     • If GDIV = 0, all group-based selection and identification mechanisms are deactivated.  
   Usage  
     • Often used in conjunction with the GRP record to define how elements are bucketed into groups for loads, supports, results extraction, etc.  
     • Changing GDIV after elements have been defined may renumber or reassign group memberships.  

4. GDIR  (Unit = LIT; Default = “*”)  
   Purpose  
     • Defines the global gravity direction.  This not only sets the direction of the gravitational load but also fixes the orientation of the two horizontal axes.  The third (vertical) axis aligns with the gravity vector.  
   Valid Literals  
     • POSX or NEGX  
     • POSY or NEGY  
     • POSZ or NEGZ  
   Implications  
     • For 3D systems, the first and second horizontal axes are assigned by cyclic permutation:  
       – GDIR = POSZ/NEGZ → X is 1st horizontal, Y is 2nd horizontal  
       – GDIR = POSX/NEGX → Y is 1st horizontal, Z is 2nd horizontal  
       – GDIR = POSY/NEGY → Z is 1st horizontal, X is 2nd horizontal  
     • For axisymmetric (2DAX) TYPE, only POSX/NEGX may be used (X = axis of rotation).  
     • All local coordinate systems and default orientations for loads, boundary conditions and graphics rely on GDIR.  

5. Related Records and Further Notes  
   • SPAC and COOR (older commands) are still supported; they map to TYPE/GDIR settings under the hood.  
   • FIX and NEGX/NEGY/NEGZ keywords appear elsewhere to define boundary fixes and negative-axis loads.  
   • CTRL REST can selectively preserve some results when TYPE = REST.  
   • GRP details grouping behavior; see the GRP record for how GDIV interacts with group creation and numbering.  

By specifying TYPE, GDIV and GDIR appropriately, you establish the fundamental coordinate framework, group-numbering schema, and gravity orientation that all subsequent definitions—elements, loads, supports and results—will reference.

The table is a concise summary of SOFiSTiK’s predefined 2D and axisymmetric system types (the “TYPE” options under the SYST record) together with their legacy names and default gravity‐axis settings. It is organized into two main columns representing two mutually exclusive global coordinate conventions:

1.  SCS (SOFiSTiK Coordinate System)  
    – z axis points into the view (DIN 1080 convention)  
    – the local working plane is the Y–X plane  

2.  WCS (World Coordinate System)  
    – z axis points out of (opposed to) the view (international convention)  
    – the local working plane is the X–Y plane  

Within each column the table lists six system types, their functional description, the default gravity‐direction code (GDIR), and the corresponding legacy mnemonic in parentheses.  

Detailed breakdown:

• 2D – Plane frame  
   • SCS:  
     – GDIR = NEGX/POSY (gravity points in negative global X or positive global Y)  
     – Legacy: (FRAM)  
   • WCS:  
     – GDIR = POSX/NEGY  
     – Legacy: (WFRA)  

• 2DSN – Plane strain  
   • SCS:  
     – Legacy only: (PAIN)  
     – (Gravity direction is inherited from the general SYST GDIR setting.)  
   • WCS:  
     – Legacy only: (WPAI)  

• 2DSS – Plane stress  
   • SCS:  
     – Legacy only: (PESS)  
   • WCS:  
     – Legacy only: (WPES)  

• 2DAX – Axisymmetric system (X is the rotation axis)  
   • SCS:  
     – GDIR = NEGX (axis of symmetry aligns with negative X)  
     – Legacy: (AXIA)  
   • WCS:  
     – GDIR = POSX  
     – Legacy: (WAXI)  

• 2DSL – Girder/slab system  
   • SCS:  
     – GDIR = POSZ (gravity in positive Z)  
     – Legacy: (GIRD)  
   • WCS:  
     – GDIR = NEGZ  
     – Legacy: (SLAB)  

• 2DPS – Prestressed plate system  
   • SCS:  
     – Legacy only: (PGIR)  
   • WCS:  
     – Legacy only: (PSLA)  

Key points for interpretation and RAG integration:

– “TYPE” selects one of the above; choosing REST under SYST will delete prior system definitions (unless CTRL REST exceptions apply).  
– GDIR sets the global gravity vector; it drives local axis orientation, special load definitions, boundary‐condition defaults, and graphical output orientation.  
– SCS vs. WCS only differ by the sense of the Z‐axis (into vs. out of the screen) and the naming convention of the horizontal plane (DIN 1080 Y–X vs. international X–Y).  
– For planar analyses (TYPE 2D, 2DSN, 2DSS, 2DPS) only the in‐plane unknowns are active; out‐of‐plane terms are suppressed.  
– Axisymmetric analyses (2DAX) always use GDIR = ± X (the rotation axis) and can only be solved as 3D elements.  
– Girder/slab systems (2DSL) and prestressed‐plate systems (2DPS) have specialized element formulations but rely on the same gravity‐axis conventions.  
– Legacy codes in parentheses (e.g., FRAM, WFRA) are supported for backward compatibility but become obsolete when you explicitly set TYPE and GDIR.  

By indexing these entries in a RAG vector store, you can quickly map any SYST TYPE + GDIR combination to its functional description, legacy alias, and axis‐orientation convention.

Summary of data‐types & units  
•  Literal flags (LIT) are on/off or sub‐keywords; defaults often shown as “!” or ON/OFF.  
•  Numeric tolerances and sizes carry SI units:

•  Pure integers or dimensionless factors have dash (–) in Unit.  

By grouping them this way, the program can quickly parse “CTRL/OPT=…”, “CTRL/HEAL=…”, “CTRL/MESH=…”, etc., allowing users to override any default. Each keyword in the “Item” column is case-insensitive and must be followed by its value (or literal) in the command file.

   • Serves as an anchor for subordinate control records (e.g. SPT, SLN, SAR, SVO—each of which further customizes different aspects of the solver).

   B. Subordinate Flag (“SUB”)  
     – Marks whether this keyword can appear as a subordinate item under another record.  
     – Here, “CTRL” is not subordinate (hence “−” in the SUB column).  

   C. No of Subdomains  
     – Specifies how many subdomain entries may be expected when running in parallel/partitioned mode.  
     – A dash (“−”) means this control record does not itself introduce subdomain‐specific entries.  

   D. – and – (two unnamed intermediate columns)  
     – Both are shown as “−” and “-” in your snippet. In the full table these columns typically indicate:  
        • Whether the entry is repeatable, optional/mandatory, or has special placement rules.  
        • Default values or allowed ranges.  
     – Here, the dashes imply “not applicable” or “no default” at this level.  

   E. Comments on “PART”  
     – In the comment column you see: “PART Controls mesh-partitioning.”  
     – Although not formally a separate column header in your snippet, this is how the table flags important subordinate keywords.  
     – “PART” is a sub‐keyword under CTRL that governs how the computational mesh is split across parallel tasks.  

   F. Final Comment/Description  
     – “This record is used to set global program control options. They can be classified as follows:”

3. How to Index in a RAG Vector Store

By structuring your table entry this way, you make it easy for the RAG system to answer questions like “Which record controls mesh partitioning?” (“PART under CTRL”) or “What top-level block configures global solver options?” (“CTRL”).

The table shown is part of the “CTRL SUB” record, which is one of the global‐control records used to drive program behavior.  In context, CTRL SUB complements other records such as SPT, SLN, SAR, and SVO.  The header text tells us that CTRL SUB can appear with two prefixes—“PART” (for mesh‐partitioning) and “SUB” (for number of subdomains)—but here the focus is on setting global control options.  

Structure of the Table  
• Columns  
  1. Item  
     – The mnemonic or keyword used in the input deck.  
  2. Description  
     – A brief English text explaining what the keyword does.  
  3. Unit  
     – Physical units where applicable; here all entries are marked “—,” indicating unitless or toggles.  
  4. Default  
     – The program default value if the keyword is omitted. A dash (“–”) means no default is applied, whereas a numeric default (e.g. “+12”) is shown explicitly.  

• Rows  
  1. POST  
     – Description: “Activate Postprocessing.”  
     – Unit: —  
     – Default: –  
     – Behavior: When POST is specified, the postprocessor routines are invoked after the main solution phase. No numerical argument is required.  
  2. INIT  
     – Description: “Controls initialization of system.”  
     – Unit: —  
     – Default: +12  
     – Behavior: INIT accepts an integer value (here defaulting to +12) to select among different initialization schemes (e.g. cold‐start, restart from checkpoint, read preconditioner, etc.).  
  3. WARN  
     – Description: “Suppress warning message.”  
     – Unit: —  
     – Default: –  
     – Behavior: The WARN keyword disables standard warning outputs; useful in batch or scripted runs to reduce log verbosity.  
  4. VAL  
     – Description: “Value of control.”  
     – Unit: —  
     – Default: –  
     – Behavior: A generic slot to pass in a primary numeric parameter associated with a custom or less common control.  
  5. V2  
     – Description: “Second value if needed.”  
     – Unit: —  
     – Default: –  
     – Behavior: Provides an optional second numeric argument.  
  6. V3  
     – Description: “Third value if needed.”  
     – Unit: —  
     – Default: –  
     – Behavior: Provides an optional third numeric argument.  
  7. V4  
     – Description: “Fourth value if needed.”  
     – Unit: —  
     – Default: –  
     – Behavior: Provides an optional fourth numeric argument.  

Key Points and Usage  
• The table is designed for extensibility. Core toggles such as POST and WARN require no units or defaults, reflecting their boolean on/off nature.  
• INIT has an explicit numeric default (+12), implying that omitting INIT still triggers a predefined initialization path.  
• VAL–V4 are catch‐all fields: they do not have intrinsic meanings until tied to a specific control item. This approach lets more advanced users pass up to four numerical parameters without altering the table schema.  
• “See also: SPT, SLN, SAR, SVO” reminds the user that other CTRL records exist to manage specialized aspects (e.g. surface processing, solver lines, source‐actions, solution vectors) in a consistent format.  

Overall, this table provides a compact yet flexible mechanism for global run‐time control, balancing well‐defined toggles with open‐ended numerical slots.

In a first processing step prior to meshing, SOFiMSHC reads in the model entered by the user or given by CAD and intersects all elements with each other in order to obtain a mechanically consistent structural system. The general behaviour during this process can be controlled using the following options.
 Stores the input model entered by the user at a reference key given at parameter V2 and activates analysis and intersection of the structural system.
 Deactivates import and analysis of the structural system entirely, even if meshing of the structure has been activated (CTRL MESH usually activates CTRL TOPO ON by default). This setting is primarily needed for debugging purposes. The model must have been already imported and analyzed in a previous run.
 Deletes the structural elements stored at the given reference key. Under normal circumstances, the database will be properly initialized and structural elements deleted, when setting the system type internally (see SYST). Hence this option is usually only necessary in order to analyze failed program runs.
 Controls the generation of structural elements between placements on a geomet- ric axis. If using the default setting SOFiMSHC automatically generates structural points and structural lines between placements on a main and/or secondary axis. The numbering of the points as well as grouping and sectional information can be controlled at the respective records GAXS and GAXP. For the global control variable, following options are possible (bit-mask):

Models from external CAD-systems or files often exhibit geometric inconsistencies resulting in failed meshing runs or poor element quality. SOFiMSHC provides a number of options for correction of geometry:
 In some cases basically connected curve or line sequences will be exported from external systems fragmented into multiple short structural lines. A large number of such short structural lines might increase the number of elements in the resulting finite element mesh unnecessarily. This options allows to join adjacent structural lines of similar type to single edges.
 Two neighboring lines will be connected, if the following requirements are met:
 - The length of the adjacent lines lies below the given parameter V2
 - The angle between the two lines is lower than V3
 - There is no other edge connected (no Y-joint)
 - Boundary and cross-section properties do not change.
 This options deletes openings with a surface area below the given value V2.

MESH This parameter activates the mesh generation for the defined model. Following options exist:
 0 deactivate meshing
 meshing of beam structures
 meshing of beam and shell structures
 meshing of beam, shell and/or volumes
 In addition to the basic options 1-3 one may add the following values:
 keep explicit old elements
 +32 triangular elements only
 +64 quadrilateral elements only
 +128 disable dupl. run with background mesh
 +256 post-processing only (partitioning, optim.)
 A CTRL MESH automatically activates the topological analysis and intersection of structural elements (STEU TOPO 0)
 Parameter HMIN controls globally the element size of the resulting finite element mesh. It defines the maximum allowed length of a beam and/or the edge of a
 HMIN
 shell or volume element. Please note, that the mesh density defines only an upper bound for the element size. Local geometric features or other constraints might require a smaller element size.
 In addition to the global setting, the mesh size can be overwritten individually for single structural objects (structural points, lines, regions).
 FINE Parameter FINE controls the mesh size at the corners of a structural area. Re- ducing the mesh size towards the corners usually lead to better element quality. The parameter allows two input options:
 V2>0.0 Mesh density in [ m]
 V2<0.0 Factor to general mesh density at HMIN
 EFAC This parameter controls the mesh density in the vicinity of short structural edges. In the neighborhood of short structural edges, whose length are below the global element size HMIN, the mesh density is reduced locally in order to avoid distorted quad elements with highly different edge lengths. The parameter describes the factor
 "Local mesh size" / "Length of short edge"
 Default setting is a factor of EFAC=1.40. For models containing many small edges, however, this setting might result in meshes with many local refinements, which increase the total number of elements considerably. In order to avoid the local refinements, this factor should be increased with the disadvantage, that the element quality might be reduced. On the other hand, if a model contains relatively long and small structural areas, whose width lies below the global mesh density, it is recommended to deactivate this parameter entirely (EFAC = 0). This avoids the reduction of the mesh density to the ends of the areas which results in a more regular mesh.

On the other hand, if a model contains relatively long and small structural areas, whose width lies below the global mesh density, it is recommended to deactivate this parameter entirely (EFAC = 0). This avoids the reduction of the mesh density to the ends of the areas which results in a more regular mesh..
 PROG This parameter defines the rate, how the mesh density is increased from a local refinement to the global part. It describes basically the maximum allowed ratio of the edge size between two adjacent quad elements. Standard setting is a progression factor of PROG = 1.5.

BSEC Controls the automatic generation of design sections. This option allows to gener- ate additional beam sections which will be evaluated during beam design in AQB. For example, design sections can be generated at support faces to allow for a rounding of the design moment at supports. Following options exist:
 Deactivate generation of design sections

 Generate design sections at support faces along beam girders. A support will be assumed at all locations where the girder is connected to a column lying below, a wall crossing the girder or at structural points containing dimensions defined at BX,BY.
 LOCA Controls the definition of the local coordinate-system of beam elements.
 local z-axis points into gravity direction resp. the local y-axis into the first global horizontal axis if the former is not possible (i.e. beam axis parallel to gravity). User defined orientations are applied to the local y-axis.
 0
 1 local z-axis points into gravity direction resp. into the first global horizontal axis if the former is not possible (i.e. beam axis parallel to gravity). User defined orientations are applied to the local z-axis.
 2 local z-axis points into global Z resp. into global X if the former is not possible (i.e. beam axis parallel to global Z). User defined orientations are applied to the local z-axis. (Default in Industry Foundation Classes, IFC)
 3 local z-axis points into global Z resp. into global Y if the former is not possible. User defined orientations are applied to the local y-axis (GENF).
 TOLN This parameter controls the detection of double finite element nodes. FE-nodes whose distance lies below the given tolerance are intersected and replaced. The parameter is given as relative factor which will be scaled internally by model di- mensions.
 PSUP For point supports or beddings special mesh macros which reflect the geometry of the supporting column can be activated. This parameter controls this generation as follows:
 -1 no special action

This parameter controls this generation as follows:. -1 no special action. generate 4 rectangular quad elements (default). increase thickness of elements at support.

In order to solve the resulting equation system in the computing kernels efficiently, the equation numbers must be given in an optimized sequence. At SOFiSTiK, this optimization step is carried out during system generation on basis of the node numbers. Depending on the type of equation solver used, different kind of optimization algorithms like band-width optimization or fill-in reducing optimization are applied.
 OPTI Creates an internal numbering which allows efficient storage and solution of the resulting finite element equation system. Following options are available:
 0 deactivate optimization

 2 extensive band-width optimization
 +49 Fill-in reducing ordering (default)
 The type of optimization should be adapted to the equation solver to be used. An improper setting may have adverse effects. Following list shows the recom- mended settings.
 CTRL SOLV 1 band-width optimization (CTRL OPTI 1,2)

The table under discussion belongs to the SOFiMSC “GRP” (group) record, which is used to collect structural lines, areas and volumes into named or numbered element‐groups.  Such groups are essential when defining construction stages, assigning loads or organising model output.  The table defines six data items (fields) that appear on a single GRP record.  Each field has a short tag (“Item”), a human‐readable explanation (“Description”), a legal unit or format (“Unit”), and a default value that SOFiSTiK assigns when the field is omitted.

1. Item: NO  
   • Description: “Group number”  
   • Unit: – / LIT  
     – The “–” indicates that this is a pure identifier (integer) or literal; “LIT” signals that the field may also be addressed symbolically (by a literal name).  
   • Default: “!”  
     – A default of “!” means SOFiSTiK will generate the next sequential group number automatically if the user does not explicitly supply NO.

2. Item: REF  
   • Description: “Span, reference or sequence number”  
   • Unit: –  
     – This is a simple integer placeholder. It can be used to order or reference groups in a user-defined sequence.  
   • Default: 0  
     – Zero indicates “no particular reference” when the user does not specify any span or sequence ordering.

3. Item: BASE  
   • Description: “Base number for this group”  
   • Unit: –  
     – Used to link primary and secondary groups.  A “BASE” value allows you to indicate that one group inherits or depends on another.  
   • Default: “*”  
     – A star means “no base group,” i.e. the group stands on its own unless the user explicitly provides a base number.

4. Item: ICS  
   • Description: “Construction stage number of activation”  
   • Unit: –  
     – This integer ties the group to a particular construction stage in a staged‐build analysis. When the stage equals ICS, the elements in this group become “active.”  
   • Default: –  
     – A blank default (dash) implies that the group is active from the very first stage, unless overridden.

5. Item: ICE  
   • Description: “Construction stage number of deactivation”  
   • Unit: –  
     – When the simulation reaches the ICE stage, the elements in the group are deactivated or removed.  
   • Default: –  
     – A dash indicates “no deactivation stage,” so the group remains alive until the end of the analysis.

6. Item: TITL  
   • Description: “Title of the group”  
   • Unit: Lit32  
     – A literal character string up to 32 bytes long.  It serves purely for user documentation, printing and post-processing.  
   • Default: –  
     – If omitted, no group title is stored.

How to interpret and use this table in practice:  
• You begin a new GRP record by specifying the group’s NO.  If you omit NO, SOFiSTiK assigns the next free number.  
• Use REF and BASE sparingly if you need ordered grouping or hierarchical grouping.  
• Use ICS and ICE to drive time‐ or stage‐based activation/deactivation of elements.  This is particularly powerful in construction‐stage analyses, demolition studies or any scenario where elements appear or disappear.  
• Always supply a TITL if you want a human‐readable label in the model output or post‐processing reports.  

In a broader context, element groups defined here can be primary (BASE = “*”) or secondary (BASE points to another group).  They serve as handles for load assignments, result extraction and construction‐stage control within the SOFiSTiK environment.

The input table is a concise worked example illustrating the calculation of a “group number” from an “element number” using a configurable “group divisor” (GDIV).  This mirrors the way SOFiMSHC assigns each element to a primary group based on integer division of its element ID by the GDIV value defined in the system record (SYST).  Below is a detailed breakdown of the table’s structure, its contextual purpose within SOFiMSHC, and how each column relates to the group‐assignment logic.

1. Table Layout and Purpose  
   • Columns:  
     – Group divisor (GDIV)  
     – Element number (unique element ID)  
     – Group number (resulting group to which the element belongs)  
   • Goal: Show four different scenarios where the same element number (in some cases) is mapped to different groups simply by changing the divisor.  This highlights how group ranges are computed on the fly, and how altering GDIV reshapes the grouping intervals.

2. Column-by-Column Description  
   • Group divisor  
     – Integer value used as the divisor for computing the group number.  
     – In SOFiMSHC, GDIV is stored in the main system record SYST and can be positive (straight integer division) or negative (interpreted as a least‐common‐multiple rule for base calculations).  
     – Typical best practice encourages GDIV values that are round multiples of 100, 1 000, or 10 000, to simplify manual inspection and automatic splitting in print outputs.  
   • Element number  
     – The unique identifier for each element.  
     – Element numbers start at 1 and can go up to 1 000 000 per group.  
     – Regardless of its absolute magnitude, the element’s membership is determined solely by dividing this number by GDIV.  
   • Group number  
     – The integer‐quotient result of “element number ÷ group divisor” (floor division).  
     – Values can range from 0 up to a maximum of 999 (as per SOFiMSHC constraints).  
     – A group number of 0 often denotes “no group” or the default group 0 (none) when the element ID is less than GDIV.

3. Row‐by‐Row Walkthrough  
   • Row 1: GDIV = 1000, Element = 1  
     – 1 ÷ 1000 = 0 (integer division)  
     – Assigned to Group 0 (none).  
   • Row 2: GDIV = 1000, Element = 3 569  
     – 3 569 ÷ 1000 = 3 (since 3.569 → floor to 3)  
     – Assigned to Group 3.  
   • Row 3: GDIV = 2000, Element = 3 569  
     – 3 569 ÷ 2000 = 1 (1.784 → floor to 1)  
     – Assigned to Group 1.  
   • Row 4: GDIV = 5, Element = 3 569  
     – 3 569 ÷ 5 = 713.8 → floor to 713  
     – Assigned to Group 713.

4. Relating Back to Group Base Ranges  
   Below this small table, the system would normally maintain a separate “Group Base” table that lists:  
   • Base number (the starting element number for that group)  
   • Optional group designation/name  
   • Implicit range end (Base + GDIV – 1)  
   By defining each group’s base and using GDIV as the width of each group interval, the software can automatically assign large contiguous blocks of element numbers to successive groups without manual intervention.

5. Additional Notes & Best Practices  
   • Automatic Base Computation: If GDIV>0, bases need not be defined manually; they are computed after element generation according to the smallest multiple of GDIV above the preceding group’s range.  
   • Negative GDIV: Interpreted as “lowest common multiple” for irregular or custom‐sized groups.  
   • Readability in Outputs: For very large element IDs, printouts split the full number into “group part” and “element‐within‐group part.” Selecting GDIV as a round number (e.g. 1 000) aids both human reading and machine parsing.  
   • Constraints:  
     – Maximum elements per group: 1 000 000  
     – Maximum group number: 999

In summary, the table demonstrates that by simply varying the group divisor, the same element ID can belong to widely differing group numbers.  This flexible mechanism underpins SOFiMSHC’s scalable grouping logic, enabling both automatic base calculations and clear, consistent grouping across very large element sets.

 SAR NO 5
 ...
 END
 defines a secondary group labeled ’GR1’, which contains all beam and area elements created on the structural lines 1, 2 and 3 and structural area 5.
 Apart from this selection mechanism, elements can also be assigned to a secondary group using attribute regions. For more information please see at the description of attribute regions at record SAR.

The table shown is part of the IMPO record, which—once defined—applies to all 3D-extrusion operations by pointing to an alternate database of mesh definitions. You may only include one IMPO record per job; it tells the system where to find the meshes and how to interpret or transform them. Below is a field-by-field breakdown:

1. Item: OPT  
   • Description: A bit-mask field named “Special options.” Each bit (power of two) enables or disables a particular behavior during extrusion.  
   • Unit: none  
   • Default: 0 (no special options)  
   • Valid bit settings:  
     – 0: No special options; use default extrusion behavior.  
     – 1: Convert input coordinates from an XYZ ordering into a YZX ordering.  
     – 2: Convert input coordinates from an XYZ ordering into a ZXY ordering.  
     – 4: Set the origin pointer to the element number (elementno). This redefines the local origin of each extruded mesh or feature.  
     – 8: Same as bit 4 but omit any group number—only use the raw element number as the reference.  
     – 16: Do not extrude any support-condition geometry. Useful if you want to skip supports or fixtures in the final mesh.  
     – 256: When selecting sub-regions of the mesh, use the “Group” identifiers rather than the default geometry numbers.  

   These bits can be combined (for example, OPT = 1 + 4 = 5 means both “xyz→yzx” conversion and “origin pointer to elementno”). If you leave OPT at its default (0), the software assumes a straight-through extrusion with no coordinate remapping, full support extrusion, and geometry-number-based selections.

2. Item: FROM  
   • Description: The name (identifier) of the external database from which to load mesh templates or definitions for extrusion.  
   • Unit: Lit96 (a literal string up to 96 characters)  
   • Default: “*”  
     – A single asterisk indicates the current or default database; any other valid name directs the system to open that database.  

3. Item: PASS  
   • Description: The password required to open or modify the named database if it is protected.  
   • Unit: Lit16 (a literal string up to 16 characters)  
   • Default: “–” (a single dash signifies “no password” or “not required”)  

How this fits in a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) pipeline  
• Key fields to vectorize or index: OPT (as numerical flags), FROM (database names), and PASS (may be redacted or excluded from indexing for security).  
• Metadata tags:  
   – tag:IMPO_record  
   – tag:extrusion_options → OPT bits  
   – tag:external_db → FROM  
   – tag:db_password → PASS (sensitive)  
• Use “FROM” as the primary retrieval key when selecting which mesh repository to query. “OPT” bits guide transformation logic, and “PASS” provides authentication if needed.  

In summary, this table defines three parameters under the IMPO record: a composite option field (OPT) controlling coordinate conversions, origin settings, support behavior, and selection mode; the external database name (FROM) housing mesh templates; and the database password (PASS). Once declared, these settings remain in effect for every subsequent 3D-extrusion call in the same session or input deck.

IMPO
 With the record IMPO you may select for the 3D-extrusions the meshes to be used for the extrusion from a different database. This record may be defined only once and is then valid for all extrusions.

The table shown documents the structure of the EXPO record used to export geometric and structural data from the CADINP database into a SOFiMSHC-compatible input file. It is arranged into four items (or parameters), each with a description, a data‐type (“Unit”) and, where applicable, a default value.

1. OPT  (Unit: LIT, Default: RAW)  
   • Purpose: Selects which category of data is written out.  
   • Allowed values:  
     – GAX  – export only geometric axes  
     – GAR  – export only geometric surfaces  
     – RAW  – export the basic structural model (nodes, elements, connectivity, etc.)  
     – FULL – export extended properties (including internal datatypes and globally unique identifiers used by various CAD systems)  
   • Behavior:  
     – If an axis or surface identifier is supplied via VAL (see below), only that single axis or surface is exported.  
     – If no VAL is provided, all items of the chosen type (all axes, all surfaces, or the entire structural model) are exported.  

2. VAL  (Unit: Lit4, Default: none)  
   • Purpose: Optionally identifies a single geometric axis or surface to export.  
   • Format: A four-character literal.  
   • When omitted, the OPT setting applies to every element of its type.  

3. TO   (Unit: Lit96, Default: “*”)  
   • Purpose: Specifies the filename for the exported SOFiMSHC input.  
   • Format: Up to 96 characters.  
   • Default behavior: If left at the default (“*”), the export is directed to “project_MEX.dat.”  

4. PASS (Unit: Lit16, Default: none)  
   • Purpose: Supplies the database password required to read from the CADINP system.  
   • Format: Up to 16 characters.  

Additional contextual rules (from the EXPO record specification):  
• Units of All Numerical Values: The physical units (length, force, etc.) appear in the export exactly as set by the current UNIE setting in the PAGE record.  
• Language: The textual language of the generated SOFiMSHC file matches that of the currently loaded CADINP input file.  
• FULL Option Details: Selecting FULL causes the export to include internal model metadata—such as datatype identifiers and globally unique IDs (GUIDs)—ensuring that each structural object remains uniquely identifiable when transferred between different CAD or analysis systems.  

In practice, a typical record might look like:  
   EXPO OPT=FULL VAL= “AX01” TO=”beam-model.dat” PASS=”s3cr3t”  
This command would export only the geometric axis named “AX01,” including all extended properties, writing the result to “beam-model.dat” under password protection.

EXPO
 Using record EXPO geometric or structural elements within the database can be exported into an input file for SOFiMSHC. This can be useful when analyzing the data after an error occured or to make further use of the data in different settings.
 If an Identifier is given additionally at GAX or GAR, only the selected geometric axis or surface is exported to the file, otherwise all elements of the given type are exported. When using option FULL, additional properties of the model are exported, including internally used datatypes and globally uniqe identifiers (GUID) of the structural elements, which will be used for idenfication of structural objects in different CAD-systems.
 If no file name is specified the data will be exported to a file named project_MEX.dat.
 The units of the values will be set to the current setting of UNIE from record PAGE. The lan- guage of the new file will be the same as the current CADINP input file.

ECHO Record Overview  
This table defines the parameters for the ECHO command, which controls the type and verbosity of output in a structural analysis run. Every time the ECHO record is invoked, its name (“ECHO”) must be repeated to disambiguate it from any other record of the same name. Two primary items—OPT and VAL—are specified. Both accept literal (LIT) values and default to FULL if no explicit entry is provided.

1. Item: OPT  
   • Description: Specifies which categories of data will be written to the output. The user must supply one of the following literal keywords:  
     – MAT: Material data—prints definitions and properties of all materials used.  
     – SECT: Section for beams—reports cross-sectional properties of beam elements.  
     – GEOM: Geometric items—lists geometric primitives and coordinates.  
     – NODE: Generated nodes—gives a complete nodal listing created during preprocessing.  
     – QUAD: Generated quadrilaterals—details 4-noded shell or plate elements.  
     – BRIC: Generated volume elements—reports volume (brick) finite elements.  
     – BEAM: Generated beam elements—lists line-element beam definitions.  
     – BOUN: Generated elastic supports—shows all spring or elastic boundary conditions.  
     – SYST: System summary—provides aggregated statistics of the model (see “See also” for advanced bitpattern options).  
     – STAT: Analysis statistics—presents solver performance and iteration counts.  
     – FULL: All the above options—equivalent to specifying every keyword in a single command.  
   • Unit: LIT (literal keyword)  
   • Default: FULL  

2. Item: VAL  
   • Description: Sets the verbosity level of the selected output categories. Must be one of:  
     – NO: no output is generated for the chosen categories.  
     – YES: regular (concise) output, containing essential information only.  
     – FULL: extensive output, providing detailed tables and parameter listings.  
     – EXTR: extreme output, with maximal detail, typically for debugging or in-depth review.  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: FULL  

Contextual Notes and Advanced Options  
– ECHO-Option SYST may also be specified numerically instead of via NO/YES/FULL/EXTR. In this mode, the numerical value is interpreted as a bitpattern enabling fine-grained statistics for:  
  • bit 1 (1): general primary group statistics  
  • bit 2 (2): beam/truss/cable statistics  
  • bit 4 (4): area element statistics  
  • bit 8 (8): volume element statistics  
  • bit 16 (16): ordered by primary groups (or by structural members for design elements)  
  • bit 32 (32): ordered by cross-sections  
  • bit 64 (64): ordered by material (not for design elements)  
  • bit 128 (128): sum of reinforcements  
  • bit 256 (256): detailed sum of area element reinforcements  
  • bit 1024 (1024): nodal masses  
  • bit 2048 (2048): life cycle assessment  
  • bit 4096 (4096): life cycle assessment per element type (only LCA, without group stats or masses)  
  • bit 16384 (16384): only sums of finite elements  
  • bit 32768 (32768): sum of tendons  
  • bit 65536 (65536): design elements  
  • bit 131072 (131072): ordered by secondary groups defined by user  
  • bit 262144 (262144): ordered by all secondary groups  
  • bit 524288 (524288): calculate statistics and save to database without printout  

– When a numeric SYST option is used, results are stored as CADINP variables: GRP_MASS, SCT_MASS, MAT_MASS (mass arrays) and GRP_REIN, SCT_REIN (reinforcement arrays). In each array, index 0 holds the total sum.  

By combining OPT and VAL, users can precisely tailor both the scope and level of detail of ECHO output for post-processing, documentation, or quality assurance.

The table shown defines the COOR record, the “set‐coordinate‐system” command in SOFiMSHC.  COOR establishes a new local coordinate system that all subsequent position or direction entries (in structural records SPT, SLN, SAR) will obey.  You may invoke COOR as often as needed; COOR WRLD returns you to the default world (Euclidean) system with origin (0,0,0) and orthonormal axes aligned to the global X, Y, Z directions.  Note that COOR does not affect the geometry record GAX/GAR—those always remain in the world system.

The table is laid out in four columns—Item, Description, Unit and Default—and can be read as two logical groups:

1.  System selection fields  
   • TYPE (LIT)  
     – WRLD: world coordinate system (resets to global default)  
     – SPT: use the local system tied to an existing structural point  
     – AXIS: use the system of an axis or line (ID gives axis name, S gives station)  
     – GAXP: use the system of a placement on an axis (ID + IDP or S)  
     – CYLI: define a cylindrical system by origin and two direction vectors  
     – SPHE: define a spherical system by origin and two direction vectors  
     Default is WRLD.  

   • ID (–/Lit8)  
     Identifier or number of the referenced item (structural point, axis, etc.).  Ignored when TYPE=WRLD or when defining a pure WRLD/CYLI/SPHE system without an external reference.

   • IDP (Lit4)  
     Only used when TYPE=GAXP to pick a specific placement by its placement‐ID.  

2.  Coordinate‐system parameters  
   • S (–)  
     Station along the axis or structural line—used with TYPE AXIS or GAXP to specify the location on the axis.  

   • X, Y, Z ([m]₁₀₀₁)  
     Coordinates of the new origin.  For TYPE WRLD, CYLI or SPHE these simply set the origin in world‐space (default 0.0,0.0,0.0).  For CYLI and SPHE, their meaning changes on interpretation of subsequent inputs:  
       ­– CYLI: X→radius, Y→azimuth angle, Z→height  
       ­– SPHE: X→radius, Y→azimuth φ, Z→inclination  

   • T11, T12, T13 (–)  
     Components of the first local axis (T1 direction).  Introduces orientation; default is (1.0, 0.0, 0.0), i.e. aligned to global X.  

   • T21, T22, T23 (–)  
     Components of the second local axis (T2 direction).  Default is (0.0, 1.0, 0.0), aligned to global Y.  The third axis (T3) is computed as the cross‐product T1×T2; if T2 is not orthogonal to T1, it will be orthogonalized automatically.

Default values summarized: TYPE=WRLD; ID, IDP undefined; S undefined; X=Y=Z=0.0 m; T11=1, T12=0, T13=0; T21=0, T22=1, T23=0.

See also GAXP (geometric placement record), SPT (structural point), SLN (structural line), SAR (structural area)—all these records will interpret coordinates according to the active COOR system.
