 This record sets a new reference coordinate system for position and direction input in SOFiMSHC. After setting the coordinate system, all succeding input of a position or a direc- tion in any structural record will be interpreted according to the given coordinate system. The coordinate system can be changed within a data record as often as desired. Setting COOR WRLD resets the coordinate system to the default, an euclidian coordinate system with origin at (0,0,0).
 This record affects only the definition of structural element records (SPT,SLN,SAR) and their property records. The coordinate system of geometry input (Record GAX,GAR) cannot be changed.
 Different types are provided to set the coordinate system:
 This type defines an euclidian (orthogonal) coordinate system with origin given at X,Y,Z. The orientation of the coordinate system can be set using the paramters T11 to T23.
 They define the first local direction T1 (T11,T12,T13) and the second local direction T2 (T21,T22,T23) . The third direction is derived from the cross product of the first and second axis. In the case that the second direction is not orthogonal to the first, it will be orthogo- nalized.
 By setting a structural point number at ID, the coordinate system will be moved to the local coordinate system of an already defined structural point.
 The coordinate system will be moved to the respective station S of an axis or a structural line and rotated according to the local coordinate system of the axis. The axis or structural line resp. is given at ID. It is also possible to reference secondary axes (e.g. ID ’A1.B’).
 The coordinate system is moved to the location of a placement, which has been defined us- ing GAXP at an axis. The second and third direction of the coordinate system (local y and local z) will be aligned according to the cut-plane of the placement (local z usually points into gravity direction). The axis is given at parameter ID. The placement can be identified by its parameter position at S or its identifier given at IDP.

The second and third direction of the coordinate system (local y and local z) will be aligned according to the cut-plane of the placement (local z usually points into gravity direction). The axis is given at parameter ID. The placement can be identified by its parameter position at S or its identifier given at IDP..
 When defining a coordinate system using GAXP, all beam elements will be aligned per- pendicular to the placement plane, i.e. the local z-axis of the beams or structural lines is oriented towards the first axis of the coordinate system (x).
 By indicating an origin at X,Y,Z and two direction vectors at T1 (T11,T12,T13) and T2 (T21,T22,T23), a cylindrical coordinate system can be defined. All succeding input of a position (X,Y,Z) or a direction (DX,DY,DZ) will be interpreted ac- cording to the following scheme:
 X: Radius (distance) from rotational axis
 Y: Azimut angle in rotational plane
 Z: Height along rotational axis
 By indicating an origing at X,Y,Z and two direction vectors at T1 (T11,T12,T13) and T2 (T21,T22,T23), a spherical coordinate system can be defined. All succeding input of a position (X,Y,Z) or a direction (DX,DY,DZ) will be interpreted ac- cording to the following scheme:
 X: Radius (distance) from origin
 Y: Azimut angle ’phi’ in equatorial plane

The table defines the keyword‐record parameters for XSUB, the command that extracts a partial structural model from a larger model for stand-alone analysis.  Each row in the table corresponds to one parameter (Item).  The four columns (Item, Description, Unit, Default) capture the parameter’s name, its meaning, its data type or allowed literal, and its default value if the user does not supply one.

1.  Column Definitions  
    •  Item: the name of the parameter as used in the XSUB record (TYPE, FIXA, FIXL, FIXM, FIXS, CDB).  
    •  Description: a short explanation of what the parameter controls.  
    •  Unit: the expected data type or literal set; e.g. “Lit4” indicates a 4-character literal, “–/Lit” means either a numeric scale factor or one of the two keywords FIX or FREE, “LIT” is a generic string.  
    •  Default: the value assumed when the parameter is omitted.

2.  Parameter Details  
    2.1  TYPE  
        –  Description: selects whether the extracted submodel is treated as a full 3D spatial system or projected into a 2D plate/girder (slab) system.  
        –  Allowed Values (Unit = Lit4):  
           •  “SPAC” (default) → retain full 3D connectivity.  
           •  “SLAB” → project all selected members onto the XY-plane at z=0.0 to form a planar plate/girder model.  
        –  Default: SPAC.

    2.2  FIXA (axial stiffness)  
        –  Description: governs the axial (tension/compression) connection behavior for any member that is “cut” at the submodel boundary.  Internally, the default stiffness c = E·A/l is computed; the FIXA value multiplies that stiffness.  
        –  Unit: “–/Lit” → either a positive numeric scale factor or the literal “FIX” (infinite stiffness) or “FREE” (zero stiffness).  
        –  Default: FIX (i.e. fully fixed axial restraint).

    2.3  FIXL (lateral stiffness)  
        –  Description: controls transverse bedding stiffness.  Default springs derive from c = 3·E·Iy/l³ (for lines) or c = 3·E·iy/h³ (for regions).  
        –  Unit: –/Lit (numeric factor or FIX/FREE).  
        –  Default: 1.0 (use the calculated default without scaling).

    2.4  FIXM (rotational stiffness)  
        –  Description: sets the rotational spring stiffness at cut connections.  Default computed as cr = 3·E·Iy/l (lines) or cr = 3·E·iy/h (regions).  
        –  Unit: –/Lit.  
        –  Default: 0.0 (no rotational restraint—hinged).

    2.5  FIXS (shear stiffness)  
        –  Description: defines shear‐spring stiffness for adjacent walls/slabs: ks = G·b/h, applied along the boundary edge.  
        –  Unit: –/Lit.  
        –  Default: 1.0 (use computed shear stiffness unmodified).

    2.6  CDB  
        –  Description: name of the output database file (planar slab or new spatial system) that will hold the extracted submodel.  
        –  Unit: LIT (string).  
        –  Default: (none) – user must supply a valid file name.

3.  Context & Cross-References  
    –  The XSUB record follows any number of selection records (SLN, SAR, GUID, BBOX) that identify which lines or regions to extract.  
    –  FIXA–FIXS let you fine-tune how the “cut” boundaries react: FIX enforces full restraint, FREE removes the degree of freedom, and numeric factors scale the stiffness computed from material (E or G), geometry (A, b, h), and length or moment of inertia terms.  
    –  TYPE determines whether the result remains a fully 3D “SPAC” system (with all z-coordinates intact) or is flattened into the XY-plane as a “SLAB” model.  
    –  Once extracted, the new model (in the CDB file) can be meshed and independently solved as a separate analysis project.

See also: XCON, GUID, BBOX
 XSUB
 This records allows to extract a partial system from a general structural model for a detailed analysis. The extracted model will be stored in a new database as planar slab or again as new spacial system, which can be then meshed and calculated in a separate independent project.
 In the case, that the partial model will be extracted as plate system (TYPE SLAB) all selected structural elements will be projected onto the xy-plane at coordinate z=0.0.
 All structural elements connected to the partial model which will be cut during the extraction, like adjacent columns or walls, will be replaced by linear elastic spring elements or fixed sup- ports approximating the stiffness at the connection. The generation of these boundary condi- tions can be controlled using the parameters FIXA to FIXS. The four parameters distinguish between axial, lateral, rotational and shear stiffness components.
 The bedding component in axial direction of connected elements will be calculated as fol- lows:
 Connected Structural line c = E*A/l
 Structural area: c = E*b/h
 ’A’ denotes the cross section area and ’l’ the length of the connected structural line (e.g. column). For adjacent structural areas the linear elastic distributed bedding replacing the area will be calculated from the thickness b and the average height/width h of the connected wall/slab.
 The stiffness in transversal direction will be calculated under the assumption, that the con- nected building element has hinged support at the bottom:
 Structural line:
 c = 3 * E Iy / l3 (bzw. 3 * E Iz / l3)
 c = 3 * E iy / h3
 Structural area:
 For an adjacent structural line two spring elements will be created for the stiffness in the direction of the local y- and z-axis of the cross section. For a connected structural region, the lateral bedding is calculated by the distributed moment of intertia iy = b3 / 12 and the medial height/width of the region.

For an adjacent structural line two spring elements will be created for the stiffness in the direction of the local y- and z-axis of the cross section. For a connected structural region, the lateral bedding is calculated by the distributed moment of intertia iy = b3 / 12 and the medial height/width of the region..
 For the computation of the rotational stiffness, it is again assumed, that the connected building element has hinged support at the bottom:
 Structural line: cr = 3 * E Iy / l (bzw. 3 * E Iz / l)
 Structural area: cr = 3 * E iy / h
 For adjacent walls or slabs the shear stiffness will be calculated as follows:
 Structural area ks = G * b / h
 The stiffness is applied in longitudinal direction along the connected boundary edge.
 In all four cases, a numerical value > 0.0 or one of the two literals FIX or FREE can be given at FIXA to FIXS. In the case, that a numerical value is given, it will be interpreted as factor multiplying the default stiffness values calculated as given above. The literal ’FIX’ creates a fixed support and the literal ’FREE’ releases the respective degrees of freedom entirely.
 The elements of the partial system are selected by entering subsequent records directly after XSUB:
 • SLN: Selection of a structural line with number NO
 • SAR: Selection of a structural region with number NO
 • GUID: Selection using a Globally Unique Identifier (GUID) A GUID uniquely identifies a structural element and will be usually set when exporting the model from a CAD system (e.g. SOFiPLUS, Extensions for Revit).
 • BBOX: Selection using a rectangular bounding box This option is especially suitable for selecting all structural elements on a specified floor level (e.g. BBOX z1 9.5 z2 10.5).
 The selection records given above can be defined in any number and any order.

The table you’ve provided is part of the “XCON” record definition in a CAD‐inP (CadInp) scripting environment. XCON is invoked after a prior subsystem definition at XSUB and gives fine-grained control over how connected building elements are “converted” into support conditions for a subsystem extraction. Below is a detailed, field-by-field breakdown of the table structure and its entries, together with how each parameter ties back to the surrounding XSUB/XCON context.

1. Overall Table Structure  
   • Columns  
     – Item: the keyword used in the XCON command.  
     – Description: a human-readable explanation of what the keyword does.  
     – Unit: the expected data type or literal class (Lit or Lit4) for the keyword’s value.  
     – Default: the value assumed if the keyword is omitted.  

2. Row: SEL (Selection)  
   • Item = SEL  
   • Description: Determines which building members, connected to the previously defined subsystem, will be reinterpreted as support conditions. Two sub-options are listed under Description:  
     – “ABOV”: selects all members lying above the subsystem (e.g., columns, walls, slabs that extend upward from the extracted area).  
     – “BELO”: selects all members lying below the subsystem (e.g., foundations, lower frames).  
   • Unit = Lit4  
     – Indicates a four-letter literal. In this case, either “ABOV” or “BELO” must be typed.  
   • Default = “–” (none)  
     – If no SEL record is provided, XCON will not assume any members by default, and connected elements must be specified explicitly (by GUIDs, element numbers, or a bounding box).  

3. Row: FIXA (Axial Stiffness)  
   • Item = FIXA  
   • Description: Controls how axial stiffness is modeled at each connection that was selected under SEL. You can either:  
     – Choose a stiffness “type” (e.g. FIX to fully fix axial movement)  
     – Supply a numeric factor (relative stiffness) to scale the axial stiffness calculated by XSUB.  
   • Unit = – / Lit  
     – The entry may be either a literal string (such as “FIX”) or a numeric literal.  
   • Default = FIX  
     – By default, axial movement is fully restrained.  

4. Row: FIXL (Lateral Stiffness)  
   • Item = FIXL  
   • Description: Analogous to FIXA, but governs lateral (in-plane or out-of-plane shear) stiffness of the connection.  
   • Unit = – / Lit  
     – Accepts either a literal keyword or numeric value.  
   • Default = 1.0  
     – Uses the full lateral stiffness that XSUB would compute.  

5. Row: FIXM (Rotational Stiffness)  
   • Item = FIXM  
   • Description: Governs rotational restraint at the connection (moment stiffness).  
   • Unit = – / Lit  
     – Again, a literal string or scalar factor.  
   • Default = 0.0  
     – The default is a free rotation (no moment stiffness).  

6. Row: FIXS (Shear Stiffness)  
   • Item = FIXS  
   • Description: Controls shear‐type restraint (only relevant for connected walls and slabs where shear springs may be generated).  
   • Unit = – / Lit  
   • Default = 1.0  
     – Uses the full shear stiffness computed by XSUB.  

How This Fits Into an XCON Block  
– You start with:  
   +PROG SOFIMSHC  
   HEAD … XSUB 3D CDB "subsystem.cdb" SAR 1  
   HEAD  
– You then invoke XCON, listing any combination of SEL, FIXA, FIXL, FIXM, FIXS.  
– You follow with a selection list (e.g. SLN or GUID or BBOX) naming the elements to which these support settings apply.  
– If any of the four “FIX” parameters are omitted, XCON falls back to whatever was defined under XSUB for that stiffness type.  

Example (simplified):  
   XCON FIXA FIX FIXL 1.0 FIXM 1.0 FIXS FREE  
   SLN 1,2,3,4  
   XCON SEL ABOV FIXA FREE FIXL FREE FIXM FREE FIXS FREE  
   SLN 5,6,7  

In this example, the first XCON line assigns fully fixed axial springs, full lateral springs, half-stiff rotation, and no shear restraint to members 1–4. The second XCON line releases all degrees of freedom for members 5–7 lying above the subsystem.  

By clearly mapping each row of the table to its role in the subsystem extraction workflow, you can store these parameter definitions in a RAG vector store alongside user queries or documentation. This lets retrieval and reasoning agents understand exactly what “FIXA” or “SEL ABOV” means whenever an XCON record is mentioned.

See also: XSUB
 XCON
 When performing a subsystem extraction, this record allows to control in detail the generation of support conditions at connected elements. This record refers to a prior subsystem definition at XSUB and defines the support conditions for the following element selection.
 Example:
 +PROG SOFIMSHC

 The given CadInp sequence extracts a subsystem consisting of the structural area no. 1. The columns with structural line numbers 1,2,3 and 4 connected with the area will be replaced by a support in axis direction of the column (FIXA) as well as elastic springs modeling the lateral and rotational stiffness of the columns. All members lying above the substructure will be completely released and thus not considered for generating support conditions.
 The computation of the support conditions can be controlled with the same parameter as in record XSUB separated into axial, lateral, rotational and shear stiffness (the latter only for connected walls and slabs). In the case that connected elements are not specified within XCON, their stiffnesses will be calculated according to the settings in XSUB.
 The elements can be selected in the same way as the elements of the subsystem at record XSUB using their structural element number, their Globally Unique Identifier GUID or a bound-
 ing box BBOX.
 Elements which are not connected with the subsystem will not be considered, even if they are listed in the selection.

The table is organized into two columns—“Record” (on the left) and “Items” (on the right)—and defines, for each record identifier, the set of field names (or “items”) that belong to it. The high-level purpose of this layout is to enumerate schema definitions for a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) vector store: each Record code (e.g., GAX, GAXB, GAR) denotes an entity or document type, and its corresponding Items are the attribute names to be indexed or stored.

1. Header  
 • Record: a short alphanumeric code, typically starting with “GA” or “G” plus two more letters.  
 • Items: a space-separated list of up to a dozen field names or abbreviations for that record.

2. Group GAX*  
 • GAX  
   – Seven primary fields: NO, TYPE, ID2, ID3, ID4, ID5, REF  
   – Seven secondary fields: SUR1, SUR2, TYP C, DEG, TITL  
 • GAXA  
   – First line: S, X, Y, SX, SY, L, R  
   – Second line: RA, RE, LA, LE, TYPS  
 • GAXH  
   – Three fields: S, H, R  
 • GAXB  
   – First row: R, XM, YM, ZM, NX, NY, NZ  
   – Second row: X1, Y1, Z1, X2, Y2, Z2  
   – Third row: Y3, Z3, X3  
 • GAXC  
   – Primary: X, Y, Z, W, NX, NY, NZ  
   – Secondary: ALFX, ALFY, ALFZ  
 • GAXN  
   – Three arithmetic operators: S, MUL, DIV  
 • GAXP  
   – First row: ID, IDS, S, TYPE, GPT, GRP, NCS  
   – Second row: Y, Z, ALF, ALFX, ALFY, ALFZ, INCL  
 • GAXS  
   – Fields: ID, IDS, GPT, GRP, Y, Z, TITL  
 • GAXV  
   – Fields: ID, NAME, S, V, DV, TYPE  

3. Group GAR*  
 • GAR  
   – Fields: NO, TYPE, DEGU, DEGV, M, N, TITL  
 • GARA  
   – First line: NO, TYPE, GIDI, GID2, X, Y, Z  
   – Second line: NX, NY, NZ, SMIN, SMAX, TMIN, TMAX  
 • GARC  
   – Numeric-UV mix: NU0, NU1, NV0, NV1, XUV1, YUV1, ZUV1, XUV4, YUV4, ZUV4  
 • GARS  
   – Simple axes: M, N, X, Y, Z, W, T  

Key observations for RAG ingestion:  
 • Record codes group related fields—GAX* covers several specialized geometries or data slices, GAR* covers grid or axis-related records.  
 • Many Items appear as abbreviations (e.g. NX, NY, ZM) or variants (ALFX vs. ALFY vs. ALFZ).  
 • Some records split their item lists across two or three physical table rows; in processing, these should be concatenated into a single item array per record.  
 • The field names include measurement units (DEG, DEGU), titles (TITL), indices (ID, IDS), scales (SMIN/SMAX, TMIN/TMAX), and multipliers or operations (MUL, DIV).  

In a vector store, each Record code would map to a JSON schema or document template with an array of its listed Items. This description enables automatic parsing, validation, and embedding of each record’s attributes when ingesting data for RAG.

This table defines the structure of the GAX record, the master definition of a geometry axis in SOFiMSHC. A “geometry axis” is a parametric curve (road alignment, bridge centerline, lane edge, tendon line, etc.) to which all dependent structural elements can be attached and automatically updated when the axis changes. Below is a field-by-field description, including data type, purpose and default behavior:

1. ID  
   – Literal(4) identifier for this axis entry.  
   – Must be unique and no longer than four characters (e.g. “AX1”).  
   – This field is mandatory (“!”).  

2. TYPE  
   – Literal tag specifying the axis category.  
   – Possible values:  
     • DEL – marks this axis for deletion  
     • NONE – no special semantic type  
     • AXIS – system or reference axis (for cross-sections, elevations)  
     • BEAM – sequence axis for beam elements  
     • LANE – traffic lane edge or centerline (default)  
     • TEND – tendon alignment (prestressing)  
   – Defaults to LANE if omitted.  

3. ID2, ID3, ID4, ID5  
   – Four additional literal slots reserved for exporting custom data or extensions.  
   – By default all are blank (“–”) except ID5 which defaults to “1.”  
   – These fields can be repurposed by downstream systems but have no intrinsic function in the core GAX specification.  

4. REF  
   – Literal(4) reference to another (master) axis ID.  
   – When specified, all subsequent curve definitions (in GAXC or other subrecords) are interpreted relative to this master axis.  
   – Enables creation of offset or parallel curves, or cloning an existing alignment with shifts.  

5. SUR1, SUR2  
   – Literal(4) references to one or two geometric surface objects.  
   – SUR1 only: the generated curve is the orthogonal projection of the axis onto that surface.  
   – SUR1 + SUR2: the resulting curve is the intersection of the two specified surfaces.  
   – Both default to blank (“–”) when no surface projection or intersection is desired.  
   – Marked with “*” to indicate they appear only in specialized use cases.  

6. TYPC  
   – Literal code defining the type of subrecord or curve generation method.  
   – Cross-references GAXA/GAXH (alignment in plan/elevation), GAXB (lines/arcs), GAXC (freeform polygonal, splines, Hermite, NURBS), GAXN (NURBS), etc.  
   – Determines which subsequent records (ARC, POLY, SPLI, HINT, NURB) will follow to build the axis shape.  

7. DEGR  
   – Integer giving the degree of the spline curve when TYPC refers to spline or NURBS types.  
   – Ignored for straight-line or simple arc definitions.  

8. TITL  
   – Literal(32) descriptive title or full name of the axis (e.g. “Main Bridge Centerline”).  
   – Optional, free-format text that can aid clarity in reports or user interfaces.  

Cross-References and Workflow  
• This record is the anchor for all downstream curve-defining records (GAXA, GAXB, GAXC, GAXH, GAXN). When you change the axis geometry here, dependent structural definitions (BEAM placements, slab sections, load lines, secondary axes GAXS, variable distributions GAXV, placement markers GAXP) update automatically.  
• Use REF, SUR1, SUR2 to create offset curves or project/intersect axes with topographic or analytical surfaces.  
• ID2–ID5 can carry client-specific attributes without altering the standard schema.  

In summary, the GAX record encapsulates all metadata needed to identify, classify, reference, and parameterize a geometric axis. Subsequent records then flesh out the actual coordinate data and interpolation method prescribed by the TYPC field.

The table under discussion defines the syntax and semantics of the GAXA record’s keyword‐value pairs in SOFiMSHC for alignment axes in plan view. It is organized into four columns—Item, Description, Unit, and Default—and can be read as follows:

1. Columns  
   • Item  
     – The keyword or parameter name used in a GAXA line.  
   • Description  
     – A brief human‐readable explanation of the parameter’s meaning or role in the axis definition.  
   • Unit  
     – The physical unit of the parameter, where applicable (“m” for metres). A dash (—) indicates a unitless quantity. “LIT” designates a literal string.  
   • Default  
     – The value assumed if the parameter is omitted. An asterisk (*) denotes that no default exists and that the parameter must be supplied whenever used in that context.

2. Groups of Parameters  
   A. Initial station‐and‐tangent definition  
   • S (Station value):  
     – A monotonically increasing or decreasing chainage along the axis (no unit).  
   • X, Y (Coordinates of startpoint / intersection point):  
     – Planimetric X‐ and Y‐coordinates in metres.  
   • SX, SY (Direction of tangent):  
     – Components of a unit vector defining the tangent direction at the station.  
     – All four of these parameters (S, X, Y, SX, SY) carry no defaults and must appear together when defining a fresh axis start.

   B. Segment‐length and curvature definition  
   • L (Length of section):  
     – Length along the axis in metres. This is the primary way to “step” along the alignment.  
   • R (Radius):  
     – Constant curvature radius for a circular segment (positive → right-hand curve; negative → left).  
   • RA, RE (Start/end radius):  
     – If present, override R at the segment’s start (RA) or end (RE). Default for both is the last supplied R value.  
     – Specifying different RA and RE triggers the insertion of transition curves (clothoids by default).

   C. Transition‐curve lengths  
   • LA (Length of first transition element):  
     – In metres. If negative, interpreted as a clothoidal parameter A via R*L = A². No default.  
   • LE (Length of second transition element):  
     – In metres. If negative, same clothoid‐parameter convention applies. Defaults to the value of LA if omitted.

   D. Transition‐curve type  
   • TYPS (Type of transition curve):  
     – A literal string indicating the shape of transition (e.g. CLOT for clothoid, CUBI for cubic parabola, BLOS for Bloss, SIN, COS).  
     – Default is “CLOT.”

3. How It Fits Together  
  – You begin an axis by issuing a GAXA line with S, X, Y, SX, SY.  
  – Subsequent GAXA lines describe each segment in turn: you either specify L alone (for straight segments), L + R (for a circular arc), or L + RA + RE (for an arc with differing start/end radii, automatically generating transitions).  
  – For more advanced control you can omit R entirely and instead specify absolute intersection points (X,Y) plus R, LA, LE: SOFiMSHC computes a “symmetric standard sequence” if only R and a total L are given (LA = LE), or an “asymmetric standard sequence” when individual LA and LE are provided.  
  – If no radius appears, the axis is purely polygonal with sharp kinks.  
  – If the transition‐element lengths are insufficient, straight-line filler segments are inserted so the tangency conditions remain consistent.  
  – Finally, alternative transition curve forms can be chosen via TYPS.

 The given record GAXA defines sections of an alignment axis in plan view. This record is a property record and refers to the preceding axis definition at GAX. For defining an alignment axis SOFiMSHC provides two different possibilities:
 Length based definition:
 In the length based definition, the axis starts by defining a startpoint (station + coordinate) and a tangential direction, e.g.
 GAXA
 S 250.0 X 0.0 Y 0.0 SX 1.0 SY 0.0
 GAXA S 250.0 X @.@ Y 0.0 SX 1.@ SY 0.0
 Following, segments are defined with their length and optional start and end radius:
 GAXA L 50.0 RA 0.0 RE 200.0
 GAXA L 50.0 R 200.0 GAXA L 50.0 RA 200.0 RE 0.0 GAXA L 50.0
 For segments with different radius between start and end, a transition curve is inserted. A radius with positive value causes a curvature to the right-hand side, while a negative radius creates a segment with a curvature to the left-hand side. Using the input above, a sequence consisting of a transition element, a circular arc, a transition element and a straight segment at the end will be created, for example.
 Tangentially based definition
 Here, the user defines the intersections of curve tangents together with a curvature radius and different length parameters, for example:
 GAXA X 0.0 Y 0.0
 GAXA X 30.0 Y 10.0 R 40.0 LA 10.0 LE 10.0
 GAXA X 60.0 Y
 0.0
 Using this parameters SOFiMSHC inserts a curve sequence such, that its end points fits tan- gentially to the predefined polygon. For the parameter following possibilities exist:

GAXA X 30.0 Y 10.0 R 40.0 LA 10.0 LE 10.0. GAXA X 60.0 Y. 0.0. Using this parameters SOFiMSHC inserts a curve sequence such, that its end points fits tan- gentially to the predefined polygon. For the parameter following possibilities exist:.
 • The minimum radius at R and the total length of the curve sequence is given at L. In this case, a curve sequence is inserted under consideration of the symmetry condition A1=A2. This is called a ”symmetric standard sequence”.
 • The minimum Radius R and the length of the two transition segments LA and LE are given. This case defines a so called ”asymmetric standard sequence”. The length of the circular segment is calculated automatically. The user may also define a start radius RA and an end radius RE. In this case, the curve sequence does not any longer fit curvature continuously to the tangents.
 If no radius is given at all, a polygonal axis with kinks is created.
 In the case that the parameters of the transition elements define a shorter length than needed, a straight segment will be inserted before the standard curve sequence and the position of the tangent points will be adjusted accordingly.
 Instead of a Clothoid, also a cubic parabola (TYPS CUBI) (not recommended) or a Bloss Curve
 (TYPS BLOS) may be used as transition element. And finally, SOFiMSHC also allows to use sinusoidal (TYPS SIN) and cosinusoidal (TYPS COS) transition elements.

The table shown is the parameter‐definition block for the GAXH element, which specifies the vertical alignment (elevation) of an already‐defined horizontal alignment axis (GAX).  In a typical road‐design workflow you first define an alignment plan in XY (via GAX, GAXA, GAXP, GAXS, GAXV) and then “drape” or assign elevations along that plan using GAXH.  The table’s four columns identify the parameter name, its meaning, its units, and its default‐value marker.

1. Column: Item  
   • S  
   • H  
   • R  

2. Column: Description  
   • Station value  
   • Height  
   • Radius of elevation  

3. Column: Unit  
   • — (unitless)  
   • m (metres)  
   • m (metres)  

4. Column: Default  
   • *  
   • *  
   • *  

Below is a detailed, field‐by‐field breakdown:

1. Item “S” (Station value)  
   – Definition: The chainage or station along the horizontal alignment where an elevation event is defined. Stations typically increment from zero at the start of the alignment and increase in the direction of travel.  
   – Unit: unitless—chainages are normally dimensioned in metres but are not re‐stated here, since they share the same linear unit convention as the underlying GAX.  
   – Default “*”: Indicates that a value must be supplied by the user; no program default is assumed.

2. Item “H” (Height)  
   – Definition: The vertical offset or elevation of the alignment axis at station S. According to road‐design convention, positive heights are oriented opposite to the world‐gravity direction (that is, upward if POSZ is up, or downward if NEGZ is defined upward in your coordinate set).  
   – Unit: metres (m).  
   – Default “*”: Must be provided to fully define the vertical profile.

3. Item “R” (Radius of elevation)  
   – Definition: The radius of the vertical curve connecting this elevation point to the previous one.  Geometry is generated using quadratic parabolas, so specifying R determines how “flat” or “steep” the curve between H at station S and the preceding station will be.  Larger R yields gentler curvature; smaller R yields sharper crest or sag curves.  
   – Unit: metres (m).  
   – Default “*”: User‐defined for each curve; no implied default.

How This Fits into the Larger GAX Workflow  
– GAX defines the horizontal alignment reference.  
– GAXA/GAXP/GAXS/GAXV commands further flesh out alignment arcs, tangents, spirals, and transitions.  
– GAXH then “lifts” that plan into 3D by specifying elevation points (S, H) and how those elevations connect via radius R.  
– In the final model, each segment between successive stations S₁→S₂ is rendered as a vertical quadratic parabola determined by R, ensuring smooth changes in gradient.

Usage Notes  
– Always list stations (S) in strictly increasing order to avoid loops or backward profiles.  
– Maintain continuity in R values to prevent sudden changes in vertical curvature.  
– Observe the sign convention for H relative to your POSZ/NEGZ settings. 

By indexing this table into a vector store, you equip downstream RAG (retrieval‐augmented generation) systems with clear, structured semantics of each GAXH parameter, its relationship to road‐design conventions, and its interplay with the broader GAX family of commands.

The illustration (Figure 4.3: Curvature radii) is a schematic cross-section through a plan-view alignment showing how a parabolic transition curve is inserted between two straight segments (tangents) at a defined station P2. The key elements and notation are as follows:

1. Tangent Lines and Points  
   • P1 (left) and P2 (center) mark two successive control stations on the horizontal alignment.  
   • From P1, a straight line (tangent) slopes gently upward and rightward toward P2.  
   • Beyond P2, another straight tangent departs at a slightly shallower downward slope to the right.

2. Parabolic Transition Curve  
   • Immediately beneath the two straight-line tangents, a thick curved line represents the quadratic (second-degree) parabola that smoothly connects the incoming and outgoing tangents.  
   • This curve eliminates the abrupt change in direction that would occur if the two straight lines met directly at P2. In road or railway design terminology, it is often called a “spiral” or “easement” curve, though here it is specifically a single-radius transition expressed as a quadratic parabola.

3. Radius Arrow (R)  
   • At the location where the parabola and the upper two tangents are closest—directly beneath the apex at P2—a single vertical arrow is drawn.  
   • The arrow points upward from the curved parabola to the intersection of the straight tangents. It is labeled “R,” denoting the radius of the curvature at that point.  
   • According to the GAXH convention (see GAX, GAXA, GAXP, GAXS, GAXV for related axes definitions), positive height (POSZ direction) is taken upward opposite global gravity (NEGZ), so R is measured in the POSZ direction from the parabolic curve to the tangent intersection.

4. Annotations and Style  
   • The diagram uses simple black lines on white background, with the parabolic segment slightly thicker to distinguish it from the straight tangents.  
   • Text labels “P1” and “P2” are placed just below the left and above the top node, respectively, in a plain sans-serif font.  
   • The figure caption “Figure 4.3: Curvature radii” appears centered beneath the drawing.

Overall, this graphic encapsulates the way GAXH defines the elevation offset (height) of an already-defined horizontal alignment axis (GAX) at a curvature point, imposing a quadratic parabola whose maximum vertical separation from the chord lines of the tangents is equal to the specified radius R. In road design practice, such a representation ensures smooth, continuous curvature between straight-line segments, improving vehicle ride comfort and safety.

 GAXH
 GAXH defines the elevation of an alignment axis defined previously at GAX. According to the convention used in road design positive height values will be placed in a direction opposite to the globally defined gravity direction (POSZ, NEGZ). Curvature radii will be applied as quadratic parabolas.

The table under the GAXB record header defines all of the numeric parameters you can supply when you want to describe one or more geometric segments—straight lines, full circles or circular arcs—in 3-D space.  Every GAXB entry “hooks” back to the most recently declared axis in the GAX record and may contain multiple contiguous segments (a polycurve), though each segment itself is defined by one of three possible parameter‐sets.  Below is a structured breakdown of the table’s four columns (Item, Description, Unit, Default) and how each row is used in practice.  

1.  Circle‐or‐arc center and normal (for full circles or arcs by center + radius)  
   •  R  
      –  Radius of circle (or arc), in meters  
      –  Unit: [m]  
      –  Default: none (required if defining by center + radius)  
   •  XM, YM, ZM  
      –  Coordinates of the circle’s center point in 3D, in meters  
      –  Units: [m] each  
      –  Default: none  
   •  NX, NY, NZ  
      –  Components of the normal vector to the circle’s plane (dimensionless)  
      –  Unit: –  
      –  Default: none  

2.  Start- and end-points (for straight lines or arcs by endpoints + radius/center)  
   •  X1, Y1, Z1  
      –  Start point of segment, in meters  
      –  Units: [m] each  
      –  Default: none  
   •  X2, Y2, Z2  
      –  End point of segment, in meters  
      –  Units: [m] each  
      –  Default: none  

3.  Third point on arc (alternative way to define an arc through three points)  
   •  X3, Y3, Z3  
      –  Coordinates of an additional point on the circular arc (meters)  
      –  Units: [m] each  
      –  Default: none  

4.  Optional chainage parameters (controls parametrization along the curve)  
   •  S1  
      –  Parameter value at start of segment (instead of true arc‐length)  
      –  Unit: –  
      –  Default: 0.0  
   •  S2  
      –  Parameter value at end of segment  
      –  Unit: –  
      –  Default: none (if omitted, uses true length)  

How to choose which rows to fill for each segment:  
•  Straight line: fill X1,Y1,Z1 and X2,Y2,Z2 only.  
•  Full circle: fill R, XM,YM,ZM and NX,NY,NZ.  
•  Circular arc (method A): fill R and NX,NY,NZ plus X1,Y1,Z1 and X2,Y2,Z2.  
•  Circular arc (method B): fill XM,YM,ZM plus X1,Y1,Z1 and X2,Y2,Z2 (center + endpoints).  
•  Circular arc (method C): fill X1,Y1,Z1, X2,Y2,Z2 and X3,Y3,Z3 (three‐point definition).  

Notes on polycurves and continuity:  
–  If you define multiple GAXB segments in sequence, the end point of one segment must coincide with the start of the next to avoid gaps.  
–  To ensure smoothness, the tangent directions at shared junctions should match; otherwise “kinks” may occur (which can disrupt downstream meshing).  
–  If a deliberate kink is desired, it’s recommended to split into two GAXB entries with a structural point.  
–  Use S1/S2 when you want a custom parameterization (e.g., non‐uniform chainage). Otherwise, the record’s natural parametrization follows true segment length.  

See also the related GAX record type and its variants (GAXA, GAXH, GAXP, GAXS, GAXV) for additional axis and placement definitions.

sections: 4.5 GAXB – Straights and circular arcs in 3D

content:
See also: GAX, GAXA, GAXH, GAXP, GAXS, GAXV
 GAXB
 S2
 Parameter at end (optional)
 −
 -
 Records of type GAXB can be used to define straight lines, circles and circular arcs in space. Records of this type always refer to the previously defined axis at GAX. Multiple segments are allowed to be entered in order to define polycurves. For the definition of a single segment following possibilities exist:
 • A straight line is defined by its start- and endpoint at (x1,y1,z1) and (x2,y2,z2).
 • A full circle can be defined by its center (xm,ym,zm), the radius and the normal on the circular plane (n,ny,nz).
 • A circular arc can be defined by its start- and endpoint at (x1,y1,z1) und (x2,y2,z2), a radius and the normal or by entering the start-, the endpoint and the center.
 • In addition, circular arcs can also be defined by entering three points on the arc. (x1,y1,z1) und (x2,y2,z2) describe the start- and the endpoint, (x3,y3,z3) a third point on the arc.
 When multiple segments are defined, the transition between two segments should be mod- eled with continuous tangents. Kinks are possible but should be avoided as they can lead to incorrect or erroneous meshes. In order to define kinks it is better to define two curves with a
 structural point in between.
 Using the parameters S1 and S2 the chainage (or parametrisation) of the curve can be set explicitly. If nothing is given at S1 and/or S2 the parametrisation is defined according to the true (arc) length of the curve.

content:
The table shown is the field‐definition for the GAXC record, which in the SOFiMSHC geometry schema is used to input one characteristic point of a freeform 3D curve.  Each GAXC line contributes exactly one control or interpolation point to the curve axis being defined in the parent GAX block.  Below is a structured, point-by-point description of all columns and rows, together with the broader functional context drawn from the accompanying text.

1. General Context  
   • GAXC belongs in the family of records GAX, GAXN, GAXP, GAXS, GAXV and specifically defines the 3D coordinates (and optional weights, chainage, orientation hints) of a single point.  
   • The parent record GAX sets the overall curve type (TYPC) and degree (DEG), e.g. polygonal line, cubic B-spline (C2 continuity), piecewise cubic B-spline (C1 continuity), or NURBS.  
   • Optionally GAX may reference another axis (REF), in which case X=station on REF, Y/Z=offsets in the local REF frame, and the resulting curve is interpolated as a cubic B-spline.

2. Table Layout  
   – Columns:  
     • Item: parameter name  
     • Description: semantic role in curve definition  
     • Unit: physical unit or “–” if unitless  
     • Default: assumed value if omitted  

   – Two logical groups of fields in the table:  
     a) Coordinates & interpolation parameters (X, Y, Z, W, S)  
     b) Directional hints (DX, DY, DZ) and local‐axis orientation (NX, NY, NZ)

3. Detailed Field Descriptions  
   A. Coordinates & Weights  
     • X (Unit: [m]₁₀₀₁; Default 0.0)  
       – Base coordinate: either the global X-axis in Cartesian or the station (chainage) along a referenced curve if REF is set.  
     • Y (Unit: [m]₁₀₀₁; Default 0.0)  
       – Global Y-coordinate or lateral offset from referenced axis.  
     • Z (Unit: [m]₁₀₀₁; Default 0.0)  
       – Global Z-coordinate (elevation) or vertical offset.  
     • W (Unit: –; Default 1.0)  
       – Weight of the NURBS control point. Values ≠1 produce true rational NURBS capable of exact circles/ellipses. Ignored for non-NURBS types.  
     • S (Unit: –; Default “–”)  
       – Explicit chainage parameter. When specified, overrides automatic parametrization. For polygonal or spline curves, S sets the point’s parameter value; if omitted, the software evenly distributes or uses geometric length as chainage.

   B. Tangential Direction Hints (only for piecewise splines, type HINT)  
     • DX, DY, DZ (Unit: –; Default “–”)  
       – Tangent vector components at this point. Used only when TYPC = “HINT” (piecewise cubic with C1 continuity). They let the user control entry/exit directions at knots.

   C. Local z-Axis Orientation  
     • NX, NY, NZ (Unit: –; Default “–”)  
       – Components of a user-defined orientation axis at the point. When omitted entirely, the local z-axis defaults toward the global gravity direction. Useful to orient cross-sections or sweep frames along the curve.

4. How It All Fits Together  
   • Each GAXC row yields one point. The parent GAX record gathers them in sequence.  
   • TYPC = “POLY”: points connect with straight segments. W, DX–DZ, NX–NZ ignored; S optional.  
   • TYPC = “SPLI”: cubic B-spline (C2 continuity). W ignored; S can tune chainage.  
   • TYPC = “HINT”: piecewise cubic with tangential hints; DX/DY/DZ define tangents.  
   • TYPC = “NURB”: NURBS curve; W mandatory for rational behavior; degree and knots defined elsewhere (SLNN record).  
   • REF on GAX transforms X into chainage on a reference axis, Y/Z into local offsets; the result is interpolated as SPLI.

By capturing X, Y, Z plus optional W, S, directional hints and axis‐orientation vectors, this single table defines every attribute needed to build, interpolate or control the shape and parametrization of an arbitrary freeform 3D curve in the SOFiMSHC/GAX framework.

See also: GAX, GAXN, GAXP, GAXS, GAXV
 GAXC
 The geometry of arbitrary freeform curves can be defined with this record by entering charac- teristic data points. Each record GAXC defines a single coordinate in 3D. The points always refer to the directly preceding geometry axis. The type and the degree of the curve is specified by the parameters TYPC and DEG within the main record GAX:
 The given points will be connected to a polygonal line.
 The given datapoints will be interpolated using a cubic B-Spline. The interpolation is carried out curvature continuous at the definition points (C2-continuity).
 The chainage (parametrisation) of the curve can be set explicitly at each datapoint using the parameter S. If no parameter values are given, SOFiMSHC assigns a parametrisation automatically. The end chainage corresponds to the geometric length of the axis in this case.
 The given datapoints will be interpolated using piecewise cubic B-Spline segments. The interpolation is carried out tangentially continuous at the definition points (C1-continuity). Using the parameters DX,DY,DZ, the tangential direction at certain points can be defined explicitly by the user. Similar to the spline interpolation, the parametrisation (chainage) along the curve can be set using the parameter S.
 A NURBS (Non Uniform Rational B-Spline) curve can be defined by entering the euclidian coordinates of the control-points at X,Y,Z. If weights < > 1.0 are given, the input results in a true ’rational’ NURBS curve, which, for example, allows to describe also circle and ellipses. The degree of the NURBS curve can be set in record SLNN, when defining the knot vector.
 It is also possible to create curves relatively to an existing axis. If a reference axis REF is given in the main record GAX, the X-values are then interpreted as station value S on the reference axis and the values Y and Z as distances relatively to the local coordinate system of the referenced axis. The thus defined points are then interpolated by a cubic B-spline (TYPC SPLI). Contrary to secondary axes at GAXS, the reference is resolved explicitly, i.e. a new independent geometry is calculated based on the definition of the data points.

If a reference axis REF is given in the main record GAX, the X-values are then interpreted as station value S on the reference axis and the values Y and Z as distances relatively to the local coordinate system of the referenced axis. The thus defined points are then interpolated by a cubic B-spline (TYPC SPLI). Contrary to secondary axes at GAXS, the reference is resolved explicitly, i.e. a new independent geometry is calculated based on the definition of the data points..
 At NX,NY,NZ a user defined orientation of the local z-axis can be set for each point on the curve independantly. This allows to define, for example, arbitrarily oriented cross-sections along a curve or an axis. If no directions are given at all, the local z-axis is oriented towards the globally defined gravity direction.

The input table defines the schema of a single GAXN record in the SOFiMSHC format. GAXN records are used whenever you want to explicitly prescribe the knot‐vector for a NURBS curve (or, in the special case of interpolation curves, set each parameter value by hand). A knot‐vector is simply an ordered list of real numbers (the “knots”) along the parametric axis of the curve; the arrangement and repetition of these numbers determine how the curve blends its control points. Within the very first GAXN record you may also declare the polynomial degree of the NURBS curve. If you omit all GAXN definitions, SOFiMSHC will assume a uniform knot spacing behind the scenes.

Table Layout  
• Columns  
  – Item: the field name used in the GAXN input line.  
  – Description: a short English label describing what the field means.  
  – Unit: physical units (if any); in this case all entries are dimensionless parameters so it is marked “–.”  
  – Default: the value assumed if the field is omitted.

• Rows / Fields  
  1. S  
     • Description: Knot value  
     • Unit: –  
     • Default: ! (mandatory)  
     • Remarks: S is the actual scalar parameter location along the curve axis. Every distinct knot you wish to introduce must appear at least once in its own GAXN record.  

  2. MUL  
     • Description: Multiplicity  
     • Unit: –  
     • Default: 1  
     • Remarks: Specifies how many times the given knot S is to be repeated in the vector. Repetition (“multiple knots”) affects continuity: a knot of multiplicity equal to the curve degree will force the curve to interpolate its control point at that location (a “clamped end”). If you want to enter two repeated knots, you can either issue two GAXN lines with the same S or give MUL=2 in one line.  

  3. DEGR  
     • Description: degree of Nurbs  
     • Unit: –  
     • Default: 1  
     • Remarks: Only valid in the very first GAXN record. DEGR sets the polynomial degree of the NURBS basis functions (degree = order – 1). After the first record, DEGR is ignored and must not be repeated.  

Contextual Notes  
• For standard NURBS, you must “clamp” the ends by repeating the first and last knot values with multiplicity equal to the polynomial degree.  
• If the user supplies no GAXN records at all, SOFiMSHC assumes a uniform knot vector (i.e., equally spaced, simple knots).  
• Related record types include GAX (geometry axis definition), GAXA (axis attributes), GAXH (axis history), GAXC (construction parameters), GAXP (parameter sets), GAXS (splines), and GAXV (vertex lists). Together they form the complete axis‐based geometric description.

sections: 4.7 GAXN – Knot value of a NURBS-curve

content:
See also: GAX, GAXA, GAXH, GAXC, GAXP, GAXS, GAXV
 GAXN
 Records of type GAXN are used to define the knot vector of NURBS-curves or to explicitly set the parametrization of interpolation curves. For each knot value of a NURBS or parameter value a single record GAXN is to be entered which refers to the previously defined geometry axis at GAX. Multiple knot-values (e.g. at the ends of a curve) can be entered in a single record using multiplicities > 1. Within the first record the polynomial degree of a NURBS-curve can be set using parameter DEGR.
 When NURBS-curves are defined in SOFiMSHC knot vectors must always be given with mul- tiple knots at the ends (”clamped ends”) with a multiplicity equal to the degree of the curve. In the case that no knot-vector is given by the user at all, a uniform distribution is assumed internally.
