content:
Below is a detailed breakdown of the GAXP input-table that defines “placements” along a primary geometry axis (GAX) (see also GAX, GAXS, GAXV). Each row in the table corresponds to one placement and the four columns are “Item” (parameter name), “Description,” “Unit” and “Default.”  

1. ID  
   • Description: Identifier for the primary axis on which this placement lies.  
   • Unit: Lit4 (4-character literal)  
   • Default: – (must be supplied)  

2. IDS  
   • Description: Selects which secondary axes (if any) also receive this placement.  
   • Allowed values:  
     – “0” for primary axis only  
     – “A” … “Z” for individual secondary lines  
     – “*” for all axes (primary + all secondaries)  
     – “+” for secondary axes only  
   • Unit: LIT (general literal)  
   • Default: “*”  

3. S  
   • Description: Station value along the axis (chainage or coordinate). You may also supply a variable name here; GAXP will then insert placements at each base-point of that variable.  
   • Unit: – / Lit (numeric or literal)  
   • Default: ! (required)  

4. TYPE  
   • Description: One or more classification flags for the placement. Combine any of:  
     – ‘S’ support  
     – ‘J’ construction joint  
     – ‘A’ start face  
     – ‘E’ end face  
     – ‘H’ horizontal connection  
   • Note: For clarity wrap multi-character literals in apostrophes (e.g. ’SJ’).  
   • Unit: Lit8 (up to 8 characters)  
   • Default: –  

5. SPT  
   • Description: Node number of the structural point created at this placement. If omitted, SOFiMSHC auto-assigns numbers starting at 1000 (step 100).  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: –  

6. GRP  
   • Description: Group number applied to all subsequent beam elements until changed.  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: 0  

7. NCS  
   • Description: Cross-section number for the beam element immediately after (and/or before) the placement. You can specify “ncs1.ncs2” to set one number before and another after.  
   • Unit: – / Lit  
   • Default: 0  

8. IDP  
   • Description: Unique identifier for this placement. Allows later reference in other records (e.g. COOR).  
   • Unit: Lit4  
   • Default: –  

9. Y  
   • Description: Explicit local-y (transverse) offset for the infinite placement plane.  
   • Unit: m  
   • Default: 0.0  

10. Z  
    • Description: Explicit local-z (vertical) offset.  
    • Unit: m  
    • Default: 0.0  

11. ALF  
    • Description: Rotation about the global Z-axis (alignment angle in plan). Values 1–360°.  
    • Unit: deg  
    • Default: –  

12. ALFX / ALFY / ALFZ  
    • Description: Rotation (skew) of the placement plane about the local x-, y- and z-axes respectively.  
    • Unit: deg  
    • Default: 0.0 / 0.0 / 0.0  

13. INCR / INCL  
    • Description: Cross-fall (camber/superelevation) of the plane.  
      – INCR: slope to the right (+Y)  
      – INCL: slope to the left (–Y)  
    • Note: INCL defaults to negative of INCR.  
    • Unit: –  
    • Default: 0.0 / –INCR  

14. TITL  
    • Description: Free-text title or comment for the placement.  
    • Unit: Lit32 (up to 32 characters)  
    • Default: –  

Usage notes (from context text):  
- Placements define infinite planes perpendicular to the axis tangent; intersections with secondary axes generate structural points there.  
- For support (‘S’), start (‘A’) or endface (‘E’) placements, SOFiMSHC automatically fills an internal S_XI() array to parameterize spans.  
- Auto-numbering of SPT and GRP can be offset per secondary axis via GAXS to avoid clashes with user-defined numbers (recommend raising CTRL NODE start index above 1000).  
- #INCR and #INCL can also be used in expressions, but represent rotation angles in radians about the X-axis (0 = along +Y).

The illustration is a schematic showing how placements (GAXP) are defined on a primary geometry axis (GAX) and how a secondary axis (GAXS) runs relative to it.  A thick solid curve in the plane represents the primary axis “GAX,” along which three sample placement points S1, S2 and S3 are marked by small red disks.  A dashed curve running above and below the main curve is labeled “GAXS,” indicating a secondary or offset axis whose shape follows but does not coincide with the primary axis.  Below the drawing is the caption “Figure 4.4: Secondary axis relative to axis.”

1.  Placement S1  
- Location: On the rising portion of the main curve.  
- Label: “GAXP” printed directly beneath the red disk.  
- Station Marker: To the left of the disk a short vertical tick is labeled “S1.”  
- Local Plane Rotation: A small 2-axis icon is drawn next to the disk—two orthogonal lines one horizontal, one vertical—and an arc between them marked “ALF.”  This indicates that at station S1 an infinite plane (the GAXP placement) is created perpendicular to the tangent of GAX but then rotated about the local axis by an angle ALF in the global X–Y plane.

2.  Placement S2  
- Location: On the peak of the main curve, roughly central in the figure.  
- Label: “GAXP” again under the red disk.  
- Station Marker: A straight vertical line through the point is annotated “S2,” showing this station value is used to compute the relative position on GAX and GAXS.  
- Secondary Axis Intersection: The dashed GAXS curve crosses near this point, illustrating how a plane at S2 would intersect both axes.  
- Plane Rotation About Z: An arc off the disk is marked “ALFZ,” signifying that this placement plane may be rotated about the local Z-axis by the specified angle before generating structural points.

3.  Placement S3  
- Location: On a descending segment of the main curve to the right.  
- Label: “GAXP” under the red disk.  
- Station Marker: A short vertical tick labeled “S3.”  
- No explicit rotation arrow is shown here, implying this placement uses default orientation of its infinite plane perpendicular to the axis tangent.

Overall, the diagram conveys the following key points:  
• Each GAXP placement is an infinite plane at a station S on the primary axis, used to generate structural points and assign identifiers or section numbers.  
• Rotations ALF, ALFX, ALFY and ALFZ allow orienting that plane relative to local or global coordinates; here ALF (in-plane rotation) and ALFZ (rotation about the local Z-axis) are illustrated.  
• The secondary axis GAXS is a separate but related curve; when you define placements on GAX, the corresponding intersection with GAXS can be used to set up point and group numbering offsets for beam-element generation on secondary lines.  
• By marking S1, S2, S3 and pairing them with GAXP labels, the figure emphasizes how SOFiMSHC reads placement definitions (IDP, TYP, SPT, etc.) to build up the structural system along both primary and secondary axes.

The image is a simple, schematic side‐view used to illustrate how an “inclination” parameter (#INCL or ALFX) tilts a placement plane about the local X-axis in a structural-modeling environment. Visually, it consists of:  
   
· A thick, black polyline made up of three straight segments.  
  – The first segment (on the left) slopes upward toward the center. Above it, the text “–INCL” denotes that a negative inclination angle has been applied to tilt the plane in the positive Y–Z sense.  
  – At the midpoint of the polyline there is a sharp “peak” or vertex.  
  – From that peak, a second segment slopes downward on the right side, implying a reversal of the sign or the application of a positive inclination (though “+INCL” is not explicitly shown).  
   
· A single‐headed arrow is drawn adjacent to the right‐hand slope, pointing straight down. Immediately to the right of the arrow is the label “Z,” indicating the direction of the global Z‐axis (vertical axis) pointing downward on the page. This clarifies the sign‐convention for height: increasing Z is downward, so a negative inclination makes the plane rise toward the left.  
   
· Beneath the drawing, centered, is the figure caption in plain text: “Figure 4.5: Inclination.” This ties the graphic directly to the manual’s narrative on how inclination angles are defined and used.  
   
The background is blank white, with no gridlines or coordinate axes drawn; only the polyline and the single axis arrow appear. The line weight is uniform, giving the plane profile visual emphasis. The label “–INCL” is set in a simple, upright font, positioned just above the rising segment so as not to obscure the geometry. The downward Z arrow is a standard straight‐line arrow, drawn thinner than the polyline for contrast.  
   
In context, this illustration appears in section 4.5 of the SOFiMSHC user manual (in the discussion of GAXP placements). It demonstrates that the placement plane—originally perpendicular to the path tangent—can be rotated about the local X‐axis by specifying an inclination angle. The variable #INCL does not hold a slope value but rather the “clockwise angle in radians about the X‐axis,” measured from the Y-axis (0 rad pointing along +Y). The diagram makes clear how a negative angle (–INCL) produces an upward slope segment when projected on the Y–Z plane, and how changing the sign reverses the slope. Engineers and modelers refer to this figure when assigning cross-fall or edge directions within sections, ensuring consistent use of sign conventions across main and secondary axes.

See also: GAX, GAXS, GAXV
 GAXP
 GAXP is used to define important sections and points, so called placements, along a geometry axis GAX at a specific station S. A placement can be defined exclusively for the main axis or for one of the secondary lines, but can also be assigned to all or all secondary lines simultane-
 ously. A combination of literals (e.g. ’SJ’) can be set at TYP for classification of the placement. In order to avoid ambiguous input it is recommended to enclose the literals in apostrophes.
 Each Placement can be assigned a uniqe identificator at IDP, which allows to reference the placement in a later calculation step (see e.g. Record COOR).
 Based on the placement definitions SOFiMSHC can create a structural system consisting of beam elements along the axis. For each placement a structural point will be created on the axis whose node number can be set at SPT. In between structural lines will be created, which get the number of their preceding point assigned. The user may specify a group or section number for a specific placement on the axis which are then used for all subsequent beam elements created unless one of the number is changed. The generation of the structural elements basically starts at the first placement which has a cross-section number assigned and ends at the end of the axis or if a placement is of type ’E = endface’.
 In order to facilitate the organization of point and group numbers the user may define offset numbers at secondary axes GAXS which are then used to set the respective group and points numbers of the placements on secondary lines. If no point number is given at a specific place- ment, SOFiMSHC assignes a number automatically starting from SPT=1000 in intervals of 100 along the axis. In order to prevent unintended interference of user defined and automatic num- bers, it is recommended to set the start index of automatically assigned number in SOFiMSHC at parameter CTRL NODE from 1000 to a sufficiently higher value.

If no point number is given at a specific place- ment, SOFiMSHC assignes a number automatically starting from SPT=1000 in intervals of 100 along the axis. In order to prevent unintended interference of user defined and automatic num- bers, it is recommended to set the start index of automatically assigned number in SOFiMSHC at parameter CTRL NODE from 1000 to a sufficiently higher value..
 A placement basically defines an infinite plane at a given station S perpendicular to the axis tangent. Structural points and other placement properties on secondary axes will then be created at the intersection of this plane with the axis. This infinite plane can be further rotated about the three local axis coordinates by setting ALFZ, ALFY and ALFX or may be aligned within the global X-Y coordinate plane by setting an angle at ALF = { 1-360 deg} . When
 placements of type support, start or endface (Type ’S’, ’A’ and ’E’) are defined, an internal variable array S_XI() is automatically set up which provides the curve parameter S with respect to span lengths between supports. For example, S_XI(0) provides the S-parameter of the start face, S_XI(1) the location of the first support, S_XI(1.5) the mid of the first span and so on.
 Instead of the station value S the user may also enter the name of a variable. In this case placements of the given type will be created for each base-point of the variable.
 Further we have two values for the cross fall. The sign of the inclination is defined that an increase of height in the direction outward is positive,
 For using the inclination two variables #INCR and #INCL may be used (e.g. for a direction of an edge within a section). However, this variable contains not the tangent value, but the clockwise angle in radians about the X-axis defined by the inclination. The value of 0 is the direction of the Y-axis to the right.

The table below defines the keywords and parameters you use when issuing a GAXS command to place a secondary axis in relation to a primary axis.  In the context of RAG’s vector‐store representation, each row corresponds to one argument you can supply to GAXS.  The four columns of the table are:

• Item: the keyword you specify in the input stream  
• Description: a short human-readable definition of what the keyword controls  
• Unit: the data type or physical unit you must supply  
• Default: the value assumed if you omit the keyword

Detailed breakdown:

1. ID  
   - Description: Identifies the primary axis to which you are adding a secondary axis.  
   - Unit: Lit4 (a 4-character literal)  
   - Default: “*” (an asterisk)  
   - Notes: This is mandatory: it anchors GAXS to an existing primary axis in your model.

2. IDS  
   - Description: The identifier of the secondary axis itself. Valid values range from “A” to “Z.”  
   - Unit: LIT (an arbitrary text literal)  
   - Default: 0  
   - Notes: If you do not explicitly name the new axis, the system uses “0” as a placeholder.

3. SPT  
   - Description: An integer offset applied to structural point numbers when you later reference points via GAXP.  
   - Unit: none (plain integer)  
   - Default: 1  
   - Notes: Useful if you want to avoid collisions with existing point IDs in your model.

4. GRP  
   - Description: An integer offset applied to group numbers used by subsequent GAXP placements.  
   - Unit: none (plain integer)  
   - Default: 0  
   - Notes: Offsetting group numbers can help you segregate the elements placed on this secondary axis from other groups.

5. Y  
   - Description: Lateral offset in the local‐y direction (transverse to the primary axis).  
   - Unit: m (meters) or Lit16 (up to 16‐character literal)  
   - Default: 0.0  
   - Notes: Specifies how far, and in which direction, the secondary axis is shifted sideways.

6. Z  
   - Description: Vertical offset in the local‐z direction (perpendicular to the primary axis and local‐y plane).  
   - Unit: m (meters) or Lit16  
   - Default: 0.0  
   - Notes: Defines the elevation difference between the secondary and primary axes.

7. TITL  
   - Description: A free-form text string naming the continuous beam or structural element associated with this axis.  
   - Unit: Lit32 (up to 32 characters)  
   - Default: “–” (dash, meaning no title)  
   - Notes: Helpful for documentation and cross-referencing in complex frame or bridge models.

Contextual remarks:  
- GAXS allows you to position a secondary axis at a fixed (constant) offset or, in combination with GAXV, to tie that offset to a varying axis parameter (for example, varying y‐ or z‐coordinates along the primary axis).  
- When you combine GAXS with GAXP, the SPT and GRP offsets ensure that all newly placed points and groups are numbered in a block distinct from those of the primary axis.  
- For further information on related commands, see GAX (defines the primary axis), GAXV (defines an axis variable for variable offsets), and GAXP (places points along axes).

See also: GAX, GAXP, GAXV
 GAXS
 GAXS defines a secondary axis relatively to a primary axis. The distance may be defined either by a constant value in local y- and z-direction or dependend on a axis variable specified with GAXV.
 It is further possible to specify an offset for point and group numbers used in GAXP place- ments.

The table shown is the record‐definition for the GAXV keyword in SOFiMSHC.  GAXV is used to define one of potentially many “additional variables” along a geometry axis (AX1, AX2, …) – for example to describe changing cross‐sections, side axes, or other secondary characteristics.  Each GAXV record (or “base point”) specifies where along the axis (station S) a variable takes a certain value V, optionally with a specified derivative DV, and how these points are to be joined or interpolated.

1.  Columns and Their Meaning  
   •  Item  
      – The field name within the GAXV record.  
   •  Description  
      – A brief English summary of the field’s role.  
   •  Unit  
      – The data type or literal size:  
        •  Lit4, Lit16, Lit20, Lit40: fixed‐length text fields of that many characters.  
        •  LIT: a small enumeration (i.e. a keyword set).  
   •  Default  
      – The default value assumed if the field is omitted.

2.  Row-by-row Breakdown  
   •  ID  
      – Id of axis (e.g. AX1).  
      – Unit: Lit4.  
      – Default: ‘*’ (means “apply to all axes” if you omit a specific ID).  
   •  NAME  
      – Name of the variable (up to 16 characters). This identifies which auxiliary variable you are defining (e.g. VAR2).  
      – Unit: Lit16.  
      – Default: ‘!’ (a placeholder indicating “no name assigned”).  
   •  S  
      – The station (position) along the axis where this base point applies. Can be a literal value or a formula.  
      – Unit: Lit20.  
      – Default: 0.0 (start of axis).  
   •  V  
      – The variable’s value (height, width, offset, etc.) at station S. Can also be a formula expression in apostrophes (see FUNC below).  
      – Unit: Lit40.  
      – Default: 0.0.  
   •  DV  
      – The derivative (slope/tangent) of the variable at station S. Used to control inclination of the connecting segment. Also a Lit40 field for formulas.  
      – Default: 0.0.  
   •  TYPE  
      – How this point should be interpreted in the interpolation. Unit: LIT (one of the keywords below).  
      – Default: POLY.

3.  TYPE Sub-Keywords  
   These determine whether the point contributes only a value, or also defines tangents for the curve connecting to its neighbors.  
   •  POLY  
      – Value only; straight‐line segments between points.  
   •  D–  
      – Sets the incoming (left) tangent only. The derivative DV applies on approach.  
   •  D+  
      – Sets the outgoing (right) tangent only.  
   •  D*  
      – Sets both incoming and outgoing tangents to the same DV value.  
   •  SPLI  
      – Marks an intermediate spline point or requests an automatically computed tangent.  
        – If every point in the set is SPLI, SOFiMSHC fits a single global C2‐continuous cubic spline with natural end conditions.  
        – If only some points are SPLI, then only those points receive interpolated C1‐continuous tangents from their neighbors.  
   •  FUNC  
      – Indicates that V (and/or DV) is given by an arbitrary formula expression. Formulas must be enclosed in apostrophes and begin with “=”.  
        – The special variable #S_ACT holds the current station and must be defined via a LET statement before it is used.  
        – A FUNC record’s formula applies from its station S up to the next GAXV record (or end of axis).

4.  Example Summaries (from the surrounding text)  
   – Defining a simple quadratic parabola via three explicit points with D* on the middle station yields a horizontal tangent at S=25.  
   – The same parabola can be defined in one FUNC record:  
     LET#S_ACT 0  
     GAXV AX1 VAR2 S 0 V ’=#S_ACT*(#S_ACT–50)/62.5+3’ TYPE FUNC  

5.  Cross-References  
   – See also: GAX (axis definition), GAXP (points on axis), GAXS (stations along axis). These keywords work together to build up full geometric descriptions in SOFiMSHC.

See also: GAX, GAXP, GAXS
 GAXV
 In SOFiMSHC an arbitrary number of additional variables can be defined along a geometry axis, which can be used, for example, to define varying cross sections or to describe the shape of a secondary axis. A variable distribution can be either defined by a number of base points and tangent directions which are interpolated or directly by entering a formula expression at V.
 * SPLI: If all data points are labeled with SPLI, a C2-continuous, global, cubic spline interpo- lation with natural boundary conditions is computed. If only individual data points are marked with SPLI, the corresponding tangent is interpolated locally from the slopes on the left and right (C1-continuous).
 Following example shows the definition of a quadratic parabola by three base points. The point in the middle is assigned a horizontal tangent and the type ’D*’, which ensures that both sections on the left and the right hand side of the point are connected horizontally:
 GAXV AX1 NAME VAR2 S 0.0 V +3.0 GAXV AX1 NAME VAR2 S 25.0 V -7.0 DV 0.0 TYPE D* GAXV AX1 NAME VAR2 S 50.0 V +3.0
 The same result could also be obtained by entering one single formula expression:
 LET#S_ACT 0
 LET#S_ACT @
 GAXV AX1 VAR2 S 0 V '=#S_ACT*(#S_ACT-50)/62.5+3' TYPE FUNC
 It is important to note, that the formula expression, which is to be evaluated dynamically, has to be specified within apostrophes and with a leading ’=’. The expression is valid from the start-
 parameter given at S (here: S=0.0) until the next base point of the variable or, if no additional record GAXV is given, until the end of the axis. The control variable must always be named by #S_ACT and must also be defined prior to its first usage.

The table under review specifies the fields and parameters that make up a “GAR” record—i.e. a raw geometric surface definition—in the data schema.  It is organized into four columns:  

• Item  
  – The mnemonic name of the field or parameter in the GAR record.  
• Description  
  – A brief plain-language explanation of what the field represents and, where applicable, the set of allowable values.  
• Unit  
  – The data type or format expected (e.g. Lit4, LIT, Lit32).  
• Default  
  – The default value or symbol used when the field is omitted.  

Below is a walk-through of each row and its subentries:

1. NO  
   • Description: “Area identifier.” This is the primary index or key for the surface record.  
   • Unit: Lit4 (i.e. a 4-character literal).  
   • Default: “!” (an exclamation mark indicates that this parameter is mandatory and must be provided).

2. TYPE  
   • Description: “Type of area.” This selects how the raw surface is to be constructed.  Several mutually exclusive keywords are allowed:  
     – DEL  
       · Meaning: Deletes (or flags for deletion) the existing record denoted by NO.  
     – Ruled surface types  
       · PLAN: Planar surface (flat).  
       · ROTA: Surface of revolution (profile spun around an axis).  
       · SWEE: Sweep surface (profile swept along a path).  
     – Coons Patches  
       · BLIN: Bilinear Coons patch (four-edge blending).  
       · COON: Bicubic Coons patch (higher-order edge interpolation).  
     – Freeform surfaces  
       · SPLI: Bi-cubic spline interpolation of a grid of points.  
       · NURB: Non-uniform rational B-spline, defined by control points and weights.  
   • Unit: LIT (i.e. an alphanumeric literal).  
   • Default: “*” (asterisk indicates that if TYPE is omitted, the system will apply its own default, which in many implementations is ROTA for GARA or BLIN for GARC, but for the generic GAR record the asterisk simply denotes optionality).

3. DEGU  
   • Description: “Degree of NURB in u direction.”  
   • Unit: “–” (not explicitly a character literal; numerics are implied).  
   • Default: “*” (if you do not specify, the system chooses a suitable polynomial degree).

4. DEGV  
   • Description: “Degree of NURB in v direction.”  
   • Unit: “–”.  
   • Default: “*” (same behavior as DEGU).

5. TITL  
   • Description: “Designation” – a free-format name or label for the surface.  
   • Unit: Lit32 (up to 32 alphanumeric characters).  
   • Default: “–” (no default; if omitted, the surface simply has no user-defined name).  

Contextual relationship to GARA, GARC, GARS:  
• This GAR record does not itself specify the detailed curves or point-grids used to build the surface. Instead, it points to one of three subordinate record types—GARA (rotational/sweep), GARC (Coons), or GARS (freeform/NURBS)—to supply the full geometry.  
• GARA and GARC allow exactly one downstream definition each. GARS may appear multiple times to accumulate control-point grids or blend patches.  
• Parameter TYPE in GAR determines which subordinate record type the parser expects next (e.g. if TYPE = SPLI, the parser looks for GARS entries).  

In sum, this table is the master template for declaring a background geometry surface in the schema, controlling how the system should interpret, generate, or delete that surface and how it links to more detailed geometric definitions.

See also: GARA, GARC, GARS
 GAR
 TITL
 Designation
 -
 This record GAR defines a raw geometric surface without any structural information. This surface can then be referenced as ’background geometry’ by a structural area SAR or can be used to create an intersection curve with another surface, for example.
 The type of the geometry to be created can be set at parameter TYPE. The geometry itself is then defined using one of the following records:
 • GARA: Definition of rotational and sweep-surfaces (default: ROTA)
 • GARC: Definition of so-called Coons Surfaces (default: BLIN)
 • GARS: Definition of a freeform surface using interpolation points or NURBS control points (default: SPLI)
 The geometry definition records must be given directly after the record GAR. For the records GARA and GARC, only one succeding entry is allowed. For the record GARS any number of items can be given.

Below is a field-by-field breakdown of the input table (“GARA” record) together with its semantics in the context of defining planar, rotational or sweep surfaces.  Use this description to populate a RAG vector store or other metadata repository.

1.  General Structure  
    •  Columns  
       –  Item:    the field name (identifier)  
       –  Description: brief human-readable label  
       –  Unit:    measurement unit or data type  
       –  Default: default value if the field is omitted  
    •  Usage modes  
       a) Planar surface  
       b) Surface of revolution  
       c) Sweep (extrusion or trajectory sweep)

2.  Fields

1.  GID1  
    –  Description: Identifier of the first generating axis  
    –  Type: Lit4 (4-character literal)  
    –  Default: none (mandatory when defining curve-based surfaces)  
    –  Notes:  
       •  Revolution: GID1 references the profile curve to be rotated.  
       •  Sweep: GID1 is the generating curve to be swept.

2.  GID2  
    –  Description: Identifier of the second generating axis  
    –  Type: Lit4  
    –  Default: none (only used for sweep along a trajectory curve)  
    –  Notes:  
       •  Sweep mode: GID2 references the trajectory curve.  
       •  Revolution and plane: GID2 is not used and should be blank.

3.  X, Y, Z  
    –  Description: Reference point in 3-D space  
    –  Unit: [m] (as per UoM code 1001)  
    –  Default: 0.0, 0.0, 0.0  
    –  Notes:  
       •  Plane: any known point on the plane.  
       •  Revolution: one point on the rotation axis.  
       •  Sweep by vector: start point of the sweep.

4.  NX, NY, NZ  
    –  Description: Direction or normal vector components  
    –  Unit: unitless (vector direction only)  
    –  Default: none (marked “*” meaning user-supplied)  
    –  Notes:  
       •  Plane: defines plane normal.  
       •  Revolution: defines axis direction.  
       •  Sweep via vector: defines extrusion direction.

5.  UMIN, UMAX  
    –  Description: Start/end parameter on generating axis GID1  
    –  Unit: unitless (parameter space of curve)  
    –  Default: “*” (if omitted, the full curve GID1 is used)  
    –  Notes:  
       •  Revolution: limits meridian curve segment to rotate.  
       •  Sweep: limits portion of the profile to extrude/sweep.

6.  VMIN, VMAX  
    –  Description:  
         VMIN = start angle or start translation  
         VMAX = end angle or end translation  
    –  Unit: unitless  
    –  Default:  
         •  VMIN default = 0 (for rotation, starts at 0°)  
         •  VMAX default = “*” (if omitted, default depends on mode)  
    –  Notes:  
       a) Revolution:  
          –  VMIN/VMAX interpreted as rotation angles in degrees.  
          –  If both are omitted: default 0° to +180°.  
          –  Advice: never define a full 360° in one go—split into two 180° shells.  
       b) Sweep:  
          –  When sweeping along a trajectory curve (GID2), VMIN/VMAX are parameters on GID2.  
          –  When sweeping by vector, VMIN/VMAX give the distance extruded.

7.  TITL  
    –  Description: Designation (user-provided name)  
    –  Type: Lit32 (up to 32 characters)  
    –  Default: none  

8.  (Optional) LAN  
    –  Description: Language indicator for textual fields  
    –  Type: Lit3  
    –  Default: 1 (usually “1” = default language)  

3.  Cross-references  
    •  See also GAR (planar surfaces only) and GAX (axis reference)  
    •  Together, GAR, GARA and GAX cover all planar, revolute and sweep definitions in the schema.

4.  Implementation Tips  
    –  Always supply at least one non-zero direction vector (NX,NY,NZ).  
    –  Use UMIN/UMAX sparingly to carve out subsections of complex curves.  
    –  For full revolutions, split into two half-shells (0→+180 and 0→−180).  
    –  Default plane spans ±100 m in U,V if UMIN/VMAX are omitted (internal fallback).

sections: 4.12 GARA – Plane, rotational and sweep surfaces

content:
See also: GAR, GAX
 GARA
 Using this record GARA planar, rotational or sweep-surfaces can be defined:
 A plane is defined by a point in space (X,Y,Z) and a normal vector (NX,NY,NZ). In order to avoid numerical problems, the dimensions of the plane should be restricted to the requred extensions using the parameters UMIN to VMAX. If no sizes are specified, a default size of -100 to +100m is set in both directions.
 A geometric curve GID1 is rotated about a straight axis in space. The rotation axis is defined by a point at X,Y,Z and a directionvector at NX,NY,NZ.
 The parameters UMIN and UMAX define the extends of the surface in meridian direction along the generating curve GID1. If nothing is given, the whole curve GID1 is taken. The extend of the rotation angle in degree is defined using the paramters VMIN and VMAX. If nothing is given, the parameters default to an angle from 0 to 180 degree.
 Important: In order to avoid ambiguity in numerical operations, surfaces of revolution should never be defined as closed surface with a rotation angle from eg. 0 to 360 degree. In these cases it is recommended to create two halfshells with angles from 0 to 180 degree and 0 to -180 degree respectively.
 A curve GID1 is swept along a so called trajectory curve GID2. Instead of the trajectory curve, a direction vector can be given at NX,NY,NZ along which the generating curve GID1 is moved. The parameters UMIN and UMAX define the extend of the surface along the generating axis GID1. If nothing is given here, the whole curve is used.
 The parameters VMIN and VMAX define the range on the trajectory axes or the length on the directon vector respectively.

The table below enumerates the complete set of input parameters required by the GARC (Generalized Area by Ruled–Coons curves) command.  GARC uses these inputs to construct a surface patch bounded by four curves.  Depending on whether a bilinear (BLIN) or bicubic (COON) blending scheme is chosen, the patch will exhibit either C0 or C1 continuity.  In the bicubic (Coons) case, the “twist” values (mixed partial derivatives at the corners) become essential.

Columns  
• Item – the parameter name used in the GARC record.  
• Description – a brief English description of what the parameter represents.  
• Unit – the data type or code expected for that field.  
• Default – the value assumed if the user does not supply one.

Rows  

1.  NU0  
 • Description: Axis for Coons patch at constant u = 0.0  
 • Unit: lit4 (a four‐character literal specifying the boundary curve)  
 • Default: “!” (mandatory field; the user must supply a curve ID)  

2.  NU1  
 • Description: Axis for Coons patch at constant u = 1.0  
 • Unit: lit4  
 • Default: “!” (mandatory)  

3.  NV0  
 • Description: Axis for Coons patch at constant v = 0.0  
 • Unit: lit4  
 • Default: “!” (mandatory)  

4.  NV1  
 • Description: Axis for Coons patch at constant v = 1.0  
 • Unit: lit4  
 • Default: “–” (optional; if omitted, some systems may assume a degenerate or flattened boundary)  

The four “axis” entries (NU0, NU1, NV0, NV1) define the four bounding curves of the patch.  They may be longer than the actual patch region so long as their intersection points at the corners can be unambiguously determined.

Twist parameters: To achieve C1 continuity with a bicubic Coons patch, GARC needs the twist (mixed second derivative ∂²X/∂u∂v, ∂²Y/∂u∂v, ∂²Z/∂u∂v) at each of the patch’s four corners.  If these are omitted, the corner twists default to zero, yielding a “flat” corner behavior.

For corner i (i = 1…4), the following three fields appear:  
• XUVi – the X-component of the twist vector at corner i  
• YUVi – the Y-component of the twist vector at corner i  
• ZUVi – the Z-component of the twist vector at corner i  

Unit for XUVi, YUVi, ZUVi is “*” (floating-point value), and the default for each is 0.0.  In practice, specifying nonzero twist values gives the designer control over how sharply or smoothly the patch bends at each corner.

Summary of twist entries by corner:  
– Corner 1: XUV1, YUV1, ZUV1 (default 0.0 each)  
– Corner 2: XUV2, YUV2, ZUV2 (default 0.0 each)  
– Corner 3: XUV3, YUV3, ZUV3 (default 0.0 each)  
– Corner 4: XUV4, YUV4, ZUV4 (default 0.0 each)  

Together, the four boundary‐curve references plus the sixteen twist components fully specify a Coons patch under GARC.  When only the four curves are given (and no twist values), the system falls back on the bilinear BLIN scheme (C0 continuity) or produces a Coons patch with “flattened” corners if COON is forced but twists are absent.

The figure is a schematic top-view sketch of a four-boundary Coons (or GARC) surface patch. It shows four planar curve segments—two “horizontal” rails and two “vertical” rails—that enclose a roughly quadrilateral domain. Each boundary curve is labeled both by its geometric role (NU0, NU1 for the left and right rails; NV0, NV1 for the bottom and top rails) and by its parametric coordinate value (u = 0.0, u = 1.0 on the vertical rails; v = 0.0, v = 1.0 on the horizontal rails). Wherever each pair of curves intersects marks one of the four patch corners.

Description of individual curves and annotations:  
• Top boundary (NV1, v = 1.0): This is drawn as a slightly undulating, gently convex curve running left to right. Its labeling “v = 1.0” sits directly above it in plain text, and “NV1” is printed beneath the curve, centered horizontally.  
• Bottom boundary (NV0, v = 0.0): A second smooth curve runs approximately parallel to the top curve but with a small positive slope from left to right. The arrowhead next to it points roughly upwards (indicating the positive v–direction), and the text “v = 0.0” is placed just above that arrow. “NV0” appears just below the curve.  
• Left boundary (NU0, u = 0.0): This curve starts near the top left, arches downwards and to the right, then curls back up slightly. It is labeled “NU0” to its right and “u = 0.0” with an arrow indicating the positive u–direction. The arrow tail lies just outside the curve, pointing upward and to the right (toward increasing u).  
• Right boundary (NU1, u = 1.0): A contrasting, more steeply curved segment descends from near the top center of the figure down toward the bottom. Its convexity bowing leftward gives it a distinctive S-shape. Immediately beside it is the text “NU1” and to its right is “u = 1.0.”

Corner intersections:  
• Upper-left corner is where NV1 meets NU0.  
• Upper-right corner is where NV1 meets NU1.  
• Lower-left corner is where NV0 meets NU0.  
• Lower-right corner is where NV0 meets NU1.

In the caption below the sketch, the author refers to this arrangement as “Definition of a Coons surface between four boundary curves.” The overhang of each curve beyond the patch’s nominal corners is deliberate: it emphasizes that the curves need not be trimmed exactly to the patch boundaries, as long as their intersection points can be computed.  

Contextual notes (from the accompanying text):  
- When using a bilinear blending (BLIN), the patch attains only C⁰ continuity at the boundaries.  
- For full bicubic Coons interpolation (COON), C¹ continuity is required. That demands not only the four boundary curves with proper local tangential directions (the little arrows for u and v) but also four “twist” derivatives at the corners.  
- Because the twist values can’t be inferred from the curves themselves, users must supply them explicitly. Absent user-provided twists, each corner will flatten out.  

Overall, the diagram cleanly visualizes the parametric setup (u, v ∈ [0,1]) of a generalized Coons/GARC patch, illustrating how the pairwise interpolation along u and v between the opposite boundary curves defines the interior surface.

See also: GAR
 GARC
 GARC defines an area by four boundary curves, where an interpolation between opposite curves will take place. This may yield a C0-continuity with a bilinear BLIN or a C1-continuity with a bicubic blending function COON. For the latter we need not only properly defined local y-coordinate directions of the curves, but also the twist values at the corners of the patch. As the twist values are not derivable from the curves itself, the user may specify them explicitly. If not defined, the area will become flat at the corners. The curves may be longer than the patch region as long as the intersections may be calculated properly.

The source table defines the six data items that make up a single record for specifying either (a) a control‐point grid on a freeform surface or (b) knot definitions when only one parametric direction is being specified.  It is normally used in conjunction with the GAR/GARS records to build a full NURBS or general freeform surface.  The table columns are:

 • Item  
 • Description  
 • Unit  
 • Default  

Below is a field‐by‐field breakdown:

1.  M  
    • Description: “Raster (1–max) in local u direction.”  
      – Specifies the number of entries (grid lines or knot definitions) along the surface’s u parameter.  
      – When generating a full M×N control‐point grid, M is the number of rows (or lines) in u.  
      – When only defining knots for u, M is the count of (value, multiplicity) pairs given for the u direction.  
    • Unit: none (—)  
    • Default: “*” (asterisk)  
      – The asterisk indicates that M has no built‐in numeric default; it must be provided by the user.

2.  N  
    • Description: “Raster (1–max) in local v direction.”  
      – Analogous to M, but counts entries along the surface’s v parameter.  
      – If defining the full grid, N is the number of columns (or lines) in v.  
      – If defining knots only in v, N is the number of (value, multiplicity) pairs for the v direction.  
    • Unit: none (—)  
    • Default: “*”  
      – Must be supplied explicitly; no predefined value.

3.  X  
    • Description: “Point coordinates.”  
      – Represents the X‐coordinate of a control point or the value of a knot in one direction.  
      – In full grid mode, this is the Cartesian X coordinate of the point.  
      – In knot mode, it is the knot value along the u or v axis.  
    • Unit: m (meters)  
    • Default: 0.0  

4.  Y  
    • Description: “Point coordinates.”  
      – The Y‐coordinate of a control point, or the knot value in the complementary direction.  
    • Unit: m (meters)  
    • Default: 0.0  

5.  Z  
    • Description: “Point coordinates.”  
      – The Z‐coordinate of the control point in 3D space.  
      – Not used when specifying knot vectors (for knot mode, only X or Y is used depending on direction).  
    • Unit: m (meters)  
    • Default: 0.0  

6.  W  
    • Description: “Weight for NURBS.”  
      – Defines the rational weight of each control point in a NURBS surface.  
      – A weight different from 1.0 skews the influence of that point on the final surface.  
      – In knot mode, W represents the knot multiplicity at the given parametric coordinate.  
    • Unit: none (—)  
    • Default: 1.0  

Usage notes and context:  
- When populating a full freeform surface grid, the record must be repeated M × N times in row‐major order. Each repetition provides one (X, Y, Z, W) tuple.  
- For knot‐vector specification (e.g., to refine or override default knot placement), you may supply only M (for u knots) or only N (for v knots). In that case, each record entry corresponds to one knot: X is the knot value, W its multiplicity, and missing fields (Y, Z) are ignored or interpolated.  
- Any omitted coordinate or weight field (other than M and N) defaults to the values shown in the table; missing knot values will be generated by interpolation.  
- Consult the GAR and GARS definitions for how these records integrate into larger spline definitions and for examples of parameter ordering.

See also: GAR
 GARS
 This record defines points on the surface or NURBS control points of a general freeform sur- face. The points must be given in a regular a m times n grid.
 Knots of a general NURBS-surface are also defined with this record in that way that only M or N is defined, then we have:
 Definition of number M, value X and multiplicity W for the u direction, definition of number N, value Y and multiplicity W for the v direction. Missing values will be interpolated.

This chapter describes the definition of structural elements. Structural elements define the calculation system and contain a geometrical description as well as structural information like cross-sections, material or support conditions which are needed to set up the calculation model. SOFiMSHC supports structural points, structural lines, structural areas and structural volumes. The structural model can then be meshed to create a finite element model consisting of beam, shell and/or volume elements.

The table before us is organized into two principal columns – “Record” and “Items” – and defines a family of record‐types used in a larger data schema (for example, a finite‐element model or a CAD/CAE interchange format). Each “Record” label (e.g. SPT, SPTP, SPTS, etc.) stands for a particular entity or construct in the data model, and the corresponding “Items” listing enumerates all the attributes or subfields associated with that record. Below is a structured walk-through of its contents, highlighting patterns and likely semantics of the various fields:

1. Top-Level Spatial (“SPT*”) Records  
   ­ SPT  
     • Core spatial point: NO (point ID), X, Y, Z coordinates  
     • References: REF, NREF (reference ID, non-reference ID)  
     • Constraints/flags: FIX (fixity code), XFLG (external flag), TITL (title or label)  
     • Auxiliary offsets: BX, BY, T, NX, NY, NZ, SX  
     • Secondary shifts: SY, SZ  

   ­ SPTP  
     • A “SPT” variant for point parameters: TYPE (type code), X, Y, REF (reference)  
     • Value slots: VAL, VALQ, VALM (primary, qualifier, modifier)  
     • Grouping: GRP, MNO  

   ­ SPTS  
     • Extended spatial section: NO, REF, TYPE  
     • Coordinate pairs/differences: CP, CQ, CM, DX, DY, DZ  
     • Group/Material: GRP, MNO  
     • Additional parameters: AR, PRE, GAP, CRAC (crack length?), YIEL (yield stress), MUE (shear modulus), COH (cohesion), DIL (dilation)  
     • Support conditions: NCS (numbered constraint set), L  
     • Shear-kn/normal-kn: PSKN, LSKN  
     • Mesh parameters: MXSK, MXPF  

   ­ SPTH  
     • Nodal cross-section data: NCS, L  
     • Plate skin data: PSKN, LSKN  
     • Maximum skin/pf thickness: MXSK, MXPF  

2. Nodal Line (“SLN*”) Records  
   ­ SLN  
     • Node connectivity: NO (node ID), NPA, NPE (node pair endpoints?)  
     • References: REF  
     • Fixity: FIX, SDIV, GRP  
     • Optional IDs: NP, KR (key reference), DRX, DRY, DRZ, DROT

The table shown is the parameter‐list for the “SPT” (Structural Point) record in SOFiMSHC.  It defines all of the input fields you can use to create or modify a structural point.  Below is a field‐by‐field description, together with units and default behaviour.  

1.  Identification and Coordinates  
   •  NO  
      –  Point number (integer).  
      –  Use a positive NO to create a new point or redefine an existing one.  
      –  Use a negative NO to modify an existing point without renumbering.  
      –  Default: “–” (no automatic assignment).  
   •  X, Y, Z  
      –  Cartesian coordinates of the point in its local system (meters).  
      –  If omitted, each defaults to 0.0.  
      –  In the absence of any REF‐option, these are interpreted in the global coordinate system.  

2.  Reference / Projection (REF, NREF, MREF)  
   •  REF (literal)  
      –  Selects how the new point is positioned or projected.  Allowed keywords:  
        •  PT, PCYL, PPOL  –  Euclidean, cylindrical or spherical coordinates relative to an existing point  
        •  AX, AXYZ, AXZX, AXXY  –  Project onto an axis or restrict to a principal plane  
        •  AR, ARYZ, ARZX, ARXY  –  Project onto a structural region or restrict to a principal plane  
        •  AXAX  –  Intersection of two axes  
        •  AXAR  –  Intersection of an axis and a region  
      –  No default—if omitted, the point is placed by absolute XYZ values.  
   •  NREF (— / Lit4)  
      –  Identifier of the primary reference entity (point, axis, line or region) used by REF.  
      –  Required whenever REF is specified.  
   •  MREF (— / Lit4)  
      –  Identifier of the secondary reference (only for REF=AXAX or AXAR).  

3.  Support / Mesh Parameters (FIX, BX, BY, T)  
   •  FIX (Lit16)  
      –  Support‐condition flags combining literals such as PX, PY, RZ, etc.  
      –  Prefix “L” or “G” forces local or global directions.  
      –  Use “->n” to couple kinematic constraints to node n.  
      –  No default—by default the node is free in all directions.  
   •  BX, BY ([m]1001)  
      –  Width of support or mesh in local x‐ or y‐direction (used when generating mesh elements).  
      –  No default (zero or unspecified width suppresses mesh thickness).  
   •  T ([mm]1010)  
      –  Plate thickness if the point lies inside a structural area (SAR).  
      –  No default.  

4.  Local Coordinate System Orientation (NX, NY, NZ, SX, SY, SZ)  
   •  NX, NY, NZ  
      –  Components of the local z‐axis unit vector.  
   •  SX, SY, SZ  
      –  Components of the local x‐axis unit vector.  
   –  If all six are omitted (default “*”), the point’s local axes are aligned with either:  
      •  The global axes (no REF)  
      •  The coordinate system of the reference axis or region (if REF used).  

5.  Superposition Control (XFLG)  
   •  XFLG (Lit)  
      –  Prevents the point from being automatically merged or constrained by other elements:  
        •  P  –  Don’t replace this point with another point at the same location.  
        •  L  –  Don’t allow this point to subdivide an existing structural line.  
        •  A  –  Don’t embed this point within a structural region.  
      –  These flags override the default superposition logic.  

See also SPTP (point properties such as mass or release definitions) and SPTS (point‐to‐surface or line‐to‐surface projections).

The table defines the fields of an SPTS record, which immediately follows a structural‐point definition and specifies additional geometric properties, kinematic constraints or coupling conditions.  It is organized in four columns—Item, Description, Unit and Default—and covers seven parameters:

1. TYPE  
   • Description: Specifies the kind of property or constraint applied at the structural point.  
     – SUPP: Periphery of a column‐head support in a slab.  
     – VOUT: Periphery of haunches or “voutes.”  
     – PNCH: Periphery of punching‐shear reinforcement.  
     – KPPX, KPPY, etc.: Literal keywords denoting coupling conditions (see coupling rules in section 2.6.2).  
   • Unit: Literal (LIT)  
   • Default: “!” (no default; must be supplied)

2. X, Y, Z  
   • Description: Local coordinate offsets or dimensions associated only with SUPP, VOUT or PNCH definitions.  For example, when TYPE=SUPP you use X and Y to define the rectangular column‐head footprint; Z can remain zero or set to a local offset if needed.  
   • Unit: metres [m] (unit code 1001)  
   • Default: 0.0 for X, Y and Z

3. REF  
   • Description: For coupling conditions (TYPE = KPPx etc.), REF holds the identifier (point number) of the structural point to which this one is coupled.  This field is ignored for support definitions (SUPP/VOUT/PNCH).  
   • Unit: not applicable (—)  
   • Default: blank (–)

4. VAL  
   • Description: The primary numeric value of the property.  In the case of SUPP or VOUT it generally represents thickness of plate or mesh‐macro depth; for coupling it may carry stiffness or multiplier values.  Example: plate thickness under column head.  
   • Unit: none specified (interpreted contextually—often [m])  
   • Default: 0.0

5. GRP  
   • Description: Optional group number.  This allows you to assign multiple SPTS records to different support sets or coupling groups.  Post‐processing logic can then apply them in batches.  
   • Unit: not applicable (—)  
   • Default: 0

Contextual notes (from SPT/SPTP specification):  
• Every SPTS record must immediately follow its parent structural‐point record.  
• Support definitions (SUPP, VOUT, PNCH) can generate mesh‐macros for slab supports, column heads or punching‐shear reinforcements when certain conditions are met—particularly that the support point is sufficiently distant from slab edges.  If a mesh macro cannot be generated, the point is meshed as a single node.  
• The orientation of supports or couplings is independent of the point’s local coordinate axes; you control direction via X, Y, Z offsets.  
• Slab‐support behavior can be tuned with the FIX type parameter (asterisks) together with CTRL PSUP:  
   – no star: monolithic support (use CTRL PSUP default)  
   – *     : increase thickness at centre (CTRL PSUP=1)  
   – **    : hinged or elastic support (CTRL PSUP=0)  
   – ***   : add kinematic constraints (special cases, CTRL PSUP=2 or 4)  
   – CTRL PSUP=−1 forces single‐node behavior regardless of geometry.

Precisely at the geometric center of the slab (where the two grid lines cross) is a solid black oval.
