The table summarizes all input parameters available on the “SPTS” record for defining individual spring (bedding) elements at a structural point in SOFiSTiK. Each row lists one field (“Item”), a brief description, its physical unit (if any), and its default value. Below is a detailed, structured description of every parameter:

1. Identification  
  • NO  
    – Spring number. Uniquely identifies the spring within the master structural point.  
    – Unit: –  
    – Default: none  
  • REF  
    – Number of a second structural point. When given, the spring connects the primary point to this reference point.  
    – Unit: –  
    – Default: none  

2. Type/Direction (TYPE; literal)  
  – Defines the principal (axial) direction of the spring. Value list LIT. Default = “C” (explicit or to-REF).  
  Sub-options:  
    • CX, CY, CZ  
      – Align spring to the local X, Y, or Z axis of the structural point’s local CS.  
    • CXX, CYY, CZZ  
      – Align to the global X, Y, or Z axis (ignoring local CS).  
    • C  
      – Use an explicit direction vector (DX, DY, DZ), or, if REF is given, use the vector from the primary to the reference point.  

3. Stiffness Parameters (per area)  
  • CP  
    – Axial (principal) stiffness, kN/m³ (stiffness per area). After scaling with AR, yields kN/m.  
    – Default: 0.0  
  • CQ  
    – Isotropic lateral stiffness in the plane normal to the axial direction, kN/m³ per area. Mechanically two orthogonal springs of equal stiffness.  
    – Default: 0.0  
  • CM  
    – Rotational stiffness about the spring axis, kNm/rad per area.  
    – Default: 0.0  

4. Explicit Direction Vector  
  • DX, DY, DZ  
    – Components of user-defined direction vector when TYPE = C.  
    – Unit: –  
    – Default: none  

5. Grouping and Material Reference  
  • GRP  
    – Group number to which the spring belongs. Enables collective assignment of non-linear laws or reporting.  
    – Unit: –  
    – Default: none  
  • MNO  
    – Reference number for a non-linear work-law (AQUA: SLFA) or a non-linear material (AQUA: NMAT). Priority: work-law over material; negative numbers force material.  
    – Unit: –  
    – Default: none  

6. Reference Area  
  • AR  
    – Reference area (m²) used to scale CP, CQ, CM and all per-area nonlinear parameters (CRAC, YIEL, COH). If omitted, AR = 1 m².  
    – Unit: m²  
    – Default: none  

7. Prestress and Gap  
  • PRE  
    – Prestress force or moment per area, kN/m². On initial rest position, the spring already exerts this axial force or torsional moment. (Lateral prestress CQ not supported.)  
    – Default: none  
  • GAP  
    – “Slip” gap in axial direction. No axial force transmits until deformation exceeds GAP.  
    – Unit: m  
    – Default: none  

8. Non-linear Parameters (per area)  
  • CRAC  
    – Failure (crack) load: tensile force or positive moment at which the spring fails (axial & lateral). Setting to zero yields immediate failure when tension is tried.  
    – Unit: kN/m²  
    – Default: none  
  • YIEL  
    – Yield load: beyond this load the spring deforms at constant force or moment.  
    – Unit: kN/m²  
    – Default: none  
  • MUE  
    – Friction coefficient for lateral spring. If given (together with optional COH), maximum lateral force = μ·Compression + C. If μ = COH = 0, lateral force transmits only under compression.  
    – Unit: –  
    – Default: none  
  • COH  
    – Cohesion (lateral spring) in kN/m². Used in friction law above.  
    – Default: none  
  • DIL  
    – Dilatation factor: lateral displacement produces an axial component.  
    – Unit: –  
    – Default: none  

Usage Notes:  
• If multiple orthogonal lateral stiffnesses are required, use multiple SPTS records or value lists on TYPE.  
• AR scaling ensures consistency between per-area definitions and point-support stiffness.  
• Non-linear effects activate automatically when any associated parameter (CRAC, YIEL, MUE, COH, DIL, or MNO) is non-zero.  
• Refer also to SPT (structural point definition) and SPRI (SOFiMSHA advanced spring) for complementary functionality.

See also: SPT
 SPTS
 This record defines beddings or spring elements on a structural point. For a given structural point SPT multiple subsequent records of type SPTS can be entered allowing to create an arbitrary number of springs, which, for example, can be assigned to different groups. Spring elements can be defined as beddings to a fixed support or relatively to another structural point.
 The stiffness of a spring element can be basically defined with three parameters: CA to CM. The first parameter CA describes an axial stiffness along the principal direction of the spring. The second parameter CQ describes a stiffness component acting in the whole plane per- pendicular to the axial direction. Mechanically, this stiffness corresponds to two identical axial
 springs lying orthogonal to each other within the plane. Since the direction of these springs inside the plane can be chosen arbitrarily, this component is also denoted as isotropic lateral spring stiffness. The third parameter CM describes the rotational stiffness about the principal spring axis.
 In SOFiSTiK, the stiffness of a spring is basically defined in the unit ’Stiffness / Area’ kN/m/m2 = kN/m3. For a spring at a point, as defined in this record, this stiffness is then scaled with the reference area given at AR:
 CP :=Cb · AR [kN/m = kN/m3 · m2]
 CQ :=Cq · AR
 If AR is not given, it defaults to 1.0m2. This means, the stiffness values given at CP and CQ are then equivalent to a standard stiffness at a singular point given in unit kN/m.
 The axial and lateral spring stiffness as well as the nonlinear parameters CRAC, YIEL and COH are given as bedding stiffness per area (e.g. kN/m/m2). These stiffness values will be scaled by the given reference area AR, resulting in a spring element with point support stiffness (kN/m). If nothing is given for AR the stiffness values will be directly taken as point stiffness value.

The axial and lateral spring stiffness as well as the nonlinear parameters CRAC, YIEL and COH are given as bedding stiffness per area (e.g. kN/m/m2). These stiffness values will be scaled by the given reference area AR, resulting in a spring element with point support stiffness (kN/m). If nothing is given for AR the stiffness values will be directly taken as point stiffness value..
 A spring can have a number and can be assigned to a group. If the identifier of a second structural point is given at REF the spring is created between the given and the referenced structural point.
 The direction of the spring can be defined as follows:
 • Along the local coordinate system of the structural point Each structural point contains a local coordinate system, which can be set explicitly at the structural point record SPT. By setting CX, CY, or CZ at parameter TYPE, the spring can be aligned to one of this local coordinate directions.
 • Along one of the global X,Y,Z - coordinate axes If CXX, CYY or CZZ is given at TYPE, the spring is oriented, indepenently of the structural point, toward one of the global X, Y, or Z-coordinate axes, respectively.
 • Along an explicitly given direction vector at DX, DY, DZ A spring can also be aligned arbi- trarily by setting a direction at DX, DY, DZ.
 • Distance between point and reference point For a spring, connecting the point with a refer- ence point, the direction to the reference point is taken as axial direction in the case, that no different settings have been given.
 In the case that no direction is given at all, the spring is aligned with the local z-axis of the structural point.
 Different stiffness values in lateral direction cannot be defined within one single record of type SPTP. However, multiple records can be given in order to create springs aligned perpendicular to each other. Using value lists, CADINP allows to handle this case efficiently. For example: SLNS TYPE CX,CY,CZ CP 1000.0, 2000.0, 3000.0 creates three orthogonal springs having each different stiffness values of 1000.0, 2000.0 and 3000.0, respectively.
 Using the parameter PRE, prestress can be activated within the spring. In its initial position
 at rest, the spring already exerts a force or a moment (if only CM is given) into or about its direction. Prestress for the lateral component CQ cannot be defined.

For example: SLNS TYPE CX,CY,CZ CP 1000.0, 2000.0, 3000.0 creates three orthogonal springs having each different stiffness values of 1000.0, 2000.0 and 3000.0, respectively.. Using the parameter PRE, prestress can be activated within the spring. In its initial position. at rest, the spring already exerts a force or a moment (if only CM is given) into or about its direction. Prestress for the lateral component CQ cannot be defined..
 At the parameters GAP, CRAC, YIEL, MUE, COH, DIL values like crack load, yield load or friction coefficients can be given in order to activate non-linear effects. Non-linear effects are activated when a non-zero value is provided, except for the failure load (CRAC), which can be set to zero:
 • Prestress: The failure and yield loads are shifted by the amount of the prestress.
 • Gap: The spring transmits forces along its axis only after its deformation has exceeded the gap.
 • Failure load: Upon reaching the failure load the spring fails in both the axial and the lateral direction. The failure load is always a tensile force or a positive moment.
 • Yield load: Upon reaching the yield load, the deformation component of the spring in- creases in its direction, without a corresponding increase of the spring force.
 • Friction coefficient: If a friction coefficient and/or a cohesion are input, the lateral spring can not sustain forces greater than:
 Frcton_coeƒƒ. · Compresse_ƒorce + Coheson
 For large tension forces or a failed axial spring (CRAC) the lateral force acts only if 0.0 has been input for both the friction coefficient and the cohesion.
 General non-linear effects can be activated by referencing an arbitrary work-law or a non- linear material at MNO. A non-linear work-law, which is described by a force-displacement or a moment-rotation curve, must be defined in advance in AQUA (AQUA: SLFA). On the other hand, also non-linear materials may be referenced (AQUA: NMAT) at MNO, from which the respective non-linear spring stiffness values are derived. If a work-law and a non-linear material are given with the same number in a project, the work-law takes precedence. This setting can be overwritten by entering a negative number in order to reference a material in this case. If a reference area is defined for the spring at AR, the work-law as well as the non-linear parameters derived from the material will be scaled accordingly.

If a work-law and a non-linear material are given with the same number in a project, the work-law takes precedence. This setting can be overwritten by entering a negative number in order to reference a material in this case. If a reference area is defined for the spring at AR, the work-law as well as the non-linear parameters derived from the material will be scaled accordingly..
 In the case that a dilatation value (DIL) is defined, a displacement in the lateral direction will generate a component in the axial direction.
 The record SPRI in program SOFiMSHA allows to create spring elements with advanced pos- sibilities. SOFiMSHA can be restarted on a database created by SOFiMSHC existing springs can be modified or to new ones created.

The table shown defines the full set of input parameters for the “PILE” record in the HASE geotechnical‐structural analysis environment.  This record describes the properties of a halfspace‐pile element that is attached to a previously defined structural point (see also records SPT and SPTH).  All of the parameters below must be specified (or accepted as default) whenever a PILE element is created; for more background on how these values interact in the numerical model, refer to the HASE manual’s PILE section.

1.  Item: NCS  
    •  Description: Cross-section number.  This integer index identifies which cross-sectional geometry (e.g. diameter, shape, reinforcement details) to use for this pile element.  
    •  Unit: – (dimensionless index)  
    •  Default: 0  

2.  Item: L  
    •  Description: Length of the pile measured in the direction of gravity.  This is the total embedded length of the pile shaft from its connection at the “structural point” down to the pile tip.  
    •  Unit: meters [m] (unit code 1001)  
    •  Default: 0.0  

3.  Item: PSKN  
    •  Description: Shaft‐skin friction percentage.  Specifies what percentage of the total axial pile capacity is assumed to be mobilized through friction along the pile’s lateral surface (as opposed to end bearing at the tip).  Values range from 0 to 100.  
    •  Unit: – (percent)  
    •  Default: 50  

4.  Item: LSKN  
    •  Description: Inactive skin length percentage.  Defines the portion of the pile’s shaft length that does not contribute to frictional resistance (for example, skirted or coated sections where skin friction is reduced or canceled).  Expressed as a percentage of L.  
    •  Unit: – (percent)  
    •  Default: (none specified; user must supply if nonzero)  

5.  Item: MXSK  
    •  Description: Maximum shaft friction capacity.  An absolute cap (in kN) on the load that can be transmitted along the pile’s lateral surface, regardless of what the percentage PSKN would otherwise imply.  Helps prevent overestimating shaft resistance.  
    •  Unit: kilonewtons [kN]  
    •  Default: – (no limit)  

6.  Item: MXPF  
    •  Description: Maximum pile foot bearing capacity.  An absolute cap (in kN) on the load that can be carried at the pile tip (end bearing).  Limits tip resistance even if PSKN would direct more load there.  
    •  Unit: kilonewtons [kN]  
    •  Default: – (no limit)  

Contextual notes:  
•  “See also: SPT, SPTH” indicates that each pile is tied to a structural point record, which defines its position, orientation, and boundary conditions.  
•  PSKN and LSKN work together to partition total axial load between frictional skin resistance and tip bearing.  MXSK and MXPF provide hard caps on those respective contributions.  
•  If you leave MXSK or MXPF blank (default “–”), no upper bound is enforced. Likewise, zero or default LSKN implies the full shaft length is active in skin friction.  
•  All percentages are entered as numeric values (e.g. PSKN = 70 means 70 % of load on the shaft).  

By capturing these six parameters, the PILE record fully describes how axial loads flow through the pile element into the surrounding half‐space model.

See also: SPT
 SPTH
 This records defines properties of a halfspace-pile connected to the previously given structural point. Information about the parameters can be found in the manual of HASE in record PILE.

Below is a structured, field-by-field description of the SLN (structural line) input table, organized by functional groups. Use this as a guide when parsing or vectorizing SLN records for a RAG-style knowledge base.

1. Identification  
 • NO (Line number)  
   – Integer identifier of the structural line.  
   – If omitted or set to zero, the system auto-assigns the next available number.  
   – A negative NO value signals an update to an existing line (e.g. “SLN –10 …” modifies line 10).  
 • TITL (Title of Line)  
   – Free text (up to 32 characters) giving a human-readable name or description.

2. End-Point References & Geometry  
 • NPA / NPE (Start point / End point)  
   – References to existing structural points defined via SPT or implicitly created when geometry is defined.  
 • REF (Reference axis)  
   – Optionally points to a previously defined geometric axis (GAX).  
   – When REF is used, all subsequent SLNB / SLNP records are ignored, and the line follows that axis.  
 • FIX (Boundary conditions along the line)  
   – Sixteen-character literal value describing support/fixity along the beam (e.g. “FFPF…”, custom codes).

3. Subdivision & Meshing  
 • SDIV (Subdivision density)  
   – Positive value: target mesh spacing in [m].  
   – Negative value: exact number of finite elements along the line.  
 • GRP (Group number)  
   – Assigns this line to a user-defined group for batch operations or load assignments.  
 • STYP (Element type)  
   – Literal code (default “SE”) indicating the type of finite element to use for subdivision (e.g. “SE” for standard beam).  

4. Section & Profile Assignment  
 • SNO (Cross-section number)  
   – References a cross-section defined elsewhere.  Default is inherited or blank.  
 • NP (Number of bore/bedding profile)  
   – References a geotechnical profile (e.g. soil bedding) for tunnel or buried pipes.

5. Local Coordinate System & Orientation  
 • KR (Direction identifier)  
   – Literal code selecting one of several predefined orientation conventions.  
 • DRX, DRY, DRZ (Direction cosines)  
   – Optional explicit direction vector for the local y-axis of the beam. Overrides KR if non-zero.  
 • DROT (Additional rotation)  
   – Angle in degrees for rotation about the beam’s longitudinal axis (twist).

6. Eccentricities (Global Coordinates)  
At the line start (suffix A) and end (suffix E):  
 • EX*, EY*, EZ*  
   – Offsets in [m] in global X, Y, Z directions  
   – Default zero yields center-to-center connection of beams.

7. Hinge Conditions  
 • FIXA / FIXE (Hinge at start / end)  
   – Sixteen-character literal, similar to FIX but only at line termini.  
 • FIMA / FIME (Hinge at all interior starts / ends)  
   – Applies hinge conditions to intermediate points if a polyline is defined by multiple SLNB/SLNP segments.

8. Intersection & Advanced Flags  
 • XFLG (Intersection properties)  
   – Literal code controlling how this line intersects with others (e.g. merge, accuracy).  
 • (Others, e.g. special SLNS sub-records can follow to add or modify sectional properties.)

Usage Notes  
– If no geometry (SLNB/SLNP or REF) is provided, SLN assumes a straight connection between NPA and NPE.  
– Modifying an existing line (negative NO) only changes the listed properties; unspecified fields remain as previously defined.  
– Always cross-reference with SPT (points), SLNB/SLNP (geometry), SLNS (sectional properties), and GAX (axes) records for a complete geometric and analytical definition.

See also: SLNB, SLNP, SLNS, SPT
 SLN
 This record defines a structural line. Start and end points of the line may be specified explicitly
 by referencing structural points which have been previously defined at SPT or implicitly using subsequent geometry records of type SLNB / SLNP . In the latter case, it will be checked if a structural point already exists at the respective end coordinate of the line and creates one if not. If no number is given for the structural line at NR, a new number will be assigned automatically.
 By entering a negative number at NO the properties of a previously defined structrual line can be changed. For example: SLN -10 SNO 1 changes the cross-section number of line no 10. All other properties of the line remain unchanged. If an additional property record of type SLNS is given when a line is being changed, it will be added to all previously defined property records of the line.
 The geometry of a line can be described by adding subsequent records of type SLNB or SLNP. SLNB allows to define straight lines and circular arcs whereas SLNP is used to create freeform curves. A third possibility is to set the geometry by referencing a previously defined axis GAX at REF. If no geometry is defined at all, a straight line between start- and endpoint is assumed.

All beam elements which will be created along the structural line have a local coordinate system assigned whose local x-axis is always aligned parallel to the structural line. For curved edges this coordinate system may vary along the line. This local beam-coordinate system determines the orientation of cross sections and, if not otherwise specified at record SLNS, the direction of local supports and kinematic couplings. The orientation of the local z-axis perpendicular to the line can be specified using special literals at KR or directly by entering direction vector at DRX,DRY,DRZ. Following possibilities exist:
 The entries DRX,DRY,DRZ define a direction vector according to which the local z-axis of the beam coordinate system is aligned. The local x-axis (= tangent) of the coordinate system remains always parallel to the structural line.
 Which of the two local directions y or z is aligned is basically determined by the global variable CTRL LOCA. If nothing is given, the local z-axis is used.
 • Predefined directions using a literal at KR Instead of an explicit direction, the user may also enter one of the literals POSX, POSY, POSZ, NEGX, NEGY or NEGZ at KR in order to align the local x-axis with one of the given global directions.
 Moreover, the local x-axis may also be aligned within one of the global coordinate planes by entering:
 KR = XY, YX: align x within global XY-plane in X- resp. Y-direction
 KR = YZ, ZY: align x within global YZ-plane in Y- resp. Z-direction
 KR = ZX, XZ: align x within global ZX-plane in Z- resp. X-direction
 • Align to other structural element KR { PT,LN,AR} NO Using this option, the local z- (or y-) axis of the beam elements along the structural line can be aligned towards another structural element. Following possibilities exist:
 KR PT: align towards a structural point
 KR LN: align towards a structrual line

• Align to other structural element KR { PT,LN,AR} NO Using this option, the local z- (or y-) axis of the beam elements along the structural line can be aligned towards another structural element. Following possibilities exist:. KR PT: align towards a structural point. KR LN: align towards a structrual line.
 KR AR: align towards a structural area
 The direction of each beam element is determined individually by calculating the projection onto the referenced structural item. If no projection exist, i.e. the distance is zero, the
 coordinate system of the referenced item is taken directly.
 • additional rotation about beam axis at DROT By indicating an angle for DROT the local coordinate system will be additionally rotated about the beam axis. The angle is to be given in degrees.

The definition of boundary or coupling conditions can be carried out by specifying one of the literals described in section 2.6.1 and 2.6.2 at FIX. If the Literal at FIX contains the character string ”->”, the following number is treated as the number of a reference line. Referenced lines will subdivided with the same number of elements and the pairwise corresponding nodes will be connected with kinematic constraints. For example, an definition of PZ->4 sets all nodal displacements in z-direction in relation to those of the referenced line nr 4. For the definition of extended coupling and interface conditions a special record SLNS is provided, which may be better used.

SDIV defines the maximum edge-length of beam or plane elements to be created along the structural line. If no mesh size is given at SDIV, the size of possibly connected structural regions or the global setting at CTRL HMIN is taken. A negative (integer) value at SDIV defines the exact number of elements to be generated along the edge.
 A set of literals at parameter STYP allows to control the generation of beam elements and the intersection behaviour of the structural line:
 ’N’ = centric beam (section at barycenter)
 ’B’ = beam with reference axis (section at origin)
 ’O’ = centric column (section at barycenter)
 ’L’ = column with reference axis (section at origin)
 ’T’ = truss element
 ’C’ = cable element
 ’S’ = use type defined at section (default)
 ’E’ = sudivide structural line in single elements (default)
 ’X’ = subdivide in elements without connecting the elements with a surrounding FE-mesh
 ’Y’ = create one single element with beam sections
 create one single element without beam sections
 If the type of beam element is set to ’truss-element’ (STYP ’T’) SOFiMSHC automatically ac- tivates option ’Z’ = ’create one element without sections’. In case of cable elements (STYP ’C’) the intersection with other structural elements is prevented by default (see option XFLG) in addition. In both cases these default settings can be overwritten by the user if any other option is given at STYP.
 Beams with linearly varying sections can be defined by entering two section numbers sepa-
 rated by a dot at NCS (i.e. ’1.2’ ). The sections at internal element nodes have to be created by running AQUA afterwards with option INTE 0.

Hinge conditions can be specified for the start and the end of a structural line individually using the parameters FIXA and FIXE. In addition to that, the options FIMA and FIME allow to define hinge conditions at all nodes created along the structural line (e.g. hinged chain). Following literals are possible:
 N,VY,VZ normal-, transverse forces
 MT,MY,MZ moments
 MB warping
 PP = NVYVZ
 MM = MTMYMZ
 The literals define the hinge condition which is to be released. The options can also be arbi- trarily combined (e.g. MYMZ), in order to release multiple degrees of freedom.
 By entering a number at FIXA to FIME it specifies the respective number of a non-linear force- work law defined in program AQUA (see AQUA: record SFLA).

Using option XFLG allows to control the behaviour, when a structural line is intersected with other structural elements. By default, structural lines which cross or lie parallel to another structural elements will be rigidly connected with the adjacent element or subdivided in case of a transversal intersection. This default behaviour can be changed using parameter XFLG. Thereby, two possibilities exist:
 Using one or a combination of the following literals allows to disable the intersection with the respective structural element types:
 ’P’: The given structural line will no longer be subdivided by structural points.
 •
 ’L’: The structural line will no longer be subdivided nor replaced by other structural lines.
 • ’A’: The structural line will no longer be subdivided by crossing structural areas and will also not be embedded within a structural region as constraining line.
 For example, the following input
 SLN 1 NPA 1 2 SNO 1 XFLG PLA
 deactivates all intersections of the structural line with other elements. I.e. the structural line no. 1 will not be subdivided. The line will also not be replaced by other lines or embedded in a structural area as constraining line.
 Please note that the intersection options only apply to the topologically internal of the structural line. They will not apply to the endpoints. In the case that the user also wants to prevent an
 intersection at the ends of the structural line, the endpoints must be defined explicitly with the respective intersection option set there.
 A second option is the definition of hinge conditions. Similar to the definition of hinge conditions at the start and the end of the structural line at parameter FIXA and FIXE, hinge conditions can also be defined relative to crossing structural members.
 For this purpose, the hinge conditions described in section 5.6.4 can be inserted at parameter XFLG. In this case, a hinge is inserted between the structural line and the adjacent member, which suppresses the transfer of the respective force condition.

Similar to the definition of hinge conditions at the start and the end of the structural line at parameter FIXA and FIXE, hinge conditions can also be defined relative to crossing structural members.. For this purpose, the hinge conditions described in section 5.6.4 can be inserted at parameter XFLG. In this case, a hinge is inserted between the structural line and the adjacent member, which suppresses the transfer of the respective force condition..
 For example, the following input
 SLN 1 NPA 1 2 SNO 1 XFLG MM
 suppresses the transfer of moment forces to adjacent crossing members. Such kind of input can be used to model the connection between a rafter and the purlin in roof constructions, in order to keep moment forces within the rafter and to prevent an input of torsional moments into the primary bearing construction.
 As in the previous case, it must be noticed, that the given options only apply to connections which cross the stuctural line in the internal. Hinge conditions at the start and the end of the structural line must be defined at the parameter FIXA and FIXE.
 A definition of internal hinge conditions at all intermediate nodes using FIMA and FIME is not possible if hinges are defined at XFLG.
 The given option does also not apply to connections between parallel members or connections between structural lines and structural areas.

This table defines the parameter‐block for a single segment in an SLNB record, which may represent a straight line, a full circle or a circular arc in 3D space. Each row (Item) names one of the numeric fields that must be supplied (or left at its default) when constructing or appending to a structural line (SLN). Columns explain what each field means, its physical unit, and its default value when no explicit value is given.  

1. X1, Y1, Z1  
   – Description: Coordinates of the segment’s start‐point in the global 3D cartesian coordinate system.  
   – Unit: meters ([m]\_1001).  
   – Default: 0.0 each.  
   – Usage: Mandatory for any segment. In a straight‐line or arc definition, these specify the first endpoint.  

2. X2, Y2, Z2  
   – Description: Coordinates of the segment’s end‐point.  
   – Unit: meters ([m]\_1001).  
   – Default: 0.0 each.  
   – Usage: Mandatory for lines and arcs. For a full circle, these fields are ignored (or may be zero).  

3. R  
   – Description: Radius of the circle or circular arc.  
   – Unit: meters ([m]\_1001).  
   – Default: “–” (no default; must be supplied if defining a circle or an arc via radius).  
   – Usage:  
     • For a full circle (no endpoints used), R defines the circle’s radius around its center (XM, YM, ZM).  
     • For an arc, R can be used together with start‐ and end‐points plus normal (NX, NY, NZ) to define curvature.  

4. NX, NY, NZ  
   – Description: Components of the normal vector of the circular plane.  
   – Unit: dimensionless (“–”).  
   – Default: “–” (no default; required when using R‐based definition of circle or arc).  
   – Usage: Together these three define the orientation of the plane in which the circle or arc lies. They must form a non‐zero vector.  

5. XM, YM, ZM  
   – Description: Coordinates of the center of the circle (or of the circle‐defining circle of an arc).  
   – Unit: meters ([m]\_1001).  
   – Default: “–” (unused for straight lines; required if defining a full circle or center‐based arc).  
   – Usage: When defining a full circle, the record uses only (XM, YM, ZM) plus R and (NX, NY, NZ). For an arc specified by its center, these three fields replace the radius‐only arc definition.  

6. X3, Y3, Z3  
   – Description: A third point on the arc, used when defining an arc by three points rather than by radius and normal or by center.  
   – Unit: meters ([m]\_1001).  
   – Default: “–” (only needed for “three‐point” arc definitions).  
   – Usage: Defines the curvature uniquely in combination with (X1, Y1, Z1) and (X2, Y2, Z2).  

Notes on usage and linkage:  
• Each SLNB entry is implicitly tied to the structural line identifier most recently created by an SLN record. You can issue multiple SLNB segments in sequence to form polycurves.  
• For smooth transitions between segments, ensure that end‐tangents coincide; avoid “kinks.” If intentional kinks are needed, split the line with an intermediate structural point (SPT record) and start a fresh SLNB.  
• See also: SLN (defines a new structural line) and SPT (inserts a structural point).

See also: SLN, SPT
 SLNB
 Records of type SLNB can be used to define straight lines, circles and cicular arcs in space. Records of this type always refer to the most recently defined structural line at SLN. Multiple segments are allowed to be entered in order to define polycurves. For the definition of a single segment following possibilities exist:
 • A straight line is defined by its start- and endpoint at (x1,y1,z1) and (x2,y2,z2).
 • A full circle can be defined by its center (xm,ym,zm), the radius and the normal on the circular plane (n,ny,nz).
 • A circular arc can be defined by its start- and endpoint at (x1,y1,z1) und (x2,y2,z2), a radius and the normal or by entering the start-, the endpoint and the center.
 •
 In addition, circular arcs can also be defined by entering three points on the arc. (x1,y1,z1) und (x2,y2,z2) describe the start- and the endpoint, (x3,y3,z3) a third point on the arc.
 When multiple segments are defined, the transition between two segments should be mod- eled with continuous tangents. Kinks are possible but should be avoided as they can lead to incorrect or erroneous meshes. In order to define kinks it is better to define two curves with a structural point in between.

The table below defines the individual data fields you supply in each SLNP record when you want to describe one control or definition point along a structural line (SLN).  SLNP records allow you to build arbitrary free-form geometry by specifying points in 3D space plus optional parameters that guide how those points are interpolated.

Columns  
• Item: the short tag you use in the SLNP record  
• Description: a brief human-readable explanation  
• Unit: physical unit or “–” if unitless  
• Default: value assumed if you omit this field  

Rows

1. X  
   – Description: X-coordinate of the point in 3D  
   – Unit: [m] (SOFiMSHC internal length unit, code 1001)  
   – Default: 0.0  

2. Y  
   – Description: Y-coordinate of the point in 3D  
   – Unit: [m] (1001)  
   – Default: 0.0  

3. Z  
   – Description: Z-coordinate of the point in 3D  
   – Unit: [m] (1001)  
   – Default: 0.0  

4. W  
   – Description: Weight of the control point (only used for NURBS curves)  
   – Unit: – (dimensionless)  
   – Default: 1.0  

5. S  
   – Description: Chainage or station along the curve at this point (used by all spline or piecewise interpolations to parameterize the curve)  
   – Unit: –  
   – Default: none (if you omit S, the system automatically assigns a parameter value to minimize oscillations)  

6. DX, DY, DZ  
   – Description: Tangential‐direction hint vector at this point (used only for piecewise cubic B-splines; enforces C1 continuity)  
   – Unit: – (direction vectors are unitless)  
   – Default: none (no explicit tangent hint)  

7. NX, NY, NZ  
   – Description: Local z-axis direction at this point (used for advanced geometric referencing, e.g. to define a local coordinate frame along the curve)  
   – Unit: –  
   – Default: none  

8. TYPE  
   – Description: Curve‐type identifier for the entire line (referencing the SLN record’s TYPE field)  
     • 1 = Polygonal interpolation (straight-line segments between consecutive points)  
     • 2 = Cubic B-spline (C2-continuous, automatic or explicit S parametrization)  
     • 3 = Piecewise cubic B-spline (C1-continuous, user-supplied DX/DY/DZ)  
     • 4 = NURBS (Non-Uniform Rational B-Spline; true rational form if W ≠ 1)  
   – Unit: –  
   – Default: inherited from SLN if un­specified here  

How it all fits together  
Each SLNP record contributes one point to a previously declared structural line (via SLN). Depending on the curve TYPE you choose in SLN (and may override here), the system will:

• Connect points in sequence (TYPE=1)  
• Build a curvature-continuous (C2) spline with or without explicit chainage (TYPE=2)  
• Build a tangential continuous (C1) spline using user-supplied tangent hints (TYPE=3)  
• Construct a weighted, rational NURBS curve of specified degree and knot vector (TYPE=4; weights from W)  

By mixing the coordinates (X,Y,Z) with optional parameters (S, DX/DY/DZ, W, NX/NY/NZ), you gain full control over both the shape and parameterization of complex structural lines. In most simple cases you need only X, Y, Z, and TYPE. Omitted numeric fields default to zero (or 1.0 for W), and omitted direction or station hints trigger automatic assignment by the software’s smoothing algorithms.

See also: SLN, SPT
 SLNP
 Structural lines with arbitrary freeform geometry can be defined with SLNP using character- istic data points. Each record SLNP defines one coordinate in 3D. They always refer to the previously defined structural line at SLN. Following types of curves are supported:
 The given points will be interpolated as polygonal sequence.
 The given datapoints will be interpolated using a cubic B-Spline. The interpolation is carried out curvature continuous at the definition points (C2-continuity). The parametrization (chainage) of the curve can be set explicitly at each datapoint using the parameter S. If no parameter values are given, SOFiMSHC assigns a parametrisation automatically. For this, special techniques are applied which minimize possible oszillations between unequally distributed definition points.
 The given datapoints will be interpolated using piecewise cubic B-Spline segments. The interpolation is carried out tangentially continuous at the definition points (C1-continuity). Using the parameters DX,DY,DZ, the tangential direction at certain points can be defined explicitly by the user. Similar to the spline interpolation, the parametrisation (chainage) along the curve can be set using the parameter S.
 A NURBS (Non Uniform Rational B-Spline) curve can be defined by entering the euclidian coordinates of the control-points at X,Y,Z. If weights < > 1.0 are given, the input results in a true ’rational’ NURBS curve, which, for example, allows to describe also circle and ellipses. The degree of the NURBS curve can be set in record SLNN, when defining the knot vector.

Below is a detailed, field‐by‐field breakdown of the SLNN parameter table. SLNN records attach directly to a previously defined structural line (SLN) and serve to specify the knot vector (for NURBS) or explicit parameter values (for interpolation curves). In a vector‐store or RAG system, you would index each of these fields to enable fine‐grained querying over curve definitions, degrees, multiplicities, etc.

1. Table Structure  
   • Columns  
     – Item: The short parameter name used in the SLNN record.  
     – Description: A concise English phrase explaining the role of the parameter.  
     – Unit: Reserved for units if applicable (none apply here, hence “–”).  
     – Default: The assumed value if the parameter is omitted. Special symbols are used:  
       * “!” denotes that the field is mandatory (no default);  
       * A numeric literal (e.g. “1”) is a hard default;  
       * “*” indicates that the field has no fixed default, but may be set only in special circumstances (here, only in the first SLNN record).  

2. Row‐by‐Row Analysis  
   2.1. Item = S  
     – Description: “Knot value.” This is the actual parameter or knot coordinate in the knot vector of a NURBS curve, or the local parameter value for an interpolation‐curve point.  
     – Unit: “–” (dimensionless). Knot parameters are normalized or user‐defined real numbers.  
     – Default: “!” (mandatory). Every SLNN entry must supply at least one S-value. If you omit it, the record is invalid.  
     – RAG indexing hints:  
       • tag = “S”  
       • type = real  
       • required = true  
       • usage notes: You may supply multiple S entries in one SLNN record if you also use a multiplicity >1.  

   2.2. Item = MUL  
     – Description: “Multiplicity.” Indicates how many times the knot value S is repeated in the full knot vector.  
     – Unit: “–” (unitless count).  
     – Default: 1. If you do not explicitly set multiplicity, the system assumes the knot appears only once.  
     – RAG indexing hints:  
       • tag = “MUL”  
       • type = integer  
       • default = 1  
       • range checks: Must be ≥ 1 and typically ≤ degree for clamped ends.  

   2.3. Item = DEGR  
     – Description: “degree of Nurbs.” Sets the polynomial degree p of the NURBS curve.  
     – Unit: “–” (order is an integer count of polynomial degree).  
     – Default: “*” (no automatic default).  
         • You may set DEGR only in the *first* SLNN record defining a particular curve.  
         • If you omit DEGR entirely (in all SLNN records), SOFiMSHC uses an internally assumed or previously declared degree.  
     – RAG indexing hints:  
       • tag = “DEGR”  
       • type = integer  
       • required in first record? Yes  
       • value domain: 1 ≤ DEGREE ≤ reasonable upper bound (e.g. 5 or 10 depending on solver).  

3. Contextual Notes  
   – Clamped Ends: For NURBS in SOFiMSHC you must explicitly “clamp” the ends. That means the first and last knot value must have multiplicity equal to the curve degree. These records allow you to set those multiplicities.  
   – Uniform vs. Explicit: If you omit all SLNN entries, the system will automatically assign a uniform knot sequence. Filling in SLNN gives you full control over parametrization—critical for advanced modeling or when matching parameter spaces across multiple curves.  
   – Interpolation Curves: When SLNN is used for interpolation (rather than NURBS), the S entries become your explicit interpolation‐point parameters. You may wish to set these to maintain consistent “speed” along different curve segments.  

4. Indexing Suggestions for RAG Vector Store  
   – Store each SLNN record as a document with fields: curve_id, record_index, S, MUL, (optional) DEGR.  
   – Tag “S” and “MUL” as repeatable fields; tag “DEGR” only in record_index = 1.  
   – Use numeric vector embeddings on S and MUL for parametric range queries; use integer embedding classes for DEGR.  
   – Add metadata for “clamped_end” when S is equal to first or last knot and MUL equals DEGR.  

This structured description captures both the semantics of each table entry and practical considerations for storing and querying SLNN parameters in a retrieval‐augmented generation (RAG) environment.

sections: 5.9 SLNN – Knot value of a NURBS-curve

content:
See also: SLN, SLNP
 SLNN
 Records of type SLNN are used to define the knot vector of NURBS-curves or to explicitly set the parametrization of interpolation curves. For each knot value of a NURBS or parameter value a single record SLNN is to be entered which refers to the previously defined structural line at SLN. Multiple knot-values (e.g. at the ends of a curve) can be entered in a single record using multiplicities > 1. Within the first record the polynomial degree of a NURBS-curve can be set using parameter DEGR.
 When NURBS-curves are defined in SOFiMSHC knot vectors must always be given with mul- tiple knots at the ends (”clamped ends”) with a multiplicity equal to the degree of the curve. In the case that no knot-vector is given by the user, a uniform distribution is assumed internally.
 When defining interpolation curves, the local parameter values at each interpolation point can also be set explicitly using this record. This can be, for example, necessary when one wants to keep the parametrization between different curves consistent. In general cases however, it is better to not set these values always since SOFiMSHC optimizes the parametrization by default such that oscillation between the different interpolation points are minimized.

content:
The SLNS record is used to define boundary conditions, elastic supports, kinematic couplings or special interface elements along a previously defined structural line (SLN).  You may supply multiple SLNS entries for the same line—for example to superimpose fixed supports and elastic bedding.  Each SLNS entry consists of a series of items (fields) with prescribed data types, units and default values.  See also SLN and SLNP for related line-geometry definitions.

Below is a field-by-field breakdown of SLNS:

1. GRP  
   • Description: Identifier for grouping multiple supports. Records sharing the same GRP number are treated as one set.  
   • Data type / format: Integer or special literal “AUTO”  
   • Unit: none (/LIT)  
   • Default: AUTO (the solver will automatically assign a group number if you omit this field)

2. FIX  
   • Description: Boundary or coupling condition specifier. It controls which degrees of freedom are fixed, free or coupled.  
   • Data type: Literal string of length up to 28 (Lit28)  
   • Unit: n/a  
   • Default: –   (you must supply a valid FIX pattern or name)

3. REFT  
   • Description: Reference type for the support or bedding. Determines whether the support is absolute, relative to a point (SPT), relative to another line (SLN), or defined as an interface via SAR keywords.  
   • Allowed values:  
     – >FIX   : absolute reference to global coordinate system  
     – >SPT   : relative to a previously defined point (SPT record)  
     – >SLN   : relative to another structural line (SLN record)  
     – +SAR, –SAR, *SAR : interface element definitions (surface-to-surface contact, etc.)  
   • Data type: Literal (LIT)  
   • Default: >FIX

4. REF  
   • Description: Numeric identifier of the referenced element (point or line) when using >SPT or >SLN.  
   • Data type: Integer  
   • Unit: none  
   • Default: –   (mandatory if REFT is >SPT or >SLN)

5. MNO  
   • Description: Material number or stress–strain curve index applied to the support or interface element.  
   • Data type / format: Integer or special literal “AUTO”  
   • Unit: none (/LIT)  
   • Default: AUTO (automatic detection based on attached elements)

6. CA, CL, CD  
   • CA (Axial bedding stiffness), CL (Lateral/transverse bedding stiffness), CD (Torsional bedding stiffness)  
   • Units:  
     – CA, CL: [kN/m^3]  
     – CD:   [kNm/m/rad]  
   • Data type: Real number  
   • Default: 0.0 for each (no elastic bedding unless specified)

7. KR  
   • Description: Direction specifier for an explicit orientation of the support or bedding.  
   • Data type: Literal of length 4 (Lit4)  
   • Unit: none  
   • Default: –   (if omitted, a default or global orientation is used)

8. DRX, DRY, DRZ  
   • Description: Components of a direction vector used when KR is set to define a local axis.  
   • Data type: Real  
   • Units: none  
   • Default: 0.0 for each component

9. DROT  
   • Description: Rotation angle about the beam (structural line) axis, in degrees. Used to twist the local support orientation.  
   • Data type: Real  
   • Unit: deg  
   • Default: 0.0

10. D  
    • Description: Distance to the corresponding interface element when REFT uses an SAR interface keyword.  
    • Data type: Real  
    • Unit: m  
    • Default: 0.0

11. BFIX  
    • Description: Width or “spread” of the support region along the line (for distributing boundary conditions over a finite width).  
    • Data type: Real  
    • Unit: m  
    • Default: 1.0

12. FCTA, FCTE  
    • FCTA: Scaling factor for bedding stiffness at the start node of the line segment.  
    • FCTE: Scaling factor for bedding stiffness at the end node of the line segment.  
    • Data type: Real  
    • Unit: none  
    • Default: 1.0 for both

13. TYPE  
    • Description: Specifies the physical type of generated element created by this support record.  
    • Allowed values (up to 4 characters, Lit4):  
      – SPRI (spring element)  
      – BOUN (boundary condition element)  
      – INTF (interface element)  
    • Unit: none  
    • Default: –   (selected automatically based on REFT and SAR usage)

Usage Notes:  
- If you omit any optional bedding stiffness (CA, CL, CD), those stiffness terms default to zero (rigid support in that direction).  
- Use accurate KR/DRX/DRY/DRZ settings to align nonsymmetric bedding when the global axes are unsuitable.  
- For contact/interface definitions, combine REFT = +SAR or –SAR with D, MNO and TYPE = INTF to generate surface-to-surface elements at a prescribed offset.  
- Group supports (GRP) to manage multiple line supports collectively in post-processing or when applying load patterns.

sections: 5.10 SLNS – Supports and kinematic couplings on a SLN

content:
See also: SLN, SLNP
 SLNS
 Item
 Description
 Unit
 Default
 This record defines boundary conditions, elastic supports, kinematic couplings or special inter- face elements for the most recently defined structural line at SLN. For a given structural line, multiple records of type SLNS can be given, e.g. in order to define elastic boundary conditions and fixed supports along the line in parallel.

metadata.sections: 5.10 SLNS – Supports and kinematic couplings on a SLN

content:
Supports or coupling conditions along the structural line can be defined at parameter FIX with the literals described in section 2.6.1: By preceding a ’L’ to the literals (e.g. LPXPY) the support conditions will be interpreted in the local coordinate system of the structural line. If multiple support and/or coupling conditions given, they will be superimposed accordingly.
 Local support conditions (e.g. LPZ) are primarily aligned according to the local coordinate system of the beam elements created along the structural line. This local orientation, however can also be set separately for this record using the parameters KR to DROT according to the description in section 5.10.3 below.
 In case that a number is given at REF a kinematic coupling is created to the referenced el- ement. All coupled degrees of freedom of the structural line are set equal to those of the reference element. A coupling condition can be defined to a structural point (REFT >SPT) or a structural line (REFT >SLN). In the latter case, both the given and the referenced line will be subdivided equally and the respective nodes will be connected with the given condition. Kine- matic couplings of warping torsion (MB) between two structural lines are not allowed. Basically, coupling conditions are defined with the same literals as support conditions, which can also be combined, e.g. FIX PXPY. Further information about couplings can be found in section 2.6.2.
 In certain cases, where the coupling of nodal displacements is desired, without considering a lever arm, couplings of type KPX0, KPY0, KPZ0 may be used, as described in section 2.6.3. These couplings may violate the equilibrium of moments, and therefore should be used cautiously.

Instead of coupling or support conditions the given record also allows to create boundary el- ements with elastic bedding or spring elements along the given structural line by setting one of the parameters at CA to CD or a material number or a work-law at MNO. If a work-law and a non-linear material are given with the same number in a project, the work-law takes prece- dence. This setting can be overwritten by entering a negative number in order to reference a material in this case. In contrast to individual spring elements, a boundary element defines a continuous bedding along the line which interpolates the displacements between the finite element nodes. If only linear parameters are given, SOFiMSHC generates basically boundary elements. In case of non-linear parameters (usually given by the material) or in case of cou- pled structural lines, spring elements will be created along the structural line. The generation of beddings and spring elements can be further controlled by setting the global parameter STEU LSUP.
 Basically, a spring or a boundary element can be assigned three parameters: axial (CA), lateral (CL) and/or rotational (CD) stiffness. These three parameters always refer to an explicit bed- ding or spring direction. An axial bedding acts radial into this direction, a lateral (or transversal) bedding in a plane perpendicular to it and a rotational bedding parameter creates a rotational stiffness around this direction. The bedding direction can be set by the user by specifying
 the parameters KR to DROT. If no direction is given, the spring or boundary elements will be aligned parallel to the structural line. SOFiMSHC provides following possibilities for setting directions of spring and boundary elements:
 Similar to coupling conditions, also linear or non-linear bedding conditions can be defined between two structural lines, if the numer of a referenced line is given at parameter REF. In this case, the given and the referenced line will be subdivided with the same number of nodes and spring elements created in between. If no direction is given at KR to DROT, the direction of the spring elements is set to the direction between the referenced nodes.

Similar to coupling conditions, also linear or non-linear bedding conditions can be defined between two structural lines, if the numer of a referenced line is given at parameter REF. In this case, the given and the referenced line will be subdivided with the same number of nodes and spring elements created in between. If no direction is given at KR to DROT, the direction of the spring elements is set to the direction between the referenced nodes..
 In the case that a material number is given at MNO, the spring constants will be calculated from the corresponding linear or non-linear elasticity properties of the material. BFIX can be set to adapt the material parameters to the width of the support. A negative value at the bedding parameters CA to CD allows to further scale the values calculated from the material. If the literal AUTO is set, SOFiMSHC automatically determines the material number from the adjacent structural area.

Supports, coupling conditions and elastic beddings or spring elements can be locally aligned using the parameter KR,DRX,DRY,DRZ and DROT independant from the orientation of the structural line. Following possibilities exist:
 • Aligned according to global directions By setting one of the literals POSX, POSY, POSZ or NEGX, NEGY, NEGZ at KR, the direction of spring elements or elastic beddings can be set according to one of the global coordinate axes X, Y or Z.
 • Align to other structural element KR { PT,LN,AR} NO Using this option, the local orien- tation of the spring element or the bedding along the structural line can be aligned towards another structural element.
 Following possibilities exist:
 KR PT: align towards a structural point
 KR LN: align towards a structrual line
 KR AR: align towards a structural area
 The direction of each beam element is determined individually by calculating the projection onto the referenced structural item. If no projection exist, i.e. the distance is zero, the coordinate system of the referenced item is taken directly.
 • Additional rotation about line axis DROT In the case that an angle is given at DROT, the direction of spring elements or elastic beddings will be additionally rotated about the axis of the structural line.
 • Local direction specifier KR LOCX, LOCY, LOCZ (only spring elements) Using this option the direction of the axial springs can be switched between the local coordinate di- rections of the structural line. Default setting is KR LOCX. In this case, the spring direction will be aligned tangentially to the axis of the structural line. LOCY and LOCZ respectively allows to align the direction with one of the local coordinate axes perpendicular to the line. The local directions LOCY and LOCZ primarily refer to the local coordinate system (y- or z-axis) of the beam elements created along the structural line.
 If no beam coordinate system is given (e.g. line is boundary of a structural region), the directions refer to the coordinate system of the structural line itself.

The local directions LOCY and LOCZ primarily refer to the local coordinate system (y- or z-axis) of the beam elements created along the structural line.. If no beam coordinate system is given (e.g. line is boundary of a structural region), the directions refer to the coordinate system of the structural line itself..
 • Explicit direction vector at DRX, DRY, DRZ A vector given at DRX, DRY, DRZ allows to align spring and boundary elements with an arbitrary global direction. An additional rotation of the springs using the parameter DROT is not possible in this case.

The options { +-*} SAR at REFT allow to create coupled interface elements along the given structural line automatically. Depending on the sub-type at SAR, SOFiMSHC creates and sets of interface edges to one or both sides of the line and disconnects connected structural regions accordingly. The direction at DRX, DRY, DRZ or, if not given, the local z-axis of the structural line defines to which side connected lines and regions will be disconnected. Thereby three possibilities exist:
 +SAR: a single interface edge is created in positive z-direction
 -SAR: a single interface edge is created in negative z-direction
 *SAR: two interface edges are created in both directions.
 If a distance is given at D a gap is created between the given and the interface line.
 SOFiMSHC creates spring elements between the coupled interface edges and assigns the linear bedding parameters given at CA to CD or possibly non-linear parameters if given at the material. The direction of the spring elements is always aligned perpendicular to the coupled lines.
 If parameter TYPE INTF is specified, SOFiMSHC will generate dedicated Rigid Frictional In- terface elements, which can currently be used in TALPA, for simulating non-linear contact in geotechnics.

Below is a detailed, field-by-field description of the input table used in the “SLSC” record for defining additional design sections along a structural line (see also SLN). These sections are inserted at fixed locations—independent of any element subdivision—and are evaluated during reinforcement design in AQB (accounting for reduced moments at supports).  

1. Item: REF  
   • Purpose: Specifies the reference point along the structural line from which the section’s position S is measured.  
   • Sub-items (literal values in column “Unit” = LIT):  
     – STRT: Distance measured from the start node of the line (default).  
     – END: Distance measured from the end node of the line.  
     – MID: Distance measured from the midpoint of the line.  
     – XI: A normalized parameter between 0 and 1 defining a relative position along the line (0 = start, 1 = end).  
   • Default REF = STRT  

2. Item: S  
   • Purpose: Numeric value giving the offset distance or position of the additional section relative to the chosen reference point.  
   • Unit: meters (m) or unitless fraction when REF = XI.  
   • Default S = 0.0  
   • Notes:  
     – A positive S moves the section in the direction from the reference towards the other end.  
     – When REF = XI, S is ignored (position entirely defined by XI).  

3. Item: TYPM  
   • Purpose: Defines the bending-moment type for the main bending plane at this section.  
   • Unit: Literal (LIT)  
   • Allowed values:  
     – SECT: Standard section (no special support treatment, default).  
     – CFAC: Section placed at the face of a clamped support.  
     – HFAC: Section placed at the face of a hinged support.  
     – IFAC: Section placed at the face of an indirect support (e.g., via structural element).  
   • Default TYPM = SECT  

4. Item: TYPT  
   • Purpose: Defines the bending-moment type for the transverse bending plane at this section.  
   • Unit: Literal (LIT)  
   • Allowed values same as for TYPM: SECT, CFAC, HFAC, IFAC.  
   • Default TYPT = SECT  

Usage Example (from context):  
+ PROG SOFIMSHC  
    HEAD  
      … SLN 1 NPA …  
      SLSC REF STRT, END 15[cm] TYPM HFAC  
    END  
+ PROG SOFIMSHC  
    HEAD  
    END  

This input creates two extra design sections located 15 cm from both ends of the specified structural line, placed exactly at the faces of hinged supports (HFAC). During the AQB reinforcement design, these sections account for moment reductions appropriate to hinged support conditions.  

Hint: If global option CTRL BSEC is activated, similar sections can be generated automatically for all horizontal beams at their column or wall support faces, without explicit SLSC entries.

sections: 5.11 SLSC – Explicit sections on structural line

content:
See also: SLN
 SLSC
 This record allows to define additional design sections along a structural line. These sections will always be placed at the same position independant from any element subdivision.
 As an example, the following input
 +PROG SOFIMSHC HEAD ... SLN 1 NPA ... SLSC REF STRT,END 15[cm] TYPM HFAC ... END
 +PROG SOFIMSHC
 HEAD
 END
 creates two additional sections at a distance of 15cm from both ends at the location of support faces of connected columns. These sections will be evaluated during reinforcement design in AQB where, according to the type of the section defined at TYPM or TYPT, a reduced moment at the respective support is accounted for.
 Hint
 Using the global option CTRL BSEC, design sections can also be automatically generated along horizontal beam members at the support faces of connected columns and walls.

metadata.sections: 5.11 SLSC – Explicit sections on structural line

content:
The table is the parameter summary for the SAR record, which defines a “structural area” in SOFiMSHC. Each row lists one parameter (“Item”), its purpose (“Description”), expected data type or unit (“Unit”), and default value (“Default”) if the user omits it.

1. NO (–/LIT, default 0)  
   • Unique area identifier.  
   • Can be a positive integer, or the keywords PROP (defines an attribute region that alters local properties without meshing) or VOID (creates an opening).  
   • If omitted, SOFiMSHC auto-assigns a number; negative numbers modify existing areas.

2. FIX (LIT8, default * )  
   • Boundary condition flag that can enforce supports within the area.

3. GRP (–, default 0)  
   • Primary group number for elements generated on this area.  
   • Elements in an attribute region (PROP) can also be assigned to a secondary group via this parameter.

4. MNO (–, default 0) & MRF (–, default 0)  
   • MNO: Material number for QUAD elements.  
   • MRF: Material number for reinforcement layers.

5. REF (LIT4, default –)  
   • Reference to an existing GAR surface definition.  
   • If omitted, geometry is inferred from the boundary loops (SARB records and optional SARP points).

6. NX, NY, NZ (–, default *)  
   • Approximate normal vector (local +Z direction) of the area.  
   • Only side matters; SOFiMSHC re-orientates it precisely.

7. NRA (–, default 0/7)  
   • Bitmask selecting element formulation:  
     – 0 = geometry only  
     +1 = plate action  
     +2 = membrane action  
     +4 = in-plane bending  

8. QREF (LIT, default CENT)  
   • Element reference point:  
     CENT = centered,  
     ABOV = toward negative global Z,  
     BELO = toward positive global Z.

9. KR (LIT/–, default *) & DRX, DRY, DRZ (–, default –)  
   • KR: Keyword or direction identifier for aligning the local X-axis of plane elements. Options include:  
     – explicit vector via DRX,DRY,DRZ  
     – global directions (POSX, NEGZ, etc.)  
     – plane alignment (XY, YZ, ZX and their reverses)  
     – “PT”, “LN”, “AR” to align toward a point, line or area (with DRX storing the target’s ID).  
   • DROT ([deg], default 0.0) applies an additional rotation about the local Z-axis.

10. T ([mm], default *)  
    • Constant thickness override for all elements in this area.  
    • If omitted, T=1 m is assumed or the global CTRL HMIN applies.

11. TX, TY, TXY, TD ([mm], default T)  
    • Orthotropic thickness components in local X, Y, cross-coupling (X–Y), and torsion.  
    • Average thickness T is used for mass calculations.

12. MCTL (–, default *)  
    • Mesh control:  
       REGM = attempt a structured mesh on quadrilateral-shaped regions,  
       SNGQ = collapse the area into a single quad element (useful when NRA=0).

13. H1 (–, default *) & H2 (–, default 0)  
    • H1: Maximum element edge length inside the area (overrides global minimum).  
    • H2: Local refinement radius around structural points (SPT records).

14. XFLG (LIT, default *)  
    • Flags (‘P’, ‘L’, ‘A’) to inhibit automatic intersections with points, lines or other areas.  
    • Enables user control of constraining geometry when combined with SARB CONS to add explicit constraints.

In combination with SARB (boundary loops), SARP (surface definition points), and SPT (thickness control points), these parameters fully determine the geometry, orientation, material assignment, thickness distribution and meshing strategy for any arbitrarily shaped region in a SOFiMSHC model.

The snippet you provided is the header and first data line of the SOFiMSHC “SAR” record (Structural Area), showing how orthotropic‐thickness and torsion parameters are specified. Below is a breakdown of each column in that mini‐table and how it fits into the overall SAR-record syntax:

1. SAR  
   • Record name. Introduces a new structural‐area definition.  
   • See also: SARB (boundary curves), SPT (thickness support points), SLN (structural lines).

2. TD  
   • Field mnemonic for the torsional thickness parameter.  
   • In a full SAR record you can specify four orthotropic‐thickness values:  
     – TX (thickness in local X‐direction)  
     – TY (thickness in local Y‐direction)  
     – TXY (coupling thickness)  
     – TD (torsional‐rigidity thickness)  

3. Orthotropic thickness torsion  
   • Human‐readable description of what “TD” means.  
   • Indicates that this column holds the torsional‐rigidity thickness value, i.e. the parameter that controls how the region resists in‐plane twisting.

4. [mm]  
   • Unit for TX, TY, TXY, and TD.  
   • All four orthotropic‐thickness parameters are entered in millimetres.

5. 10 10  
   • Example data values for two of the thickness entries.  
   • In this snippet “10 10” likely stands for TX = 10 mm, TD = 10 mm (or TXY = 10 mm, TD = 10 mm), depending on column ordering in your full table.  
   • It demonstrates that you can specify distinct thicknesses; here the torsional thickness is set to 10 mm.

6. T  
   • The final column header. In the full SAR record, T is the **average** or **nominal** thickness (in m) used for mass‐and‐inertia calculations.  
   • If you leave T unspecified, SOFiMSHC defaults it to 1.0 m.  
   • When using SPT points or SARB edge‐thickness definitions to vary the thickness, you set T = 0.0 to activate interpolation from those support entities.

––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––  
How this ties into the SAR record as a whole:  
 • You begin an area‐definition with the “SAR” keyword and optionally give it an ID number.  
 • You define its outer boundary via SARB records (and inner holes if needed).  
 • You may supply a reference surface (GAR) or let the mesher infer the shape.  
 • You specify the local normal (NX, NY, NZ) and how the in‐plane axes align (DRX/DRY/DRZ plus KR, or one of the POSX/POSY…/XZ options).  
 • You define a base thickness T (in m), and—if you need orthotropic stiffness—you add TX, TY, TXY, TD (in mm).  
 • You can override the default uniform thickness by distributing support points (SPT) or edge loads (SARB-T).  
 • Finally, you control mesh density with H1/H2 and meshing modes (MCTL) or disable intersections with XFLG.

In your RAG-vector‐store context, this table row therefore points to how the torsional orthotropic thickness (TD) is read from the SAR record, in millimetres, alongside the other thickness fields. It also reminds you that the overall thickness parameter T is distinct, measured in metres, and has its own default behavior unless you explicitly zero it out to invoke variable‐thickness interpolation.

The table shown defines a subset of parameters available on the SAR record (structural area definition) in SOFiMSHC.  It is organized into four columns—“Item,” “Description,” “Unit,” and “Default”—and lists eight parameters controlling bedding, meshing and auxiliary region‐level settings.  Below is a detailed, parameter‐by‐parameter description suitable for indexing in a RAG vector store:

1.  CB  
    •  Description: Factor (negative) or bedding modulus for normal sub-grade bedding.  This parameter governs the Winkler‐type vertical spring stiffness assigned beneath the entire area.  A negative number is interpreted as a constant factor, whereas a positive value is taken as an absolute stiffness in kN/m³.  
    •  Unit: [kN/m³]  
    •  Default: –1 (interpreted as “use global default” or “no bedding” depending on context)

2.  CT  
    •  Description: Factor (negative) or bedding modulus for transverse sub-grade bedding.  Analogous to CB but acting in the plane of the surface, CT controls in-plane spring stiffness for pavement or slab‐on‐grade modeling.  
    •  Unit: [kN/m³]  
    •  Default: –1

3.  MCTL  
    •  Description: Mesh control directive for this structural region.  Four literal options are allowed:  
      – AUTO: automatic/unstructured meshing (default behavior)  
      – REGM: attempt structured, rectangular‐style mesh when the boundary has four sides and near‐right angles  
      – SNGQ: collapse the region into one single quadrilateral element (useful for pressure or load distribution areas)  
      – OFF: deactivate meshing entirely (region exists only for grouping or property assignment)  
    •  Unit: dimensionless control code  
    •  Default: AUTO (represented by code 0 in SOFiMSHC input)

4.  H1  
    •  Description: Target element edge length for the entire region.  Overrides the global minimum mesh size (HMIN) set in CTRL.  SOFiMSHC will refine or coarsen the mesh so that no edge exceeds H1.  
    •  Unit: [m]  
    •  Default: inherited from CTRL HMIN

5.  H2  
    •  Description: Local refinement size applied around structural points inside the region.  Points tagged with thickness or stiffness variations (SPT records) cause mesh to reduce to edge lengths not exceeding H2 in their immediate vicinity.  
    •  Unit: [m]  
    •  Default: inherited from H1/global

6.  H3  
    •  Description: Minimum element thickness enforced only within a structured boundary‐layer mesh defined via the DFIX option on SARB curves.  This parameter ensures that boundary layer prismatic elements do not collapse below a user‐specified thickness.  
    •  Unit: [m]  
    •  Default: same as H1/H2 or global mesh defaults

7.  XFLG  
    •  Description: Literal flags disabling automatic geometric intersection between this region and other model entities.  Flags may be combined:  
      – ‘P’: do not snap/intersect points inside the region  
      – ‘L’: do not intersect other lines (SNL)  
      – ‘A’: do not intersect or generate intersection lines with other areas (SAR)  
    •  Unit: LIT (literal string)  
    •  Default: none (automatic intersection on)

8.  TITL  
    •  Description: Free text title or name of the structural region (up to 32 characters).  Useful for annotation, grouping, or reference in postprocessing.  
    •  Unit: Lit32 (32‐character literal)  
    •  Default: blank

By cataloging each parameter’s purpose, data type and default behavior, this description helps a retrieval‐augmented system to answer questions such as “Which SAR record field controls mesh density?” or “How do I turn off intersection with other areas?” and to point users back to the appropriate section of the SOFiMSHC documentation.
