 The given record defines a structural area, a two-dimensional arbitrarily shaped region which can be meshed with triangular or quadrilateral elements. If no identifier NO is given, SOFiMSHC assigns one automatically. A negative identifier changes the existing definition of a previously defined record.
 Two special literals (PROP, VOID) indicate that the record defines an attribute region or an opening instead of a regular area. These special type of regions can be placed arbitrarily within the model on top of other surfaces in order to change selected properties locally or to create openings. They will not be meshed for themself. SOFiMSHC intersects these regions geometrically with other structural regions and changes the given properties in the intersected part or cuts out an opening respectively.
 In addition to changing the properties the elements within an attribute region can also be assigned to a secondary group (see record GRP). For this the secondary group identifier, given as text string of at most four characters, has to be set at parameter GRP. In this case, all elements remain in the primary group defined for the original structural area and will be additionally assigned to the secondary group of the attribute region.
 The shape of a structural region is defined by its boundary and possibly a geometric surface description. A valid region requires at least one closed loop of outer boundary curves which are defined by following SARB records. Inner boundaries may be added to create openings. For more complex geometric shapes an additional surface definition is needed in order to describe the geometry inside the outer boundary. This geometry can be either defined by referencing a GAR record at REF or by adding succeding SARP records describing points on the surface.
 In most cases however, an explicit geometry is not necessary as SOFiMSHC determines it automatically on basis of the boundary description.
 The orientation of a structural region is basically defined by specifying a normal direction at NX,NY,NZ. This direction defines the local z-axis of all plane elements created on the struc- tural region, which are oriented to the opposite side of the normal. It can be entered only approximately by the user, only specifying the side as SOFiMSHC calculates its exact direction according to the given geometry afterwards.

This direction defines the local z-axis of all plane elements created on the struc- tural region, which are oriented to the opposite side of the normal. It can be entered only approximately by the user, only specifying the side as SOFiMSHC calculates its exact direction according to the given geometry afterwards..
 The orientation of the elements within the structural region can be specified by different meth- ods. By default, the local x-axis of the plane-elements will be aligned:
 A direction vector at DRX, DRY, DRZ defines a direction to which the local x-axis of all plane elements created on the structural region will be aligned. This direction must not be defined perpendicular to the surface, as no uniqe direction can be determined in this case then.
 By setting one of the literals RADI or TANG at KR it can be further specified which of the two local coordinate axes x or y is to be aligned.
 Instead of an explicit direction, the user may also enter one of the literals POSX, POSY, POSZ, NEGX, NEGY or NEGZ at KR in order to align the local x-axis with one of the given global directions.
 Moreover, the local x-axis may also be aligned within one of the global coordinate planes by entering:
 KR = XY, YX: align x within global XY-plane in X- resp. Y-direction
 KR = YZ, ZY: align x within global YZ-plane in Y- resp. Z-direction
 KR = ZX, XZ: align x within global ZX-plane in Z- resp. X-direction
 Using this option, the local x-axis of the area elements on the structural region can be aligned towards another structural element whose number must be given at DRX. Following possibilities exist:
 KR PT: align towards a structural point
 KR LN: align towards a structrual line
 KR AR: align towards a structural area
 The direction of each area element is determined individually by calculating the projection onto the referenced structural item. If no projection exist, i.e. the distance is zero, the coordinate system of the referenced item is taken directly.
 In order to align the local y-axis, the local coordinate system can be rotated by 90 degrees.
 •
 additional rotation about beam axis at DROT By setting an angle for DROT the local coordinate system of each plane element will be additionally rotated about its local z-axis.

the distance is zero, the coordinate system of the referenced item is taken directly.. In order to align the local y-axis, the local coordinate system can be rotated by 90 degrees.. •. additional rotation about beam axis at DROT By setting an angle for DROT the local coordinate system of each plane element will be additionally rotated about its local z-axis..
 The thickness of the elements in a structural region can be defined by setting the parameter T. If no thickness is given, it will be set to a constant value of 1.0 m. In addition to a constant distribution of the thickness, SOFiMSHC also allows to define varying thicknesses within a region. Therefor two possibilities exist:
 • Thickness at boundary edges in record SARB: By setting the thickness value at the outer boundary edges of a region, a varying thickness can be defined.
 • Thickness at structural points within the region: For this, structural points with thickness properties (SPT ... T) can be defined within or on the boundary of the region in order to describe a variable thickness distribution. Since one of these points may be shared by multiple structural regions, the region thickness value at SAR must be set explicitly to T=0.0 in order to activate this setting. Only structural points with no additional geometric information like column sizes etc. will be considered in calculating the thickness distribution.
 In both cases a least square method is applied, which interpolates the thickness values at the support points or lines. In most cases this interpolation reduces to a planar distribution of the thickness values across the region, but may also be higher polynomial in the case that a higher number of support points is given.
 Different stiffnesses in different local directions can be defined by setting orthotroptic thick- ness values (TX, TY, TXY, TD). An average thickness T should be given which will is used for calculating masses etc.
 Meshing of the region can be controlled using a general parameter and different density values. By setting MCTL=REGM SOFiMSHC tries to create a regular (structured) mesh on structural regions with 4 boundary edges. The structured mesh is created as long as the ratio of edges and angles corresponds approximately to a rectangular shape. By default, a unstructured mesh consisting of quadrilateral or triangular elements is created. The parameter H1 sets the element size within the region overwriting the global setting in CTRL HMIN. The value given at H1 defines the maximum length of an element edge. Additionally, H2 can be set to create refinements around structural points inside the region.

By default, a unstructured mesh consisting of quadrilateral or triangular elements is created. The parameter H1 sets the element size within the region overwriting the global setting in CTRL HMIN. The value given at H1 defines the maximum length of an element edge. Additionally, H2 can be set to create refinements around structural points inside the region..
 By setting MCTL=SNGQ the structural region will be converted into a single quad element. The region should have a triangular or quadrilateral structure. This option is useful for defining load distribution areas whose stiffness is deactivated using NRA=0. Since no nodes are created in the interior of the region, problems with large deflections might not occur.
 Option XFLG allows to prevent the automatic intersection of the given structural region with other structural elements. The following options are provided, which can also be combined:
 • ’P’ Structural points will no longer be automatically added as constraining points to the region.
 • ’L’ Other structural lines will no longer be automatically added as constraining lines to the region.
 • ’A’ The structural region will not be intersected with other structural regions. I.e. no inter- section lines will be created automatically. Two structural regions can be placed parallel on top of each other without warning.
 Please note that the above mentioned options only apply to the internal of the structural region. They will not apply to edges and points on the boundary. In the case that the user also wants to prevent intersection on the boundary, he has to create the lines and points with the respective settings explicitly.
 Independently from the settings in XFLG it will always be possible to add single structural points and lines as constraining points and lines explicitly to the region using the command SARB
 CONS. Contrary to the default behaviour of SOFiMSHC, this allows to add only a selection of structural elements as constraints to a region.

The table below specifies the fields of the “boundary‐edge” record used when defining one edge of a structural region (SAR) in SOFiMSHC.  Each entry may refer either to an existing geometric line (SLN) or be defined explicitly by its start/end points (SLNP).  At least one closed loop of outer edges (TYPE=OUT) is required; inner loops (TYPE=IN) define holes or openings, and TYPE=CONS marks interior constraint edges.  Unless noted otherwise, omitted numeric fields default to zero and literal fields to “–” or asterisk as indicated.

1.  TYPE (literal, default = OUT)  
   •  OUT – outer boundary edge  
   •  IN – inner boundary edge (hole)  
   •  CONS – interior constraint  
  
2.  NL (integer, default 0)  
   Reference index of a geometric line (SLN). Mutually exclusive with NP.  
  
3.  NP (integer, default 0)  
   Reference index of a geometric point. Used when building an edge from points (SLNP). Cannot be used with NL.  
  
4.  NA (integer, no default)  
   Number of the start point when constructing an edge via SLNP records. Required if NL=0 and NP>0.  
  
5.  NE (integer, no default)  
   Number of the end point for an explicitly defined edge. Paired with NA.  
  
6.  T (thickness, [Lit16/mm] or literal, default = *)  
   •  Constant thickness at this boundary edge.  The overall region thickness (SAR-T) must be zero if any T is specified here.  
   •  When used with VAXI, T becomes the name of a variable (literal) whose value varies along the specified axis—ideal for decks or tapered members.  
  
7.  MNO (integer, default 0)  
   Material number for an elastic (possibly non-linear) bedding layer attached to this edge.  
  
8.  FIX (literal, default = –)  
   Hinge‐release specification: any combination of PX, PY, PZ, MX, MY, MZ to release the corresponding local degree of freedom.  
  
9.  DFIX (distance, m, default 0)  
   Offset gap for interior spring‐edge generation when FIX or bedding is applied. A small gap “pulls” the spring elements into the domain.  
  
10. CA (axial bedding stiffness, [kN/m²], default 0)  
11. CL (lateral bedding stiffness, [kN/m²], default 0)  
12. CD (torsional bedding stiffness, [kNm/m/rad], default 0)  
   – These define linear spring constants in the local-x (axial), local-y/z (lateral), and rotational directions.  If MNO is used instead, non‐linear behavior may be defined via that material.  
  
13. VAXI (literal, default –)  
   Identifier of the axis along which T varies. Only valid when T is given as a variable name rather than a numeric thickness.  

Notes and usage tips:  
- Edges may be entered in any order; SOFiMSHC will sort and join them into closed loops when common end points exist.  
- If no outer boundary is explicitly provided, edges are auto‐created from the underlying surface (especially for rotational/free‐form SARR/SARP regions).  
- Interior constraints (TYPE=CONS) are typically detected automatically; explicit use of NP/NA/NE for constraints is only needed if automatic detection fails.  
- Thickness interpolation along boundaries uses least‐squares fitting; higher polynomial distributions require more definition points.

 This record describes one single edge of an outer or inner boundary of a preceding structural region defined at SAR. A valid structural region requires at least one closed loop of outer boundary edges but may also have a number of inner boundaries to describe openings or constraining edges. The edge can be given as reference to a structural line SLN or can be established directly by adding subsequent SLNB or SLNP records.
 In the case, that no outer boundary is explicitly given for a structural area, SOFiMSHC creates the edges on the boundary automatically on basis of the underlying geometric surface defini- tion, if one exists. This option is especially helpful when defining rotational (SARR) and free form surfaces (SARP).
 The edges of the boundaries can be entered in any sequence and orientation. SOFiMSHC sorts and connects the edges, provided that common end points exist and a closed sequence of edges can be found.
 Additional point or line constraints in the interior of the domain may be defined for supports, columns or other selected points using TYPE CONS. As SOFiMSHC however, automatically incorporates points and lines lying inside a region as constraint, there is usually no need for this option. Only in cases, where the automatic detection fails, it can be useful to add points or
 lines as constraints explicitly.
 For boundary edges and constraining points a thickness may be set at T in order to define a varying thickness distribution over the structural region. The thickness is approximated be- tween the given points and lines using a least squares method. Depending on the number of definition points linear and higher polynomial distributions of the thickness are possible. If the thickness is given at boundary edges, the general thickness of the region at SAR must be set explicitly to 0.
 Alternatively, it is possible to define the thickness along a boundary line as a variable along an axis, specified at parameter VAXI. In this case, the name of the variable is specified in parameter T, as a literal. This feature may be used to define a bridge deck, with a variable thickness distribution along its axis.

Alternatively, it is possible to define the thickness along a boundary line as a variable along an axis, specified at parameter VAXI. In this case, the name of the variable is specified in parameter T, as a literal. This feature may be used to define a bridge deck, with a variable thickness distribution along its axis..
 Hinge- and bedding conditions can be defined for outer and inner edges. Hinge conditions are defined at FIX, where the literals PX, PY, PZ, MX, MY, MZ which can also be combined are possible and which defines the respective local degree of freedom to be released.
 In order to define elastic bedding conditions on the boundary, linear bedding constants can be given at CA, CL and CD for axial, transversal and rotational bedding or a material at MNO which allows to define also non-linear conditions. This will generate one set of spring elements, with their axial direction aligned along the local-x direction of the edge and constant CL applying to both local-y and local-z directions.
 When boundary conditions are defined, additional edges will be created in the interior of the region and connected with the respective boundary. If a distance is given at DFIX, these internal edges will be additionally set off with a small gap to the interior of the region.

The table shown is the parameter definition for the SARR record, which in the SOFiMSHC schema attaches a rotational or sweep‐surface geometry to a previously defined structural area (SAR). Only one SARR record is allowed per SAR, and it may describe either a surface of revolution (ROTA) or a sweep‐surface (SWEE). Below is a breakdown of each column and row in the table:

1. Columns  
   • Item: the identifier or field name in the SARR record.  
   • Description: a short natural‐language description of what the field represents.  
   • Unit: the physical unit or data type of the field (where applicable).  
   • Default: the default value or symbol if the field is omitted in the input.

2. Rows (Fields)  

  a. Type  
     – Description: Selects the kind of structural surface geometry.  
     – Allowed values (Lit4, a 4‐character literal):  
       • “ROTA” – Surface of revolution  
       • “SWEE” – Sweep‐surface  
     – Default: “ROTA” if not explicitly provided.

  b. GID1  
     – Description: The identifier (curve ID) of the first generating curve, GID1.  
       • For ROTA, this is the meridian or generating curve to be revolved.  
       • For SWEE, this is the profile to be swept.  
     – Type: – / Lit4 (an optional 4‐character literal referencing an existing curve definition)  
     – Default: “*” (mandatory – must be provided for either geometry type)

  c. GID2  
     – Description: The identifier of the second generating curve, used only for SWEE.  
       • For SWEE, GID2 is the trajectory curve along which GID1 is swept.  
       • For ROTA, GID2 is not used.  
     – Type: – / Lit4  
     – Default: “–” (dash indicates “not applicable” for ROTA)

  d. X, Y, Z  
     – Description: Coordinates of a reference point in 3D space.  
       • For ROTA, this point lies on the rotation axis.  
       • For SWEE with direction vector, this may serve as the start point of the vector.  
     – Unit: meters [m]_1001  
     – Default: 0.0 (origin) for each coordinate if omitted.

  e. NX, NY, NZ  
     – Description: Components of a direction‐vector.  
       • For ROTA, defines the direction of the axis of revolution.  
       • For SWEE, if no GID2 (trajectory curve) is given, the profile is swept along this vector.  
     – Unit: dimensionless  
     – Default: “*” (mandatory if needed by geometry type)

  f. UMIN, UMAX  
     – Description: Parametric extents along the U‐direction (first parameter) of the surface.  
       • For ROTA, U corresponds to the generating curve parameter on GID1 (meridian).  
       • For SWEE, U corresponds to the sweep direction along GID2 or along the direction vector.  
     – Unit: dimensionless  
     – Default: “*” (if omitted, the full domain of the curve or vector length is used)

  g. VMIN, VMAX  
     – Description: Parametric extents along the V‐direction (second parameter) of the surface.  
       • For ROTA, V corresponds to the rotation angle in degrees.  
         – VMIN defaults to 0.0° (start angle) if omitted.  
         – VMAX defaults to “*” (must be provided if not a full half‐shell).  
       • For SWEE, V corresponds to the parameter along GID1 (the profile).  
     – Unit: degrees (deg) for ROTA; dimensionless for SWEE  
     – Default:  
         • VMIN = 0.0°  
         • VMAX = “*” (mandatory unless using the implicit 180° default for a half revolution)

Notes on usage:  
- For ROTA surfaces, avoid specifying a full 0°–360° sweep in one record; instead split into two half‐shells (0°–180° and 0°––180°) to prevent numerical ambiguity.  
- Boundary edges (SARB records) normally need not be defined explicitly: the software will generate edges at the parameter limits automatically. Only define SARB if you require openings or non‐coincident structural boundaries.

This table provides a concise but complete reference for populating the SARR record, ensuring correct interpretation of geometry parameters for revolved and swept structural surfaces.

See also: SAR
 SARR
 The given record SARR defines the geometry of rotational or sweep-surfaces. The record is a property record and refers to the directly preceding definition of a structural area SAR. Only one record SARR is allowed or each structural area.
 The following types of geometry can be described with this record:
 • ROTA: Surface of revolution A given structural line or geometric curve GID1 is rotated about a straight axis in space. The rotation axis is defined by a point at X,Y,Z and a direc- tionvector at NX,NY,NZ.
 The parameters UMIN and UMAX define the extends of the surface in meridian direction along the generating curve GID1. If nothing is given, the whole curve GID1 is taken. The extend of the rotation angle in degree is defined using the paramters VMIN and VMAX. If nothing is given, the parameters default to an angle from 0 to 180 degree.
 Important: In order to avoid ambiguity in numerical operations, surfaces of revolution should never be defined as closed surface with a rotation angle from eg. 0 to 360 degree. In these cases it is recommended to create two halfshells with angles from 0 to 180 degree and 0 to -180 degree respectively.
 A structural line or geometric curve GID1 is swept along a so called trajectory curve GID2. Instead of the trajectory curve, a direction vector can be given at NX,NY,NZ along which
 the generating curve GID1 is moved.
 The parameters UMIN and UMAX define the extend of the surface along the trajectory curve GID2 or the direction vector, respectively. If nothing is given here, the whole curve or the length of the direction vector is used.
 The parameters VMIN and VMAX define the extend of the surface along the generating curve GID1.
 In general cases, there is no need to define the boundary edges of the structural area explic- itly, when rotational or sweep surfaces are defined with this record. SOFiMSHC creates the edges automatically at the boundary of the geometry surface. Only in cases if openings or constraining edges should be defined or the boundary of the structural area does not coincide with the extends of the geometric surface, the boundary edges have to be defined explicitly using records of type SARB.

The input table defines the format and semantics of a single SARP record, which in turn describes one point of a freeform surface patch used to build up arbitrary surface geometries on top of a structural region (SAR).  Each row of the table specifies one field (Item) of the record, together with its meaning (Description), its physical or logical unit (Unit) and any default value assumed when the field is omitted or set to a placeholder.  Below is a detailed breakdown:

1.  Overall Context (from additional text)  
    -  SARP records follow a SAR structural definition and supply the geometry of a freeform surface over that area.  
    -  A collection of SARP records, typically arranged in an m-by-n grid, define either a bicubic-spline surface (TYPE SPL ILIKE) or a NURBS surface (TYPE NURB).  
    -  For NURBS, each point can carry an optional weight W to describe rational surfaces; if W is omitted, it defaults to 1.0 (non-rational).  
    -  The tool (SOFiMSHC) will automatically create boundary edges along the outermost rows/columns of the grid unless explicit boundary edges (SARB) are required.

2.  Field-by-Field Description  
    • TYPE  
      – Description: Literal keyword that selects the interpretation of the point data. Typical values are “SPL” for bicubic‐spline interpolation or “NURB” for NURBS control points.  
      – Unit: Lit (literal).  
      – Default: none (this field is mandatory for each record).  

    • M  
      – Description: Integer index in the u-direction of the grid (ranges 1 . . . m).  
      – Unit: none (dimensionless index).  
      – Default: “!” (an explicit user value is required).  

    • N  
      – Description: Integer index in the v-direction of the grid (ranges 1 . . . n).  
      – Unit: none.  
      – Default: “!” (must be provided to place the point in the correct grid row).  

    • X  
      – Description: Global X‐coordinate of the surface point.  
      – Unit: meters ([m], unit code 1001).  
      – Default: 0.0  

    • Y  
      – Description: Global Y‐coordinate of the surface point.  
      – Unit: meters ([m], unit code 1001).  
      – Default: 0.0  

    • Z  
      – Description: Global Z‐coordinate (elevation) of the surface point.  
      – Unit: meters ([m], unit code 1001).  
      – Default: 0.0  

    • W  
      – Description: Weight of the point when TYPE = NURB. If omitted or set to 1.0, the surface is non-rational (uniform weight).  
      – Unit: none (relative weight).  
      – Default: 1.0  

    • T  
      – Description: Local plate thickness at this point (not currently supported by the solver). Reserved for future use.  
      – Unit: millimeters ([mm], unit code 1010).  
      – Default: none  

3.  Usage Notes  
    -  To define a complete freeform surface, supply SARP records for all combinations of M = 1…m and N = 1…n. The software will then either interpolate those points (bicubic) or treat them as NURBS control points.  
    -  If the structural boundary coincides exactly with the outer grid limits, you need not issue any SARB records; otherwise, use SARB to carve openings or impose non-rectangular boundaries.  
    -  For purely spline‐based surfaces, omit W; for rational surfaces, W allows bulges or “pinched” corners.  
    -  Always include X, Y, Z with correct metric units to guarantee the proper spatial placement of each control point.

See also: SAR, SARN
 SARP
 With records of type SARP an arbitrary freeform surface geometry can be defined for a pre- ceding structural region at SAR. A single record SARP describes one point on the surface. The points will be usually given in a m x n-grid like pattern.
 Depending on the parameter TYPE, following types of surface geometries can be defined:
 The given data points will be interpolated by a bicubic spline surface. The points must be given in a m x n-grid like pattern.
 The given data points correspond to the control points of a NURBS surface. The points must be given in a m x n-grid like pattern. In order to describe non-rational NURBS-surfaces (e.g. rotational or spherical surfaces), each point can also be assigned a weight W < >1.0. Additional information about the definition of NURBS curves and surfaces can be found in chapter 2 of this manual.
 In general cases, there is no need to define the boundary edges of the structural area explic- itly, when a freeform surface geometry is defined with this record. SOFiMSHC creates the edges automatically at the boundary of the geometry surface. Only in cases if openings or constraining edges should be defined or the boundary of the structural area does not coincide with the extends of the geometric surface, the boundary edges have to be defined explicitly using records of type SARB.

See also: SAR
 SARC
 Item Description Unit Default TYPE Type of surface interpolation Lt BLIN
 SOFiMSHC allows to create curved structural areas only by definition of an outer boundary. In these cases - if the user has not explicitly defined the geometry of the area (SARR, SARP) - the surface geometry is interpolated from the pairwise opposite boundary curves (Coons-Patch or Gordon-Surfaces). With this record the type of this interpolation can be set:
 • BLIN: bilinear interpolation The surface geometry is defined by linear interpolation of oppo- site boundary curves
 • BCUB: bicubic interpolation A bicubic interpolation also considers the inclinations of the boundary cuves. This allows to define surfaces with smooth transitions between adjacent structural areas.
 SOFiMSHC automatically performs a linear interpolation of the boundary edges, if the edges are not lying within a plane and no surface geometry has been set explicitly. Thus, this record must only be given if a cubic interpolation is desired.
 In order to perform a Coons-Patch interpolation, at least three closed boundary edges must be given. If more than four edges are given, they will be joined conveniently.

The table under discussion specifies all of the fields you need to set up boundary conditions—either fixed supports or elastic/kinematic couplings—for the most recently defined structural area (SAR).  It is intended for inclusion in a RAG-backed vector store so that each parameter is indexed and retrievable by name, unit and default.  Below is a field-by-field breakdown:

1.  REFT (Type of support / bedding)  
    •  Purpose: Selects the kind of constraint applied to the SAR surface.  
    •  Possible literals (Unit: LIT):  
       –  “>FIX”  →  Use a fixed support (no movement allowed).  
       –  “>SAR”  →  Elastic or kinematic coupling to another surface.  
    •  Default: “>FIX”.  

2.  REF (Number of the referred element)  
    •  Purpose: When REFT=“>SAR”, REF identifies the target element number (ID) of the surface to which the SAR area will be coupled.  
    •  Unit: –  
    •  Default: –  

3.  FIX (Support / kinematic coupling element)  
    •  Purpose: Index of the special coupling or support element (often a “Lit28” element in your element library) that implements the kinematic link or fixed support.  
    •  Unit: Lit28  
    •  Default: –  

4.  CA (Axial bedding stiffness)  
    •  Purpose: Defines the normal-direction (axial) elastic stiffness of the bedding or coupling springs in kN/m³.  
    •  Unit: [kN/m³]  
    •  Default: 0.0  (i.e. no axial stiffness unless explicitly set)  

5.  CL (Lateral (transverse) bedding stiffness)  
    •  Purpose: Defines the in-plane or transverse elastic stiffness of the bedding springs in kN/m³.  
    •  Unit: [kN/m³]  
    •  Default: 0.0  (i.e. no lateral stiffness unless explicitly set)  

6.  GRP (Group number of the support / coupling elements)  
    •  Purpose: Logical grouping identifier. You can assign multiple SAR support or coupling elements to the same group number for batch activation, deactivation or post-processing.  
    •  Unit: –  
    •  Default: –  

7.  MNO (Number of stress-strain curve / material)  
    •  Purpose: If you want your bedding springs to follow a nonlinear stiffness law, MNO picks which predefined stress-strain curve or material definition to use.  
    •  Unit: –  
    •  Default: –  

8.  RCTL (Control parameter for surface coupling)  
    •  Purpose: Dictates how the mesh is generated on the SAR coupling surface when REFT=“>SAR.”  
    •  Options:  
       –  0 → Always generate a new mesh for the coupling surface, regardless of the referred surface’s mesh.  
       –  +1 → Try to reproduce the exact same mesh topology as that on the referred surface (if feasible).  
    •  Unit: –  
    •  Default: 1  

See also the SAR record (where the area is first defined) and the SLNS coupling routines for details on how “>SAR” connections are implemented. This table allows you to fully parameterize boundary conditions—fixed or elastic—on any SAR surface in your structural model.

sections: 5.17 SARS – Support and coupling of structural areas

See also: SAR, SLNS
 SARS
 This record defines boundary conditions, kinematic or elastic couplings for the last defined structural area SAR.

metadata.sections: 5.17 SARS – Support and coupling of structural areas

content:
If option FIX is specified at REFT and no reference surface is defined at REF, the resulting boundary conditions are those of a fixed support. In this case, there is the possibility to define an axial bedding perpendicular to the surface and a lateral bedding within the surface plane, using the parameters CA and CL or a material number or a work-law at MNO. If a work-law and a non-linear material are given with the same number in a project, the work-law takes prece- dence. This setting can be overwritten by entering a negative number in order to reference a material in this case. Alternatively, a fixed support can be defined by specifying the correspond- ing degrees of freedom using FIX. Local degrees of freedom (e.g. ’LPXPY’) are considered in the local coordinate system of the structural area. Rotational degrees of freedom are ignored.
 In contrast to parameters CB, CT of the structural area record SAR, which are processed as bedding constants during quad element generation, with this record spring elements with the corresponding constants are created. The properties of the spring elements are scaled according to their area of influence, in order to achieve a uniform bedding effect across the structural area. The spring elements, as well as the fixed supports, can be assigned to a group, regardless of the group of the structural area.

With the input of option >SAR at REFT and a number at REF, it is possible to couple two structural areas with each other, as in the following example:
 +PROG SOFIMSHC
 HEAD
 ...
 SAR 1 T 200 ... SARB OUT ... SARS REFT >SAR 2 CA 10000.0 CL 1000.0 ... END
 END
 In this example, structural area 1 is coupled with structural area 2 and an elastic bedding is generated between the two, with an axial stiffness of 10000.0 kN/m3 and a lateral stiffness of 1000.0 kN/m3. The bedding is modeled by means of individual spring elements between corresponding nodes, which are then scaled according to their area of influence.
 By default, if the geometry of the structural areas allows it, the resulting meshes of the coupled areas will have the same pattern of subdivision, so that every node of the generated mesh can be coupled with a node of the reference mesh. This behavior can be disabled with the use of parameter RCTL. In case that, due to the areas’ geometry or use of RCTL, such a correspondence does not exist for the two meshes, the kinematic coupling will be generated directly on the reference area, if necessary.

The table shown is the definition template for an SVOB (Structural Volume) record, which is used in SOFiMSHA (or related CAE pre-/post-processors) to declare and parameterize a three-dimensional volume region that will later be meshed with volumetric elements (in this case tetrahedra). In a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) vector store context, this table serves as a schema or “knowledge chunk” describing how users specify each volume and control its meshing and material attributes. Below is a detailed, field-by-field breakdown:

1. Overall Layout  
   - Four columns:  
     • “Item” – the mnemonic code for the parameter.  
     • “Description” – a short English phrase explaining the parameter’s role.  
     • “Unit” – the physical unit or data‐type (when relevant).  
     • “Default” – the assumed value if the user omits this entry or uses a negative index (to modify an existing volume).

2. NO (Number of structural volume)  
   - Description: Unique identifier for the volume element set.  
   - Unit: none (just an integer index).  
   - Default: “*” (mandatory; user must supply a positive number for a new volume).  
   - Notes: Entering a negative NO value signals modification of an existing volume’s properties rather than creation of a new one.

3. FIX (Boundary condition within the volume)  
   - Description: Specifies internal constraints or linkage conditions (for instance, rigid-body or kinematic couplings) that apply inside this 3D block.  
   - Unit: LIT (literal toggles or keywords).  
   - Default: “*” (user mandated).

4. GRP (Group number of volume elements)  
   - Description: Assigns the resulting tetrahedral elements to a named or numbered group for post-processing organization (e.g., applying loads or results extraction).  
   - Unit: none.  
   - Default: 0 (no grouping).

5. MNO (Material number of volume elements)  
   - Description: Links the volume to a material definition (elastic, plastic, hyperelastic, etc.) by its numeric ID.  
   - Unit: none.  
   - Default: 0 (unassigned).

6. MRF (Material number of reinforcement)  
   - Description: If the volume contains embedded reinforcement (rebar, fibers), this index points to that reinforcement material definition.  
   - Unit: none.  
   - Default: 0 (no reinforcement).

7. TYPE (Type of element)  
   - Description: Defines what kind of finite element to generate in the volume. In this table the only listed option is TET (unstructured tetrahedral mesh).  
   - Unit: LIT.  
   - Default: TET.  
   - Context: Tetrahedral elements are simple to generate for arbitrary geometries but generally provide lower numerical accuracy compared to structured hexahedral meshes. For higher‐quality hexahedral meshes, SOFiMSHA provides specialized “extrude,” “loft,” and “brick” routines (see records EXTR, LOFT, BRIC). An alternative unstructured approach with more sophisticated surface control is available via the UMSH record in SOFiMSHA.

8. TITL (Title of volume)  
   - Description: A free‐form, 32-character text string (Lit32) used for identification in pre-/post-processing reports and GUIs.  
   - Unit: Lit32.  
   - Default: “–” (empty).

Usage Notes & Context  
• When creating a new volume, supply positive NO, FIX, and (optionally) GRP, MNO, MRF. The TYPE defaults to TET unless overridden.  
• To revise an existing volume’s settings, enter NO as a negative integer; the rest of the fields will overwrite the previous record.  
• Although this SVOB record automates an unstructured tetrahedral mesh, users needing superior element quality for high-gradient regions should explore SOFiMSHA’s structured meshing tools or the UMSH record, which offers additional surface and volume control.  
• In a RAG system, each of these table entries, units, defaults, and contextual pointers (EXTR, LOFT, BRIC, UMSH) would be stored as discrete, retrievable embeddings, enabling a conversational agent to reconstruct syntax, warn about defaults, or suggest alternatives based on query intent.

See also: SVOB
 SVO
 This record defines a structural volume, which can be meshed with volumetric elements (Tetra- hedrons). The geometry of the volume is defined by succeding records of type SVOB. By entering a negative number, the properties of an existing structural volume can be changed.
 This record allows to generate an unstructured mesh consisting of tetrahedral elements. The numerical quality of tetrahedrons however are inferior to hexahedral elements. A generation of a structured hexahedral mesh can be carried out within SOFiMSHA by extrusion, lofting and interpolation of 2D quad meshes. See records SOFIMSHA: EXTR, SOFIMSHA: LOFT, SOFIMSHA: BRIC for additional details.
 An unstructured tetrahedral mesh can also be defined using record SOFIMSHA: UMSH in SOFiMSHA. This records provides additional means to define the volume to be meshed and its enclosing surfaces.

The table in question specifies two parameters that define how boundary surfaces of a structural volume are recorded in the input deck. It is intended to be used immediately after a structural‐volume definition (SVO) and acts as a property record (SVOB) that assigns surface types and links them to structural‐area identifiers. In unstructured tetrahedral meshing, these surfaces must form a closed shell around the volume.

1. Table Structure  
   - Item: The mnemonic or keyword that identifies the parameter.  
   - Description: A concise explanation of what the parameter controls or references.  
   - Unit: The kind of data expected (“LIT” for literal, “–” for unit‐less integer).  
   - Default: The default value assumed if the parameter is omitted.

2. Parameter Details  
   A. TYPE  
     • Description: Specifies what kind of boundary surface this record refers to.  
       – OUT: Marks the surface as an outer boundary of the structural volume.  
     • Unit: LIT (a literal string token is expected).  
     • Default: OUT  
       – If the user does not supply a TYPE entry, the surface will be treated as the outer surface by default.  
     • Notes:  
       – In more complex models there could be additional surface types (for example, inner interfaces or partition surfaces), but in this table only “OUT” is defined and assumed.  
       – Because the structural‐volume record (SVO) may list multiple boundary surfaces, each SVOB entry with TYPE=OUT contributes one facet to the overall closed shell.

   B. NO  
     • Description: Identifies which structural‐area definition (SAR) this surface belongs to. In other words, it cross‐references an SAR record number that groups surfaces into logical patches or categories.  
     • Unit: – (an integer index; it does not carry a physical unit).  
     • Default: !  
       – The exclamation mark indicates that this parameter is required—no default number can be assumed.  
     • Notes:  
       – The NO field must match the number assigned in an earlier SAR record.  
       – This linkage is essential when meshing complex geometries that use multiple material regions or when assigning boundary conditions to particular surface sets.

3. Relationship to Other Records  
   – This SVOB record must follow directly after the last SVO record that defines a structural volume. It inherits the context of “the current volume.”  
   – It is common to see a sequence:  
     1) SVO (define volume geometry)  
     2) SVOB (list boundary surfaces for that volume)  
         • TYPE, NO entries for each shell face  
     3) SAR (if not already defined, assigns areas to surfaces)  
   – For a valid unstructured tetrahedral mesh, the collection of SVOB entries (with TYPE=OUT by default) must enclose the volume completely, creating a watertight shell. Any gap or mismatch will cause meshing or solver errors.

4. Cross References  
   – See also: SVO (Structural Volume definition)  
   – See also: SAR (Structural Area grouping)  

In summary, this table documents how to tag and organize each facet of a structural‐volume boundary: you give each surface a literal type (defaulting to “OUT”) and an integer label tying it to a structural‐area definition. When all SVOB entries are collected, they form the closed shell required for robust tetrahedral meshing.

See also: SPT, SLN, SAR, SVO, SLVL, TOWR
 GUID
 Item Description Unit Default ID 128 bit code given as hexadecimal string Lt !
 This record allows to assign a Globally Unique Identifier to a structural element. A Globally Unique Identifier (GUID) is a worldwide unique reference number usually stored as 128-bit integer, which is primarily used for the unique identification of objects, when data is exchanged between different computer systems. It must be given at parameter ID as hexadecimal string, like for example:
 +PROG SOFIMSHC HEAD ... GUID ID '3F5A9ECC-145B-4093-9D16-E6F48732F569' ... END
 +PROG SOFIMSHC
 HEAD
 The GUID is a property record and must be given directly after the definition of the structural element at SPT, SLN, SAR, SVO, SLVL or TOWR. GUIDs will be assigned to all structural elements exported from SOFiPLUS or Autodesk Revit Structural. When describing the model using the CADINP language in text mode, it is usually not necessary to set a GUID.

The table in question defines the six scalar parameters that make up a BBOX (“bounding box”) record. In this context, a BBOX is a simple, axis‐aligned rectangular prism used to select structural elements in a 3D model—either as part of an explicit subsystem (see XSUB) or as a secondary grouping mechanism (see GRP). Below is a detailed, field‐by‐field breakdown suitable for indexing in a RAG/vector‐store pipeline:

1. Purpose of the BBOX Record  
   - Establishes a filtering envelope in X–Y–Z space.  
   - Any structural entity whose coordinates lie inside or on the faces of this box will be included in the selection.  
   - Primary use cases:  
     • Defining a subsystem via XSUB, where the “subsystem” is literally the set of all elements inside the box.  
     • Defining a secondary group via GRP, for ad‐hoc grouping or downstream processing.

2. Column Layout  
   - Item: the symbolic name of the parameter.  
   - Description: a human‐readable label of what the parameter represents.  
   - Unit: the physical unit in which the value is expressed. In all six fields it is meters ([m]_1001).  
   - Default: the value assumed if the user does not explicitly supply one.

3. Parameters  
   A. Minimum Coordinates  
     • XMIN  
       – Description: “Minimum coordinates” on the X-axis.  
       – Unit: meters.  
       – Default: –1.0 × 10¹⁰.  
     • YMIN  
       – Description: “Minimum coordinates” on the Y-axis.  
       – Unit: meters.  
       – Default: –1.0 × 10¹⁰.  
     • ZMIN  
       – Description: “Minimum coordinates” on the Z-axis.  
       – Unit: meters.  
       – Default: –1.0 × 10¹⁰.  

   B. Maximum Coordinates  
     • XMAX  
       – Description: “Maximum coordinates” on the X-axis.  
       – Unit: meters.  
       – Default: 1.0 × 10¹⁰.  
     • YMAX  
       – Description: “Maximum coordinates” on the Y-axis.  
       – Unit: meters.  
       – Default: 1.0 × 10¹⁰.  
     • ZMAX  
       – Description: “Maximum coordinates” on the Z-axis.  
       – Unit: meters.  
       – Default: 1.0 × 10¹⁰.  

4. Interpretation of Default Values  
   - The extremely large default ranges (±1 × 10¹⁰ m) effectively mean “no clipping” unless overridden.  
   - If a user only sets XMIN and XMAX, but leaves YMIN/YMAX and ZMIN/ZMAX at their defaults, the bounding box will span the entire model in Y and Z, but will be restricted in X.

5. Downstream Usage  
   - When constructing a query to the model database or to a RAG system, these six parameters become part of the query vector.  
   - Typical vector representation: [XMIN, YMIN, ZMIN, XMAX, YMAX, ZMAX] normalized or scaled as needed.  
   - Combined with the “record type” (BBOX) and context pointers to XSUB or GRP, the RAG store can quickly retrieve all relevant geometry or metadata subsets.

See also:  
- XSUB – “explicit subsystem record,” used to package selections into named submodels.  
- GRP – “secondary grouping record,” used to define ad‐hoc collections of elements.

See also: XSUB, GRP
 BBOX
 This record defines as rectangular bounding box for the selection of structural elements. The record can be used for selecting the elements of a subsystem (see XSUB) or as secondary group (see GRP).

The table in question defines the structure of an SLVL record, which is used to specify the individual storey (floor) levels of a multi-storey building in a finite-element modeling environment. Below is a detailed breakdown of each column and entry, together with contextual hints and usage notes drawn from the accompanying documentation.

1. Record Purpose  
• SLVL: This record is dedicated to defining storey levels. It relies on a global Cartesian coordinate system where the Z-axis (ZLVL) always points upwards (opposed to gravity). All floor elevations are given relative to the global origin, and lateral extents lie in the X–Y plane.  
• Automatic numbering: If the user does not supply a storey number, the system will assign one sequentially. If the user writes “DEL” in the NO field, all previously defined SLVL entries are purged from the current session.

2. Column Layout  
– Item: Identifier of each field in the record.  
– Description: Explanation of the field’s purpose and permissible values.  
– Unit: Data type or measurement unit.  
– Default: Value assumed if the user omits this field.

3. Field-by-Field Analysis  
a. NO  
   • Description: This optional field serves two roles:  
       – As a user-specified index (storey number) of type Lit4 (4-character literal).  
       – As a delete command: entering “DEL” will erase all existing storey-level definitions.  
   • Unit: Lit4 (four-character text).  
   • Default: “–” (none). If omitted, the software auto-increments the level index.  
  
b. ZLVL  
   • Description: The vertical elevation of the storey level, always taken positive in the upward direction of the global Z-axis. This value positions the floor relative to the model origin.  
   • Unit: [m]\_1006 (meters, following internal unit code 1006).  
   • Default: “!” This symbol indicates that a value is required; there is no meaningful default elevation.  
  
c. TITL  
   • Description: A user-provided name or label for the storey level (e.g., “Ground Floor,” “Level 1,” “Penthouse”). This helps in identification and reporting.  
   • Unit: Lit32 (up to 32 characters of text).  
   • Default: “*” If omitted, the system may auto-generate a generic label or leave it blank depending on software settings.

4. Usage Hints and Cross-References  
• Gravity Alignment: Storey levels assume the global Z-axis aligns with gravity. If the user’s gravity vector is inverted, ZLVL positive still points “up.”  
• Relationship to Other Records: SLVL entries often pair with TOWR (tower definitions), GUID (unique IDs for structural entities), XSUB (substructures), and GRP (group assignments).  
• Deletion Behavior: As soon as “DEL” appears in any SLVL.NO field, the software removes the entire set of previously defined levels—use with caution.  
• Further Reading: For advanced functionality—such as automatic story grouping, inter-storey drift checks, and specialized output—refer to the “Storey Analysis” section in the FEABENCH manual and the corresponding online documentation.

This description captures all key aspects of the table—its structure, field definitions, units, and default behaviors—so that it can be indexed effectively in a RAG-style knowledge base.

The illustration (captioned “Figure 5.2: Definition of storeys in a multi‐storey building”) combines a simple three‐storey portal frame elevation with a right‐hand schematic of global storey‐level definitions.  It is intended to clarify how SLVL records (storey‐level definitions) relate to the structural model and the global Z‐axis.

Centerpiece (portal frame):  
‐ Three horizontal beams stacked at three elevations, supported by two vertical columns.  
‐ At each beam–column interface a short horizontal line and the legend “Shear force” indicate that lateral shear is applied or resisted at every storey diaphragm.  
‐ The bottom of the columns is shown “fixed” (hatched base symbol) at what is defined as LVL 0 (the base level, or ground/foundation).  
‐ The mid‐storey (between LVL 1 and LVL 2) is highlighted to illustrate in‐plane displacement (drift) and the total lateral displacement vector u:  
   • A dashed vertical line rising from LVL 1 marks the undeformed (original) column position.  
   • A solid, oblique line rising to the beam at LVL 2 marks the actual displaced location of that same column top, labeled “u.”  
   • A double‐headed arrow at the beam level, annotated “drift,” spans the gap between the dashed original and solid displaced column lines, denoting storey drift.  

Right‐hand storey‐level schematic:  
‐ A vertical reference axis, labeled “LVL 3” at top down through “LVL 2,” “LVL 1,” and “LVL 0 (base level).” Each level is shown as a short horizontal tick‐mark crossing the axis.  
‐ The inter‐level heights are annotated as h₃ (between LVL 2 and LVL 3), h₂ (between LVL 1 and LVL 2), and h₁ (between LVL 0 and LVL 1).  
‐ This illustrates that SLVL entries define storey elevations along the global Z‐axis, with level numbers either automatically assigned or user‐provided (and removable via the ‘DEL’ keyword).

Gravity and global‐axis orientation:  
‐ In the lower‐left corner, a composite arrow shows “Z/L” pointing upward and “G” (gravity) pointing downward.  
‐ This reinforces the requirement that the gravity vector must be aligned with the global Z‐axis (positive Z up or negative Z down) for proper storey‐level definition.

Contextual notes (from additional text):  
‐ SLVL records establish the vertical coordinates of storey levels in a multi‐storey building model.  
‐ The lateral extent of each storey (in X–Y global axes) is implicitly tied to these Z‐levels.  
‐ Unique level identifiers are generated unless overridden, and a ‘DEL’ command clears previously defined levels.  
‐ For more on towers, groups, and the SLVL functionality see the FEABENCH manual’s “Storey Analysis” section and the online documentation (keywords: TOWR, GUID, XSUB, GRP).

See also: TOWR, GUID, XSUB, GRP
 SLVL
 This record defines the storey levels for a multi-storey building. The ZLVL axis has its origin at the global coordinate system origin and always points upwards (opposed to gravity), see figure 5.2.
 Hint
 The definition of storey levels requires the gravity direction to be aligned with the global Z-coordinate axis (positive or negative); lateral storey extension is associated with global coordinates in X- and Y-direction.
 Storey levels will be automatically assigned a unique number, or it may be provided by the user. If the literal ’DEL’ is given at NO, all previously defined storey levels will be deleted from the system.
 For more information about storeys, towers and related functionality, please refer to Section
 Storey Analysis in the manual FEABENCH: storeys and to the online documentation.

The table shown defines the fields, units and defaults for the “TOWR” record in a seismic‐response model. A TOWR record groups storeys into an independent structural unit (a “tower”), allowing multiple towers or mechanically independent parts of the same building to be analysed separately. Below is a field‐by‐field breakdown:

1. ID  
   • Description: Unique tower identifier (4-character literal)  
   • Unit: Lit4  
   • Default: none (mandatory)  
   • Notes: Must be unique among all towers. Used to tag subsequent SLVL (storey level) entries that belong to this tower.

2. ZBAS  
   • Description: Elevation of the tower’s base relative to model datum  
   • Unit: metres ([m])  
   • Default: “!” (indicator that user input is required)  
   • Notes: Specifies the vertical offset from the global origin. Implicitly, the top of the tower is determined by the highest SLVL.ZLEV that follows.

3. X1, Y1 … X4, Y4  
   • Description: Coordinates of the tower’s lateral bounding polygon on the XY-plane  
   • Unit: metres ([m])  
   • Default: ±∞ (each coordinate can default to an unbounded value if omitted)  
   • Usage patterns:  
     – Rectangle via diagonal: define only (X1,Y1) and (X2,Y2). The engine assumes a rectangle whose corners are these two points.  
     – Arbitrary polygon: define up to four points (X1,Y1)…(X4,Y4) in sequence to trace out the polygon boundary.  
   • Notes: If fewer than four vertices are supplied but a non-rectangular shape is needed, the remaining points default to ±∞ which effectively disables a hard boundary in that direction.

4. WIDE  
   • Description: Width of a rectangular tower when only an edge (via X1,Y1–X2,Y2) is specified  
   • Unit: metres ([m])  
   • Default: none (interpreted as “–”)  
   • Notes: Defines the extent perpendicular to the edge given by (X1,Y1)–(X2,Y2). Mutually exclusive with supplying X3…Y4.

5. TITL  
   • Description: Textual designation or title for the tower  
   • Unit: Lit32 (up to 32 characters)  
   • Default: “*” (optional; may be omitted if not needed)  
   • Notes: Free text field for user convenience. Not used in analysis logic.

How TOWR Is Used in Practice  
• The record always begins with TOWR, followed by ID and ZBAS, then any combination of X/Y or WIDE to establish lateral limits, and finally TITL if required.  
• Immediately following a TOWR block, one or more SLVL (storey level) records are listed, each associating a new storey elevation (ZLEV) and optional title with the current tower ID.  
• Multiple towers may share the same floor elevations but remain distinct by virtue of different ID literals.  
• If no lateral bounding is needed—i.e. the user wishes to let storey slabs or other definitions implicitly carve the plan—X1…Y4 and WIDE can all be omitted.  

Default and Constraint Summary  
• Mandatory: ID, ZBAS  
• At least one lateral‐limit specification: either X1/Y1–X2/Y2 (plus X3/Y3–X4/Y4 for polygons or WIDE for rectangles)  
• Optional: TITL  
• Units consistency: all linear measures in metres; ID/TITL in fixed-length string fields.

See also: SLVL, GUID
 TOWR
 This record can be used to define a tower, i.e. a collection of storeys, which belong to the same structural unit of a multi-storey building, in the context of seismic response analysis. The use of towers allows the existence of multiple independent structures within the same model, or the seismic assessment of mechanically independent parts of the same structure.
 The definition of a tower consists of an ID, given as a 4-character literal, and the elevation of its base, defined by parameter ZBAS. The height of a tower is implicitly defined by the topmost storey level that is associated with the tower. The lateral limits of a tower may be defined by a bounding polygon, using parameters X1...Y4. If only X1...Y2 are provided, then these points define the diagonal of a rectangular bounding box. It is also possible to define a rectangle by specifying an edge, using X1...Y2, and a width through the parameter WIDE.
 The storey levels associated with the tower must be defined right after the tower definition. Different towers may have storey levels at the same elevation. These storey levels are unique and independent of each other.
 Example:
 TOWR ID 'TLFT' ZBAS 0.0 X1 0 Y1 0 X2 10 Y2 0 $$ X3 10 Y3 10 X4 0 Y4 10 TITL 'Left Tower' SLVL ZLEV 3.0 TITL 'Left bottom' SLVL ZLEV 6.0 TITL 'Left middle' SLVL ZLEV 9.0 TITL 'Left top'
 TOWR ID 'TRGH' ZBAS 0.0 X1 15 Y1
 0 X2 25 Y2 10 TITL 'Right Tower'
 SLVL ZLEV 3.0 TITL 'Right bottom' SLVL ZLEV 6.0 TITL 'Right middle' SLVL ZLEV 9.0 TITL 'Right top'

The table under discussion defines the header‐record fields that initiate a predefined Result Set (RSET) when using the SRES command within SOFiMSHA. Predefined RSETs differ from free‐format RSETs in that their content and structure are fixed in advance; they are generated automatically according to the RSET type and the structural model elements to which they apply. The moment an SRES header is encountered, the system begins assembling a new RSET of that type; subsequent records list its elements, and the RSET terminates either when a new command appears or when an empty SRES row is inserted. The table below summarizes the key header fields (Item column), explains their meaning (Description), indicates the storage or data‐type (Unit), and shows the default value that applies when the header line omits an explicit entry (Default).

1. Columns and Their Purpose  
- Item: the keyword or identifier used in the SRES header record. It tells the parser which attribute is being defined.  
- Description: human‐readable explanation of what the Item represents and, where relevant, lists any permitted values.  
- Unit: the data type or literal length in which the field must be expressed. “Lit4” denotes a 4‐byte literal (typically integer or small text), “Lit32” denotes a 32‐byte literal (longer text).  
- Default: the value assumed when the user omits this field in the SRES header.

2. Detailed Item Descriptions  
A. TYPE  
• Description: Specifies the kind of predefined Result Set to generate. This choice controls which structural entities and associated properties the RSET will automatically include.  
• Allowed Values:
  – NONE: indicates no predefined structure (effectively an empty or null RSET).  
  – BEAR: requests an Elastic Bearing result set at each node in the model.  
• Unit: Lit4  
• Default: NONE (if the user leaves TYPE blank, the system defaults to creating no RSET).

B. ID  
• Description: A user-supplied identifier (number or short code) that uniquely names this particular RSET instance. It allows subsequent commands or data lines to refer back to the same result set.  
• Unit: Lit4  
• Default: “–” (no default; the ID field must be filled in explicitly when a predefined RSET is requested).

C. TITL  
• Description: An alphanumeric designation or title for the RSET. This can be any descriptive text up to the length limit, helping users recognize the purpose of the set in printed reports or graphical listings.  
• Unit: Lit32  
• Default: “*” (an asterisk indicates that, if omitted, the system will automatically generate a generic title based on the RSET type and ID).

3. How the Header Table Fits into SRES Usage  
When a user issues an SRES command line, they begin by specifying TYPE, ID, and TITL according to the definitions above. For example:  
   SRES, TYPE=BEAR, ID=10, TITL='Node‐Bearing Forces'  
This line tells SOFiMSHA to start building a predefined elastic‐bearing result set at each node, tag it with ID 10, and assign the title “Node‐Bearing Forces.” After that header, the system automatically emits one record per structural element (bearing) until the RSET ends. If the header omits TITL, the default “*” causes the software to insert a generated title; omitting ID altogether is not permitted; leaving TYPE blank yields a no‐op RSET of type NONE. By enforcing this fixed header schema, SRES ensures consistency in the structure and naming of result sets used downstream in report generation, post-processing or archiving.

SRES
 With the use of SRES, it is possible to define Result Sets of predefined structure and proper- ties, which correspond to a specific modeling entity or concept. In contrast to the free structure of the RSETs, which can be defined in SOFiMSHA, the items of predefined RSETs are auto- matically generated, based on the type of the RSET, as well as the structural elements that are associated with it. The definition of a predefined RSET is initiated by a header record, which specifies the ID and type of the generated RSET, followed by the records of the asso- ciated structural elements. The termination of the RSET is done automatically, when a new command is issued, or by using an empty SRES record. Currently, the following types of predefined Result Sets are supported:

This predefined RSET can be used for sets of spring elements that act on a node, as in the common case of bridge bearings. A number of following SPTS records are expected after the SRES record, which correspond to the springs that act on different directions at the bear- ing. The individual springs are allowed to have either an axial or a rotational stiffness. The generated RSET contains one force and one displacement item per spring.
 Example:
 +PROG SOFIMSHC
 HEAD
 HEAD
 ...
 SPT NR 1 X 0 Y 0 Z 0 SRES TYPE 'BEAR' ID 'BR01' TITL 'Bearing at Node 1' SPTS TYPE 'CX' CP 1000 SPTS TYPE 'CY' CP 1000 SPTS TYPE 'CZ' CP 1000 SPTS TYPE 'CX' CM 1000 SPTS TYPE 'CY' CM 1000 SPTS TYPE 'CZ' CM 1000 ...
 END
 With the above input, an RSET of 12 items will be generated: 3 forces, 3 moments, 3 dis- placements and 3 rotations, referring to the support springs of Node 1, with respect to its local coordinate system.
